A book payment, also called an in-house payment or an on-us payment, is a transfer of money between two accounts that both sit with the same bank. The payer and the payee may be different customers, or the same customer moving money between their own accounts. Because both accounts live on the same core banking ledger, the bank does not need to send the payment anywhere else. It simply updates its own books, which is where the name comes from.

The process is straightforward. The payer instructs the bank, through online banking, a branch, a mobile app, or a standing instruction. The bank validates the instruction first. It checks that the payer account exists and is active, that the payee account exists, that the payer has enough available funds including any overdraft limit, and that no block, freeze, or fraud hold applies to either account. If any check fails, the payment is rejected before any money moves, and the payer is told why.

When the checks pass, the bank posts two accounting entries at the same moment in its general ledger. It debits the payer account, which reduces the payer balance and reduces the amount the bank owes that customer. It credits the payee account, which increases the payee balance and increases the amount the bank owes that customer. The bank total liability to customers does not change, because one liability falls by the same amount the other rises. No cash moves, no central bank account is touched, and no external settlement account is involved. The entries are normally final and available immediately, so the payee can usually see and use the funds straight away.

This is very different from a local payment through a clearing house. In a clearing payment, the payer bank and the payee bank are different institutions. The payer bank must send a payment instruction through a clearing system, such as a local ACH or a national clearing house, the two banks must settle the net or gross amount between them, usually across accounts at the central bank, and the payee bank must then credit its customer. That chain takes time, creates settlement risk between banks, and can fail at several points. A book payment skips all of it, because there is only one bank and one ledger.

Failures in a book payment are normally simple and contained. The most common failure is insufficient funds, in which case no entry is posted and the payment is returned or held as pending, depending on the product. A wrong account number usually fails validation, because the bank can check the payee account directly on its own system. If a payment is posted to the wrong account by mistake, the bank can reverse it with a correcting debit and credit, subject to its error correction and customer consent rules. A system outage can delay posting, but because no external party is waiting for settlement, the payment can normally be reprocessed once the system is back, without any interbank claim.

Book payments matter for three practical reasons. First, they are fast and cheap, which is why banks encourage customers to pay other customers of the same bank this way, and why salary payments, internal loan repayments, and transfers between a customer own accounts are usually book payments. Second, they carry almost no settlement risk, because the bank is not exposed to another bank failing to pay. Third, they still need strong controls. A book payment that is posted in error, duplicated, or made under fraud is just as real as any other payment, and the bank must be able to trace, reverse, and evidence every entry. For a payments professional, the test is simple. If both accounts are on the same ledger, it is a book payment. If a second bank is involved, it is not.

Cheque conversion is the process of turning a paper cheque into an electronic payment instruction at the point where the cheque is presented. Instead of sending the physical paper through the clearing system, the bank or merchant captures the key data from the cheque, creates an electronic debit against the payer account, and processes that debit through an electronic clearing or ACH system. The paper cheque becomes the source of the data, not the payment instrument that travels.

Conversion usually starts when a cheque is received by a merchant, a biller, or a bank branch. The person accepting the cheque reads the MICR line printed along the bottom of the cheque. MICR, which stands for Magnetic Ink Character Recognition, carries the cheque number, the payer bank sort code or routing number, and the payer account number, printed in magnetic ink that a reader can scan reliably. The amount is keyed in or read from the written amount, and the payer may be asked to sign an authorisation allowing the cheque to be converted to an electronic debit. In some models, the customer is told at the till or counter that the cheque will be processed electronically and the paper will not be returned through the normal clearing cycle.

Once the data is captured, the converting party creates an electronic debit instruction. That instruction carries the payer bank identifier, the payer account number, the amount, the cheque number as a reference, and the date. It is sent into the electronic clearing system in the same way as a direct debit or an electronic funds transfer. The payer bank receives the instruction, validates the account and the available funds, and either pays it or returns it. If it pays, the payer account is debited electronically and the payee is credited through the normal electronic settlement route.

What happens to the paper depends on the local rules. In many conversion models, the paper cheque is voided, stamped as converted, and retained by the converter for a defined period for audit and dispute handling, then securely destroyed. It is not sent onward to the paying bank. That is the key difference from traditional cheque clearing, where the physical cheque, or at least its image, travels to the paying bank. The customer should not expect the original cheque back with a statement, and the electronic debit will appear on the statement instead, usually with the cheque number shown as a reference.

Failure cases are important to understand. If the MICR line cannot be read, because the print is damaged, smudged, or the cheque is not MICR encoded, the cheque cannot be converted reliably and must be handled as a paper cheque or returned to the presenter. If the payer account has insufficient funds, the electronic debit is returned unpaid, in the same way as a bounced cheque, and the payee may charge a return fee. If the amount captured does not match the amount written on the cheque, the conversion is wrong, and the dispute must be resolved from the retained paper and the capture record. A duplicate conversion, where the same cheque is converted twice, creates a duplicate debit that the payer bank must reverse on evidence.

Cheque conversion matters because it is faster and cheaper than moving paper, and it gives the payee earlier certainty about whether the payment will clear. It also changes the risk picture. The payer loses the float that paper clearing used to give, because the debit can arrive much sooner. The converter takes on responsibility for accurate capture and for holding the paper safely. For a payments professional, the practical checks are whether the MICR data is complete and readable, whether the customer authorisation is properly recorded, whether the electronic instruction carries the cheque reference so it can be traced, and whether the paper retention and destruction process meets the scheme and legal requirements in that market.

Cheque truncation is the process of stopping the physical movement of a paper cheque early in the clearing cycle and continuing the clearing process using its electronic data and image instead. The word truncation means the paper journey is cut short. The cheque is captured at the bank of first deposit, or at a central capture point, and from that point onward the paying bank works from the image and the data, not from the original paper.

The process works step by step. A customer deposits a cheque at a branch, an ATM, or through a mobile deposit. The collecting bank scans the front and back of the cheque at high resolution, creating a digital image that shows the payer details, the payee, the amount in words and figures, the date, and the signature. At the same time, the bank captures the MICR data from the bottom of the cheque, which gives the cheque number, the payer bank identifier, and the payer account number. The bank validates the image quality and the data, checks the amount, and creates an electronic clearing file containing the image and the data fields. The physical cheque is then retained securely by the collecting bank for a defined period and is not sent to the paying bank.

The clearing file travels through the cheque clearing system to the paying bank. The paying bank does not receive paper. It receives the image and the data, and it verifies the payment from those. Its checks include confirming the account exists and is active, confirming the signature on the image matches the mandate held on file where signature verification is required, checking the amount and the date, checking for stop payment instructions, and confirming there are sufficient funds. If everything passes, the paying bank debits the payer account and the clearing system settles the amount between the two banks, usually on a net basis through central bank accounts. The collecting bank then credits the payee.

Timelines depend on the market, but truncation is materially faster than the old paper exchange. In many systems, the cheque image reaches the paying bank the same day or the next working day, and funds are available to the payee within one to two working days. Some markets now clear cheque images almost in real time during the business day, while others still run on a daily clearing cycle with a defined cut off. The collecting bank must tell the customer when funds will be available, and that availability date is based on the image clearing timetable, not on the physical movement of paper.

When a cheque is returned, the process runs in reverse using the same image. If the paying bank dishonours the cheque for insufficient funds, a closed account, a stop payment, or a signature mismatch, it sends a return instruction through the clearing system, referencing the original image and data. The collecting bank reverses the provisional credit to the payee account and notifies the payee, usually with a return reason. The payee can then pursue the payer directly. The original paper, if still held, can be produced as evidence, but the return itself does not require the paper to travel back.

Truncation and conversion are often confused, but they are different. In truncation, the cheque remains a cheque. It is cleared through the cheque clearing system, the paying bank verifies the cheque image, and cheque law, including the rules on dishonour and stop payment, still applies. In conversion, the cheque stops being a cheque at the point of capture. It is turned into an electronic debit and cleared through an electronic or ACH system, and the cheque clearing rules no longer govern the payment. Truncation keeps the cheque clearing route and changes only the transport. Conversion changes the payment route itself. For a payments professional, the practical points are image quality, because a poor image can cause a valid cheque to be rejected, the retention period for the paper, the return timetable, and the need to explain to customers that the original cheque will not be returned and that the image is the legal record of the cheque.

text:
A hybrid payment system is a payment system that combines the features of gross settlement and net settlement in a single system, so that it can settle some payments immediately and individually and others more efficiently through netting. It is designed to get the best of both models. Gross settlement gives certainty and finality, but it needs a lot of liquidity. Net settlement saves liquidity, but it delays finality. A hybrid system lets the operator and the participants choose, payment by payment, which treatment is right.

The core idea is that the system holds a central queue and a settlement engine that can work in two modes. Urgent, high value, or time critical payments are settled gross, one by one, in real time, with immediate finality, in the same way as in a pure RTGS system. Lower value, routine, or liquidity sensitive payments are held in the queue, offset against incoming payments from other participants, and settled on a net basis, either continuously in small batches or at defined settlement windows during the day.

Liquidity saving mechanisms are the heart of a hybrid system. The most common is bilateral or multilateral offsetting, where the system looks at payments waiting in the queue and finds pairs or groups that cancel each other out, so only the net difference needs central bank money. Another is queue optimisation, where the system reorders queued payments to find the largest set that can settle with the liquidity available. Some systems use a central queue with a gridlock resolution process, which runs at intervals to break a logjam where several banks are each waiting for funds from another bank. These mechanisms let banks settle more payments with less liquidity held at the central bank, while still giving finality to the payments that settle.

Examples help to make this concrete. Several modern large value systems operate as hybrids, even if they are often described simply as RTGS systems. They offer gross settlement for urgent payments and a liquidity saving queue for the rest, with frequent settlement cycles during the day. Some systems also offer a choice at the payment level, so a participant can flag a payment as urgent for immediate gross settlement, or as normal for queueing and netting. The exact design varies by country, but the pattern is the same. One system, two settlement modes, and a queue that manages the trade off between speed and liquidity.

Whether a payment settles gross or net depends on rules set by the system operator and choices made by the sending bank. The operator may set a value threshold, so payments above the threshold must settle gross and payments below it may be queued. The sending bank may flag a payment as urgent, for example a payment linked to a securities settlement, a central bank operation, or a customer payment with a strict deadline. The state of the queue also matters. A queued payment may settle gross if the bank has enough liquidity at that moment, or it may settle net when an offsetting payment arrives. The participant can usually see its queued payments and can change their priority, cancel them before settlement, or inject more liquidity to release them.

Failure handling in a hybrid system has to cover both modes. A gross payment that fails for lack of funds stays in the queue until liquidity arrives, or it can be cancelled by the sender. A net settlement that fails, because a participant cannot fund its net debit at the settlement window, can block the whole batch, so the system needs a clear rule for unwinding the batch, removing the failing participant payments, and resettling the rest. The system also needs controls for a participant failure during the day, including limits on queued exposures and a procedure for handling payments that are already final. A payment that has settled gross is final and cannot be unwound. A payment that is still queued is not final and can be stopped. For a payments professional, the key questions are which payments are eligible for netting, how often the netting cycle runs, and what happens to queued payments if a participant fails before the settlement window.

RTFS and RTNS are two settlement models that both operate in real time, but they give finality in different ways. RTFS stands for real time final settlement. RTNS stands for real time net settlement. The difference is not about speed. Both work continuously during the operating day. The difference is about when a payment becomes final and irrevocable, and whether settlement happens payment by payment or on a net basis.

RTFS means each payment is settled individually, in real time, with immediate finality. When a payment is accepted into the system, the sending bank central bank account is debited and the receiving bank central bank account is credited straight away, for the full amount of that payment. Once that entry is made, the payment is final. It cannot be revoked, unwound, or reversed by the system, and the receiving bank can safely credit its customer knowing the funds are good. RTFS is in practice the same model as RTGS, which stands for real time gross settlement. The two terms describe the same thing from slightly different angles. Gross describes that each payment settles for its full amount. Final describes that settlement is immediate and irrevocable. Many central banks use the terms interchangeably.

RTNS means payments are settled continuously, but on a net basis. As instructions arrive, the system records them and updates each participant net position in real time, but it does not move central bank money for every payment. Instead, it settles the net amounts at very frequent intervals, so the gap between instruction and final settlement is very short. A payment in an RTNS system is not finally settled until the net settlement for that cycle is completed. Until then, it can be held or caught in an unwind if a participant fails to fund its net position.

The practical difference is about risk and liquidity. RTFS needs more liquidity, because every payment requires the full amount in central bank money when it settles. A bank must hold or borrow that amount, even if it expects an incoming payment of the same size minutes later. RTNS needs less liquidity, because incoming and outgoing payments offset each other and only the net difference moves. The trade off is that RTNS carries a short window of settlement risk. If a participant fails between the time its payments are recorded and the time the net settlement is completed, the system must decide how to handle those payments, and other participants may face a delay or a shortfall. RTFS removes that window entirely, because finality is immediate.

Where each model is used depends on the market and the payment type. RTFS, or RTGS, is the standard for high value, time critical, and systemically important payments, such as interbank transfers, securities settlement funding, and central bank operations, where immediate finality matters more than liquidity cost. RTNS is more common for lower value or higher volume flows where liquidity saving matters and a very short settlement delay is acceptable, and in systems that run frequent net settlement cycles during the day, sometimes every few minutes. Some modern systems blend the two, offering RTFS for urgent payments and RTNS style frequent net settlement for the rest, which is the hybrid model covered in a separate lesson.

DNS, which stands for deferred net settlement, is the older model that both RTFS and RTNS improve on. In DNS, payments are exchanged during the day and settled on a net basis only at the end of the day or at a few fixed times, so finality is delayed by hours. RTNS shortens that window to minutes or less by settling nets continuously. RTFS removes it entirely by settling each payment gross and final in real time. For a payments professional, the question to ask about any system is when finality happens. A payment that is processed in real time but settles net later is not the same as a payment that is final in real time, and the difference matters for credit decisions, for customer funds availability, and for what happens if a participant fails.

text:
Payment systems move large amounts of money quickly, so they carry real risks. A single failure can leave a bank out of pocket, delay thousands of customer payments, or threaten the stability of the financial system. Risk mitigation means the controls, rules, and tools that the operator and the participants use to reduce those risks to a level they can accept and manage. A payments professional needs to know each risk by name, and the control that matches it.

Credit risk is the risk that a participant cannot pay what it owes. In a net settlement system, this is the risk that a bank builds up a large net debit during the day and then fails before settlement. The mitigations are prefunding, where participants hold funds or collateral in advance to cover expected net debits, exposure limits, which cap how much one participant can owe another, and loss sharing arrangements, where surviving participants agree in advance how a default loss will be shared. In a gross settlement system, credit risk is much lower, because each payment settles in central bank money with immediate finality.

Liquidity risk is the risk that a participant has enough assets overall but does not have enough usable funds at the exact moment a payment must settle. This is the most common day to day risk in RTGS systems. The mitigations include intraday liquidity from the central bank, usually against eligible collateral, queueing and liquidity saving mechanisms that let payments wait for incoming funds, and throughput rules that require participants to send a proportion of their payments early in the day. Banks also manage this risk with intraday liquidity monitoring, payment flow forecasting, and a buffer of central bank reserves.

Settlement risk, including Herstatt risk, is the risk that one leg of a payment settles but the other does not. Herstatt risk is named after the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in 1974, where payments in one currency were made but the corresponding payments in another currency were never made. The mitigation for cross currency settlement is payment versus payment, often shortened to PvP, where both currency legs settle at the same time or not at all, so neither party pays without receiving. For securities, the equivalent is delivery versus payment, or DvP, where cash and securities move together. For domestic payments, immediate finality in an RTGS system removes most settlement risk.

Operational risk is the risk of failure in systems, processes, or people. Examples are a core banking outage, a cyber attack, a failed software release, or a manual error in a payment instruction. The mitigations are resilient design with backup sites and failover, regular testing of contingency procedures, straight through processing to reduce manual handling, validation and duplicate checks on payment files, and clear incident procedures. Reconciliation is a key operational control. Banks must reconcile payment accounts daily and investigate breaks quickly.

Fraud risk and legal risk sit alongside these. Fraud risk includes authorised push payment fraud, business email compromise, and internal fraud by staff. The mitigations are confirmation of payee checks, payment limits and dual authorisation for high value payments, real time transaction monitoring and sanctions screening, and segregation of duties so that one person cannot create, approve, and release a payment alone. Legal risk is the risk that a payment is not legally final, or that the system rules do not hold up in insolvency. The mitigation is a clear legal framework, settlement finality legislation where it exists, and system rules defining when a payment is final and what happens on a participant default.

In practice, no single control covers every risk. A well run payment system layers them. Prefunding and limits control credit risk, intraday liquidity and queueing control liquidity risk, PvP and finality control settlement risk, resilience and reconciliation control operational risk, and screening controls fraud risk. The operator sets the rules and monitors compliance, and each participant must manage its own exposures within them. For any payment flow, ask what can go wrong, who bears the loss, and which control stops it or limits it. If you cannot answer those three questions, the risk is not yet properly mitigated.

A mandate is the authorisation a customer gives to allow a creditor to collect payments directly from their bank account on a recurring or one off basis. Without a valid mandate, a direct debit collection has no authority and must be returned. Mandate management is the end to end process of creating, validating, storing, amending, and cancelling mandates. It matters because a weak mandate process creates failed collections, customer disputes, and indemnity claims.

The lifecycle starts with creation. The debtor, who is the customer, agrees the mandate with the creditor, the organisation collecting the money, such as a utility, a lender, or a subscription provider. The mandate must capture the debtor name and bank account details, the creditor name and identifier, the purpose and frequency of collections, and the debtor signature or electronic consent. On paper, the customer signs a physical mandate form. Electronically, the customer authorises online or through a bank portal, and the authorisation is recorded with a timestamp and an audit trail.

After creation comes validation and activation. The creditor, or its bank, checks that the account details are complete and correctly formatted, that the account can accept direct debits, and that the consent matches the account holder. In some schemes, the debtor bank validates the mandate before it becomes active. In others, the creditor holds it and the debtor bank only sees it when the first collection arrives. Either way, a mandate is not usable until validated and activated and, where required, registered with the scheme or the debtor bank.

Who holds the mandate depends on the scheme. In the SEPA Direct Debit scheme, the creditor holds the mandate, and the debtor bank does not normally hold a copy. The creditor must be able to produce it if the debtor disputes a collection, and must store it for a defined period after the last collection. In the Indian NACH system, the mandate is registered with the debtor bank and the National Payments Corporation of India, and the bank validates it before collections can start. NACH mandates can be paper based or electronic, and electronic mandates use authentication such as internet banking, debit card, or Aadhaar based approval. The point is the same in every scheme. Somebody must hold a provable record of the customer consent, and that record must be retrievable on demand.

Amendment and cancellation are part of normal mandate life. A customer may change bank account, amount, or collection date, or cancel the mandate entirely. An amendment must be recorded, validated, and applied before the next collection, or the collection will go to the wrong account or for the wrong amount. Cancellation can be instructed to the creditor or directly to the debtor bank, depending on the scheme rules. Once cancelled, no further collections may be made, and any collection presented after cancellation must be returned.

When a collection fails, the mandate is often part of the cause. If it was never activated, the collection is rejected as no mandate. If the mandate details do not match the account, it is rejected as invalid mandate. If the customer cancelled the mandate, the collection is returned as mandate cancelled. If funds are insufficient, the collection is returned unpaid, but the mandate remains valid and the creditor can retry on the next due date, subject to scheme rules. If the customer disputes a collection and the creditor cannot produce a valid mandate, the debtor bank will refund the customer under the scheme guarantee or indemnity, and the creditor bears the loss. A mandate that cannot be found is as bad as one that never existed.

Good mandate management is a practical discipline, not just a filing task. The creditor needs a single system of record for mandates, with status tracking from created to active to amended to cancelled, and an audit trail for every change. For a payments professional, the checks are simple. Can you prove the customer authorised this collection, can you find the mandate quickly, is it still active, and does the collection match its terms. If any answer is no, the collection should not go out.

MT102 is a SWIFT message that lets a bank send many individual customer credit transfers in one single message. Instead of sending a separate MT103 for every customer payment, the sending bank groups a batch of payments that share the same value date, the same currency, the same sending bank and the same receiving bank into one MT102. The receiving bank then splits the bulk message back into its individual payments and credits each beneficiary separately. It is a bulk instruction, not a single payment, and the total amount settled between the two banks is the sum of all the individual transactions inside it.

A bank uses MT102 when it has many small customer payments going to the same destination bank on the same day. Typical examples are payroll files, pension payments, dividend payments, bulk supplier payments, and remittance batches collected by a money transfer operator. The individual payments are too small to justify a separate SWIFT message and a separate settlement for each one, but they still need to reach different beneficiaries with different references. MT102 also suits a bank that has collected customer instructions through the day and wants to clear them in one evening batch.

The structure has three sequences. Sequence A (General Information) carries information that applies to the whole batch, including the file reference in field 20 and the bank operation code in field 23, with the value date and currency. Sequence B repeats once for every individual transaction. Each repeat carries its own related reference in field 21, its own instructed amount in field 32B, the ordering customer in field 50, the beneficiary customer in field 59, remittance information in field 70, and the details of charges in field 71A. Sequence C (Settlement Details) carries the total interbank settled amount in field 32A. The sum of all the amounts in field 32B must agree with the total in field 32A, plus the receiver's charges where the charge code is OUR, and that agreement is one of the first checks the receiving bank makes.

When the receiving bank gets an MT102, it first validates the whole message, checking that the total matches the sum of the individual transactions and that the value date and currency are correct. It then splits the bulk into its parts and processes each transaction as if it were a separate customer payment. Each beneficiary account is credited for its own amount, each beneficiary advice carries its own remittance information from field 70, and each transaction is posted and reconciled separately. The single interbank settlement in field 32A is settled once, through the Nostro or Vostro account, while the customer postings underneath it are many. Compared with many MT103s, one MT102 means one message, one settlement, and one reconciliation at interbank level, which is cheaper and faster. The trade off is flexibility, because every transaction in the batch must share the same value date, currency, and receiving bank, and a format error in the common part can hold up the whole batch.

If one transaction inside the bulk is rejected, the whole bulk is not normally rejected with it. The receiving bank processes the good transactions and isolates the bad one. A transaction can fail because the beneficiary account is closed or does not exist, the account number does not match the name, or the payment is stopped by a sanctions or compliance check. In that case the receiving bank holds the amount for that one transaction, notifies the sending bank, and returns the funds for that transaction only, normally by a separate payment back to the sender. The sending bank then corrects the details and sends the payment again as a new MT103 or in a new MT102. MT102 matters because bulk payments are a large part of everyday cross border banking. When it works, hundreds of beneficiaries are paid from one message. When it fails, the skill is in isolating the one bad transaction without stopping the rest, and in reconciling the bulk total against the individual credits.

text:
MT103 STP is the straight through processing version of the MT103 single customer credit transfer. It is the same basic payment instruction as a normal MT103, but it is built to be processed from end to end by computer, with no manual reading, no rekeying, and no human intervention at any bank in the chain. STP stands for straight through processing, and the message is only accepted as STP if it meets a strict set of format rules. If it meets the rules, each bank in the chain can validate it, route it, and post it automatically. If it does not, it is not rejected outright, but it falls out of the STP flow and has to be handled manually.

The STP rules are about cleanliness and completeness. Field 50 must be complete: option A (account + BIC/BEI), F, or K (account + full name and address) are all STP-valid; what breaks STP is a missing account identifier, a missing name/address where the option used requires it, or a free-text party. The beneficiary customer in field 59 must also be given with an account number and a full name and address. The value date, currency, and interbank settled amount in field 32A must be present and valid, the bank operation code in field 23B must be present, and the details of charges in field 71A must be present with a clear code for who pays the charges. Every institution in the payment chain, including the intermediary institution and the account with institution, must be identified by a valid BIC, not by a free text name and address that a computer cannot match.

MT103 STP differs from MT103 CORE in purpose, not in the payment itself. MT103 CORE is the general purpose version. It allows free text, incomplete addresses, identification of banks by name instead of BIC, and extra narrative that a person can read and act on. That flexibility is useful for unusual payments, but it forces manual work. MT103 STP removes that flexibility on purpose. It trades freedom for speed. The underlying payment, one customer paying another customer through the correspondent banking chain, is identical. What changes is how much a computer can do without help, and how much the message costs to process.

Banks prefer MT103 STP because it is faster, cheaper, and less prone to error. An STP payment can move through several banks in minutes, with each system validating the format, checking sanctions lists, checking the account, and posting the credit without a clerk opening the message. A manual MT103 has to sit in a queue, be read by an operator, have missing details chased, and be rekeyed into the next system, which adds hours, adds cost, and adds the risk of a typing error in an account number or an amount.

A payment fails STP for simple, practical reasons. The most common is an incomplete or badly formatted ordering customer or beneficiary, for example a missing address line, a truncated name, or an account number that does not match the format the receiving system expects. Another common cause is a bank identified by name instead of by BIC, or a BIC that is invalid or retired. Free text in field 72 that asks for something unusual, a missing charges code in field 71A, or remittance information that is too long or unstructured can also break STP. In all of these cases the message is still a valid MT103, so it is routed to a repair queue. An operator then fixes it, for example by adding a missing address line from the customer record or correcting a BIC, or contacts the sending bank with an MT195 query, which can delay the payment by a day or more. The lesson is that STP is not a different payment, it is a discipline. Clean data in, fast payment out. Dirty data in, manual work, delay, and cost.

text:
MT103 REMIT is the remittance version of the MT103 single customer credit transfer. It is identified by the bank operation code REMIT in field 23B, and it is used when the payment is a remittance, typically a personal or family payment sent by an individual, often through a money transfer operator or a bank acting for a remitter, rather than a normal commercial payment between businesses. The underlying instruction is still an MT103, one ordering customer paying one beneficiary customer, but the REMIT code tells every bank in the chain that this is a remittance flow, with different expectations about the information available and the way the beneficiary will receive the funds.

MT103 REMIT is used in several common situations. A migrant worker sending money home to family is the classic case. A money transfer operator collects cash or a debit from the sender in one country, aggregates many such remittances, and instructs its bank to send them onward. The bank then sends an MT103 REMIT for each beneficiary, or groups them in an MT102. In those cases the payment still travels through the correspondent banking chain, but the last step may be a cash payout by an agent rather than a credit to a bank account.

The fields that matter in MT103 REMIT are the same fields that matter in any MT103, but they are used differently. Field 23B carries REMIT, which is the signal that sets this variant apart. Field 50 carries the ordering customer, who is the remitter, and in a remittance flow that may be an individual whose full address is not held in the same way as a corporate customer. Field 59 carries the beneficiary customer, who may be identified by name and a collection reference rather than a full bank account number, if the payout is in cash. Field 70, remittance information, is especially important, because it often carries the reference number the beneficiary must quote to collect the funds, or the purpose of the remittance.

MT103 REMIT differs from MT103 CORE and MT103 STP in intent and in strictness. MT103 CORE is the general purpose version, used for ordinary commercial and personal customer payments, with full flexibility in how the fields are completed. MT103 STP is the strict, machine readable version, designed for automatic processing with complete BICs, full names and addresses, and no free text. MT103 REMIT sits apart from both. It does not have to meet the STP cleanliness rules, because remittance data is often incomplete, a beneficiary may have no account number, and an address may be partial. The REMIT code tells the receiving bank to apply remittance handling, which may mean a cash payout process, a different compliance check, and a different way of advising the beneficiary.

A worked flow makes this clear. A sender in London pays 500 pounds in cash to a money transfer operator, to be sent to her mother in Manila. The operator takes the sender details, the beneficiary name, and a payout location, and instructs its bank in London. The London bank sends an MT103 REMIT to its correspondent in the Philippines. Field 23B says REMIT, field 50 names the sender, field 59 names the mother with a collection reference, field 70 carries that reference and the purpose, and field 32A carries the value date, currency, and settled amount. The correspondent bank receives the message, checks it against sanctions lists, and passes it to the local payout agent. The mother goes to the agent, shows identification, quotes the reference from field 70, and collects the funds in local currency, less any charges shown in field 71A. MT103 REMIT matters because remittances are one of the largest cross border flows in the world, and they do not behave like corporate payments. The amounts are small, the volumes are high, the senders and beneficiaries are individuals, and the last mile is often cash.

When a REMIT payment fails, the handling depends on where it stopped. If the payout agent cannot pay because the beneficiary does not come forward, the funds are held for the collection period and then returned to the sender, normally by an MT202 or a new MT103 back to the ordering bank. If the beneficiary's identification does not match, the agent refuses the payout and the case goes to the remitter for correction. If the payment is rejected by a bank in the chain, for example because the beneficiary name is on a sanctions list, the sending bank is told by MT199 or by a return, and the funds come back to the remitter. If the reference in field 70 is wrong or missing, the beneficiary cannot collect, and the agent must check with the sender's bank before releasing the cash. A remittance that is never collected is not kept by the agent: it is returned to the sender after the holding period, and the sender is told why.

text:
MT191 is a SWIFT message used by one bank to request payment of charges, interest, or other expenses from another bank. It is not a customer payment and it is not a cover payment. It is a bank to bank claim. When a bank has incurred a cost while handling a payment for another bank, or when interest is owed because funds were held or delayed, it sends an MT191 to ask the other bank to pay that amount. The receiving bank then decides whether the claim is valid, and pays it or queries it. The message is short, but it carries a clear audit trail back to the original transaction.

A bank sends an MT191 in a few common situations. The first is charges. A correspondent bank may have paid charges to a third bank, or incurred its own handling charges, while processing a customer payment, and those charges were not covered by the charges code on the original MT103. The second is interest. If a payment was delayed, if funds were held because of a query, or if a bank had to fund a payment before it was reimbursed, interest may be owed for the days the money was outstanding. The third is other expenses, for example the cost of a repair, a trace, or a manual intervention that one bank carried out at the request of another. In each case the claiming bank needs a formal way to ask for the money, with a reference the other bank can match to its own records.

The flow starts with the original payment. Suppose Bank A sends a customer payment to Bank B, and Bank B has to pay a fee to an intermediary bank to complete it, or has to hold the funds for two days while a compliance check is done. Bank B calculates the amount owed, prepares an MT191, and sends it to Bank A. The MT191 carries the sender reference in field 20, a related reference in field 21 that links it to the original payment, the currency and amount claimed, and a description of what the amount is for, whether it is charges, interest, or another expense, including the period the interest covers or the reason for the charge. It also tells Bank A which account should be debited, so the payment can be made without further correspondence.

The receiving bank, in this example Bank A, does not pay automatically. It first checks the claim. It matches the related reference in field 21 to the original payment in its own system, checks that the amount is reasonable and that the charge or interest was actually incurred, and checks whether the original payment instruction already covered the cost, for example through the charges code in field 71A. If the claim is valid, Bank A pays it, normally by a separate MT202 bank to bank payment, or by authorising a debit to its account with Bank B. If the claim is not valid, or if the amount or the period is wrong, Bank A does not just ignore it. It answers with an MT196, explaining why it will not pay, or it asks a question with an MT195.

MT191 relates closely to MT192 and MT195, and the three are often confused. MT191 is a request for money, charges or interest. MT192 is a request for cancellation of a payment that has already been sent. MT195 is a question about a payment, asking for information or clarification. All three are bank to bank messages that refer back to an earlier payment, and all three are answered by MT196. The difference is what the sender wants. MT191 wants payment of an amount. MT192 wants a payment stopped or reversed. MT195 wants an answer. MT191 matters because charges and interest are where correspondent banking relationships are tested. Small amounts can sit unpaid for months if there is no clear claim and no clear answer, and they can damage a relationship out of proportion to the amount. A well written MT191, with a clear related reference, a clear amount, and a clear reason, gets paid quickly. A vague one gets queried, delayed, or refused.

text:
MT192 is a SWIFT message used by one bank to request the cancellation of a payment that has already been sent. It is a request, not an instruction that automatically cancels the payment. The sending bank is asking the receiving bank to stop the payment if it still can, and to return the funds if it has already received them. Whether cancellation is possible depends on where the payment is in its journey, whether the beneficiary has already been paid, and whether the receiving bank has already passed the payment onward. MT192 is the formal way to start that process.

A bank sends an MT192 for several practical reasons. The customer may have made a mistake, for example a wrong account number, a wrong amount, or a duplicate payment sent twice. The sending bank may have discovered a compliance problem after the payment left, for example a sanctions concern that was not caught in time, or a fraud report from the customer. In each case the sending bank needs to act quickly, because every hour that passes makes cancellation less likely. MT192 is sent as soon as the problem is known.

The cancellation flow for a customer payment, originally sent by MT103, works in stages. First, the sending bank sends the MT192 to the bank that received the MT103, quoting the sender reference and the related reference that identify the original payment, and the message type and date of the original message so the receiving bank can find it without doubt. The MT192 also carries a narrative explaining why cancellation is requested. Second, the receiving bank searches for the original payment. It checks whether the payment is still held in a queue, whether it has been credited to the beneficiary account, and whether it has been passed on to another bank. Third, if the payment is still held and has not been paid out, the receiving bank stops it, returns the funds to the sending bank, and answers with an MT196 confirming the cancellation. If the payment has already been credited, the receiving bank cannot simply reverse it without the beneficiary consent, and it must contact the beneficiary and ask for the funds back.

The flow for a bank to bank payment, originally sent by MT202, is similar but more direct. An MT202 is a payment between banks, with no customer beneficiary in the same sense, so there is no customer account to credit and no beneficiary consent to seek in the same way. If the MT202 has not yet been settled, the receiving bank can stop it and return the funds. The key point is the same in both cases. Cancellation is only possible while the receiving bank still controls the funds. Once the funds have left the receiving bank, cancellation becomes a recovery, not a stop.

Cancellation is possible when the payment is still in flight, still held for a value date in the future, or still sitting in a queue waiting for a compliance check or a repair. It is too late when the beneficiary account has already been credited and the beneficiary has withdrawn the funds, when the payment has already been settled through a clearing system and cannot be recalled, or when the receiving bank has already passed the payment onward and no longer holds it. In those cases the sending bank cannot cancel, it can only ask for a return of funds, which depends on the beneficiary agreeing to give the money back. The difference from a return is important. A cancellation is a request to stop a payment before it is completed. A return is what happens after a payment has been completed and the funds are sent back, for example because the beneficiary account does not exist or the beneficiary refused the payment. A cancellation, if successful, means the payment never reaches the beneficiary. Knowing when to send MT192, and when it is already too late, is one of the most practical skills in payments operations.

text:
MT196 is a SWIFT message used by a bank to answer a request it has received from another bank. It is the reply message for MT191, MT192, and MT195, and for other request messages in the same family. When one bank asks for charges, asks for a cancellation, or asks a question about a payment, the receiving bank does not reply with a free format message. It replies with an MT196, which carries a structured answer that the requesting bank system can read, match to the original request, and act on. MT196 closes the loop that the request opened.

A bank sends an MT196 whenever it has received a request that needs a formal answer. If it receives an MT191 asking for charges or interest, it answers with an MT196 to say whether it will pay, and if not, why not. If it receives an MT192 asking for cancellation, it answers with an MT196 to say whether the payment has been cancelled and the funds returned, or whether cancellation is not possible and why. If it receives an MT195 asking a question about a payment, it answers with an MT196 to give the information asked for, for example the status of the payment, the value date applied, or the charges deducted.

The flow end to end is straightforward, but the discipline matters. First, Bank A sends a request, for example an MT192 to cancel a customer payment. The MT192 carries a sender reference in field 20 and a related reference in field 21 that identify the original payment. Second, Bank B receives the request, finds the original payment, and investigates. It checks whether the payment is still held, whether it has been credited, and whether it has been passed onward. Third, Bank B sends an MT196 back to Bank A. The MT196 carries its own sender reference in field 20, a related reference in field 21 that links it to the MT192 it is answering, and an answers field that states the outcome in a coded form, with a narrative to explain the detail. Fourth, Bank A reads the answer, updates its own records, and tells its customer what has happened.

The possible answers depend on the request. For an MT191 charges request, the answers are normally that the charges will be paid, that the charges will be paid in part, or that the claim is refused, with a reason such as the charges were already covered by the original payment instruction, the amount is incorrect, or the claim is out of time. For an MT192 cancellation request, the answers are normally that the payment has been cancelled and the funds have been returned, that cancellation is not possible because the payment has already been credited to the beneficiary, or that cancellation is not possible because the payment has already been passed onward. For an MT195 question, the answer is the information requested, for example the payment was credited on a given value date, the beneficiary account was closed, or the payment is still held for a compliance check. In every case the answer must be clear enough for the requesting bank to act without having to ask again.

MT196 is not a payment message and it does not move funds by itself. If an MT196 says that a cancelled payment will be returned, the actual return of funds is made by a separate payment message, normally an MT103 or MT202 in the opposite direction. If an MT196 says that charges will be paid, the payment of those charges is also made separately. The MT196 is the message that says what will happen, and the payment message is the one that makes it happen. Confusing the two is a common error. MT196 matters because correspondent banking runs on questions and answers, and without a structured answer the requesting bank cannot close its case. A good MT196 is prompt, specific, and linked clearly to the request it answers.

text:
MT210 is a SWIFT message used by a bank to tell its correspondent bank that funds are coming. Its full name is Notice to Receive, and its purpose is to fund a Nostro account. A Nostro account is an account a bank holds with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency, for example a bank in India holding a US dollar account with a bank in New York. When the bank knows it will need funds in that account to meet outgoing payments, it sends an MT210 to the correspondent, giving advance notice of the incoming funds, so the correspondent knows to expect them, can identify them when they arrive, and can make the funds available on the right value date.

A bank sends an MT210 when it is moving its own funds, not customer funds, to top up a Nostro account. Typical situations are daily liquidity management, where a bank forecasts the payments it will have to make in a currency that day and funds the account to cover them, and planned funding, where a bank is sending a large amount to its correspondent ahead of a known outflow, for example a bulk customer payment run or a settlement.

The flow starts with the sending bank deciding how much it needs and when. It checks its Nostro balance, its forecast of outgoing payments, and any minimum balance it must keep with the correspondent. It then arranges the funding, normally by instructing a payment from its account elsewhere, and sends the MT210 to the correspondent bank. The MT210 carries the sender reference in field 20, the account identification in field 25, which identifies the Nostro account to be credited, the value date in field 30, which is the date the funds should be available, and the currency and amount to be received in field 32B. It also identifies the ordering institution and, where relevant, the intermediary or account with institution that will send the funds, so the correspondent can match the incoming payment to the notice.

When the correspondent bank receives the MT210, it does not credit the account immediately. It records the notice, checks that the account in field 25 is a valid Nostro account held for the sending bank, and waits for the funds to arrive. When the funds arrive, normally by an MT202 bank to bank payment or through a clearing system, the correspondent matches the incoming payment to the MT210 by amount, currency, value date, and sender. If the match is good, it credits the Nostro account on the value date in field 30 and the sending bank can use the funds for its outgoing payments. If the match is not clear, the correspondent holds the funds in a suspense account and queries the sender, which delays availability.

If the funds do not arrive, the correspondent bank does not credit the account, and the sending bank has a problem. It may have already instructed outgoing customer payments on the assumption that the funding would arrive, and those payments may now fail or be delayed. The sending bank must first check whether the funding payment was actually sent, whether it was sent to the right correspondent, and whether it is held somewhere in the chain, for example by an intermediary bank or by a compliance check. It can send a query, an MT195, to trace the funds, and it can arrange emergency funding from another source if the original funding is lost. MT210 matters because Nostro funding is the plumbing that makes cross border customer payments possible. A customer payment cannot be made in US dollars if the sending bank has no dollars in its Nostro account with its US correspondent. The MT210 is the advance warning that keeps that plumbing working, it lets the correspondent prepare, it lets the sending bank plan, and it creates a clear record when funds go missing.

text:
MT195 is a SWIFT message used by one bank to ask another bank a question about a payment. It is the enquiry message in the correspondent banking family. When a bank does not know where a payment is, why it has not arrived, why an amount is different from expected, or what happened to a payment it sent or expected to receive, it sends an MT195 to the other bank involved and asks for the information it needs. The receiving bank answers with an MT196. Together, MT195 and MT196 form the question and answer pair that keeps cross border payments traceable.

A bank sends an MT195 in many everyday situations. A customer complains that a payment has not arrived, and the sending bank needs to know whether the receiving bank has credited it. A payment arrives for a lower amount than expected, and the receiving bank needs to know what charges were deducted and by whom. A payment is held for repair, and the sending bank needs to know what information is missing. A payment cannot be applied because the beneficiary account number is wrong, and the receiving bank needs the correct details. In each case the MT195 is the formal way to ask, with a reference the other bank can use to find the payment quickly.

The enquiry flow is simple and disciplined. First, the asking bank identifies the payment it is asking about, using the sender reference and the related reference that link to the original MT103 or MT202, and the message type and date of the original message so there is no doubt which payment is meant. Second, it sends the MT195, stating its question clearly in the queries field and adding a narrative with the detail the other bank needs, for example the amount expected, the value date, and the beneficiary name. Third, the receiving bank searches its system for the payment, checks its status, and prepares an answer. Fourth, it replies with an MT196, giving the information asked for, or explaining why it cannot give it yet, for example because the payment is still held for a compliance check. The asking bank then updates its records and tells its customer.

The common questions asked by MT195 fall into a few groups. Status questions ask where the payment is, whether it has been credited, and on what value date. Amount questions ask why the amount received is less than the amount sent, and what charges or deductions were taken. Beneficiary questions ask whether the beneficiary account exists, whether the name matches the account, and whether the beneficiary has been contacted. Value date questions ask why a payment was credited late, or why the value date applied is different from the one instructed.

Worked examples make the use clear. In the first example, a bank in Mumbai sends an MT103 for 10,000 US dollars to a bank in London, but the customer in London says nothing has arrived after three days. The Mumbai bank sends an MT195 to London, quoting the original reference and asking whether the payment was received and credited, and if not, why not. London replies by MT196 that the payment was received but held because the beneficiary account number did not match the name, and asks for the correct account number. Mumbai gets the correct number from its customer and sends it, and London releases the payment. In the second example, a bank receives 9,850 dollars when it expected 10,000 dollars. It sends an MT195 asking for a breakdown of the charges deducted. The sending bank replies by MT196 that an intermediary bank deducted 150 dollars in charges, and the receiving bank can then explain the shortfall to its customer and reconcile its account. MT195 matters because payments go wrong, and when they do, the only way to fix them is to ask the right bank the right question with the right reference.

text:
MT199 is a SWIFT free-format message that one bank sends to another. It is used when no dedicated structured message fits what the bank needs to say. In a gpi payment flow, it carries status updates, queries, and confirmations. It is the general purpose message that keeps a payment visible after the instruction has left the sending bank.

A gpi payment travels through several banks. Each bank must keep the chain informed about where the payment is. The main instruction travels as an MT103. The cover, where one is used, travels as an MT202 COV. Neither message can carry a free text status update. That is the gap MT199 fills. A bank uses it when it credits the beneficiary, deducts a charge, holds a payment for a check, or must explain a delay.

The structure is simple. The message carries the sender and receiver, a reference to the payment, and a free text narrative. The reference is what makes the message useful. Without it, the receiving bank cannot match the MT199 to the right payment. The usual references are the sender's reference and the gpi unique end to end transaction reference. A good MT199 starts by identifying the payment precisely. It then states the point in plain terms. It ends by giving any action needed.

In a typical flow, the ordering bank sends the MT103. Each intermediary bank processes it and passes it on. The beneficiary bank credits the beneficiary account. That bank then sends a confirmation back up the chain, often as an MT199. It states that the payment has been credited. It gives the value date and the amount credited after any charges. Intermediary banks may also send MT199 messages to report a forwarding, a charge deduction, or a hold pending further information.

MT199 is also used for queries. If a bank has not received a confirmation it expected, it can ask for the status by MT199. The receiving bank answers with another MT199. This query and answer pattern is one of the oldest uses of the message. It matters in gpi because the tracker depends on banks reporting status. A missing report is often chased with an MT199.

MT199 differs from MT299 in purpose. MT199 is used in the course of a live payment. It is the message most often used for gpi status and confirmation traffic. MT299 is also free format, but it is used for bank to bank queries that sit outside a specific payment instruction. In practice, teams choose MT199 when the message is tied to a live payment flow, and MT299 when it is a standalone enquiry. The receiving bank routes and prioritises the two differently.

A worked example makes this concrete. A beneficiary bank in Singapore receives a gpi payment, credits the customer account on the value date, and deducts a small handling charge. It sends an MT199 to the bank that sent it the payment. The narrative identifies the payment by its reference, states that the account has been credited, gives the amount and value date, and notes the charge. The sending bank can then update the tracker and answer the ordering customer with confidence. Another example is a delay. An intermediary bank holds a payment because the beneficiary name does not match its records. It sends an MT199 explaining the hold and asking for the correct name.

If the MT199 is not sent, the consequences are immediate. The tracker shows a gap, because no bank has reported the next status. The ordering bank cannot tell its customer whether the payment has arrived. The sending bank keeps the payment as an open item, which creates reconciliation work. In the worst case, a payment that has been credited is treated as missing, and a second investigation starts for a payment that has already completed. The money has moved, but the information has not. Send MT199 promptly, reference the payment precisely, state the facts plainly, and say what happens next. A short, accurate MT199 prevents a long investigation later.

text:
MT299 is a SWIFT free-format message that one bank sends to another. It asks a question, gives an answer, or passes on information that has no dedicated structured message type. It is the general enquiry message in the MT family. It is used when a bank needs to communicate about a matter that is not tied to a single live payment instruction, and when the subject needs free text rather than fixed fields.

Not every bank to bank communication fits a structured message. MT103 is for a customer payment. MT202 is for a bank to bank transfer. MT900 is for a debit confirmation. Each has fixed fields for a fixed purpose. When the question is open ended, a free-format message is needed. MT299 provides that channel.

MT299 is used instead of MT199 when the subject is a query rather than a status update inside a live payment flow. The line is not always sharp, and different banks draw it slightly differently. The working rule is still useful. If the message asks a question, seeks information, or replies to such a question, MT299 is the usual choice. A bank that receives an MT299 expects a question or an answer. It routes the message to the team that handles enquiries and investigations.

The query and answer flow is simple. The enquiring bank sends an MT299 to the bank it needs information from. The narrative must identify the subject clearly. For a payment query, that means the payment reference, the value date, the amount and currency, and the names of the ordering and beneficiary parties. For a non-payment query, it means the account or arrangement the question relates to. The message then states the question in plain terms. Where relevant, it gives the date by which an answer is needed.

The receiving bank reads the MT299, finds the underlying record, and replies with its own MT299. The reply should quote the original reference, so the two messages can be matched. It should answer the question directly and state any action taken or still needed. If the receiving bank cannot answer immediately, a good reply says so, gives a reason, and gives a date for a full answer. Silence is the worst response. The enquiring bank then has no way to know whether the message was received, is being worked on, or has been lost.

A worked example shows the pattern. A bank receives a customer complaint that a payment sent two weeks ago has not arrived. Its operations team confirms the payment was sent and sends an MT299 to the next bank in the chain. The receiving bank replies by MT299, quoting the same reference. It states that the payment was held because the beneficiary account number was incomplete, and asks the sending bank to confirm the correct account number. The sending bank obtains it, replies, and the payment is released.

Another example is a charges query. A bank notices that the amount credited to its customer is less than the amount sent, and the difference is larger than the charges it expected. It sends an MT299 to the bank that deducted the charge, asking for a breakdown. The reply lists the charges deducted, the reason for each, and the value date applied. The enquiring bank can then explain the deduction to its customer with facts instead of guesses.

The risks of a poorly written MT299 are the same as for any free-format message. If the reference is missing or wrong, the receiving bank cannot find the payment, and the query sits unanswered. If the question is vague, the reply will be vague. Good practice is to trace the chain first, identify the right bank, give the full reference, and ask one clear question at a time. MT299 matters because payments do not always go smoothly. When they do not, banks need a reliable way to ask each other what happened. The structured messages move the money. MT299, together with MT199, moves the explanation.

The Relationship Management Application, known as RMA, is the SWIFT mechanism that controls which banks can send SWIFT messages to each other. It also controls which types of message they can send. It is a permissioning system. Before one bank can send a message to another bank over the SWIFT network, an RMA must exist between them that authorises that type of message. Without it, the network will not deliver the message.

A bank cannot simply send a SWIFT message to any other bank. That restriction exists for a clear reason. SWIFT messages move money and create binding instructions. It also limits acceptance to the message types the receiving bank has agreed to accept.

Think of RMA as a bilateral agreement recorded on the network. Each bank decides, for each other bank it deals with, which message categories it will accept. A bank may accept payment messages from a correspondent bank it has an account relationship with. It may not accept payment messages from a bank it has no relationship with. RMA records those choices, and the network enforces them.

Setting up RMA is a controlled process. First, the two banks agree commercially that they will exchange SWIFT messages. This is usually part of a correspondent banking relationship or a specific service agreement. Second, each bank's SWIFT operations or network management team creates the RMA record for the other bank. The record specifies the message categories and types that are authorised. The authorisation is directional. Each direction is set up separately.

Third, the banks exchange the RMA authorisation over the network. Each side confirms that the record is in place. Only then does message traffic flow normally. In practice, setup is done in advance of the first live payment, as part of onboarding a new correspondent. It is tested with a test message before live traffic begins.

Scopes are central to RMA. An RMA authorisation is not a blanket permission to send anything. It is scoped to message categories, and often to specific message types within a category. A bank may authorise another bank to send customer payments, but not bank to bank cover payments. It may authorise both. It may authorise securities messages for one relationship and trade messages for another. The scope reflects the business relationship.

When RMA is missing, the consequence is immediate. The sending bank transmits the message. The network checks the RMA record, finds no authorisation for that message type, and rejects the message. The sending bank receives a rejection, and the payment does not reach the intended receiver. No money moves. The payment sits as a failed instruction in the sending bank. Operations must investigate, find that RMA is missing, arrange for it to be set up, and then resend the payment. That takes time. If the payment was urgent, the delay can breach a customer expectation or a value date.

RMA can also be missing in a subtler way. The RMA may exist, but for the wrong message type. Or the RMA may exist in one direction only, so messages flow one way but not the other. These partial gaps are a common cause of failed first payments with a new correspondent. They are found by checking the RMA scope before the first live message, not after it fails.

Maintaining RMA is an ongoing job, not a one-off setup. Relationships change. A bank may add a new service, which needs a new message type authorised. A bank may close a relationship, which means the RMA should be removed so no further messages can be sent. A bank may change its SWIFT address, which means the RMA records must be updated. Good practice is to review RMA records regularly and remove authorisations that are no longer needed. An old, unused RMA is a risk, because it leaves a channel open that no one is monitoring. RMA is also a security control, because it stops unauthorised payment instructions at the network boundary. If a message is rejected and no other reason is obvious, check RMA before assuming a system fault.

text:
ACK and NACK are the SWIFT network's short answers to a message a bank has sent. ACK means the network has accepted the message. NACK means the network has not accepted it. Together they tell the sending bank, quickly and definitively, whether its message has entered the SWIFT network properly, or whether something is wrong and the message needs to be fixed and sent again.

The distinction matters because sending a message is not the same as delivering it. A bank's own system may show a payment as sent, but that only means it left the bank's internal system. The network then checks the message before it forwards it to the receiving bank. The ACK or NACK is the result of that check. Until the ACK arrives, the sending bank should not treat the payment as safely on its way.

When a bank sends a message, the SWIFT network runs a series of validation checks. These are network level checks, not business checks by the receiving bank. If all checks pass, the network accepts the message, stores it, and forwards it to the receiver. It then sends an ACK back to the sender.

If any check fails, the network does not forward the message. It sends a NACK back to the sender instead. The NACK is not a vague failure notice. It carries a reason, or an error code, that identifies what failed. The sending bank's operations team uses that reason to find the fault.

An ACK means several specific things. It means the message passed network validation. It means the network has accepted responsibility for delivering it to the receiver. It means the sender and receiver addresses were valid, and the RMA check passed. It does not mean the receiving bank has read the message, agreed to it, or acted on it. It does not mean the payment has been credited to the beneficiary. Those are business outcomes. They are confirmed separately, by the receiving bank, through a confirmation message or a status update. Confusing a network ACK with a business confirmation is a common and costly mistake.

A NACK means the message has not entered the network and has not reached the receiver. The sending bank must act. The first step is to read the NACK reason and find the fault in the original message. The second step is to correct the fault in the bank's own system, by creating a corrected version. The third step is to resend the corrected message and wait for the ACK. The original message should not be treated as sent. The payment should not be treated as in progress until the corrected message receives its ACK.

Some NACKs are easy to fix. A formatting error, a missing field, or a mistyped receiver address can be corrected quickly and the message resent. Others take longer. A NACK caused by a missing RMA authorisation cannot be fixed by correcting the message. It needs the RMA to be set up, which involves the network management team and the other bank. A NACK caused by a system fault needs the technical team.

The end to end flow looks like this. The sending bank creates the payment instruction and transmits it to the SWIFT network. The network validates it. If it passes, the network sends an ACK to the sender and forwards the message to the receiver. The receiver's system accepts the message and processes it as a business instruction. If the validation fails, the network sends a NACK to the sender and does not forward the message. The sender corrects the fault and resends. The cycle repeats until an ACK is received.

A bank's operations team should monitor ACK and NACK traffic as a routine control. Every sent message should have a matching ACK. Any message without an ACK after a reasonable interval should be investigated. A customer who asks whether a payment has arrived needs the business confirmation, not the ACK. Giving the ACK as if it were proof of arrival overstates what the bank knows.

text:
CGI-MP stands for Common Global Implementation Market Practice. It is a set of usage guidelines that banks and corporates use when they implement ISO 20022 messages. Its aim is that the same message means the same thing wherever it is used. Its purpose is simple: one common implementation instead of many local flavours that do not work together.

ISO 20022 is a standard, but a standard on its own does not guarantee that two banks will use it in the same way. The standard defines message types and fields, but it leaves room for choice. One bank may use a field in one way, another bank may use it differently, and a third may leave it out. A corporate that sends payment instructions to several banks would then need a different version of the same message for each bank. That defeats the purpose of a common standard. CGI-MP exists to close that gap by agreeing, in detail, how the standard should be used in practice.

CGI-MP is maintained by a group of banks and corporates working together. Its guidelines are published for the industry to use. The guidelines do not replace ISO 20022. They sit on top of it. ISO 20022 says what a message can contain. A bank that follows CGI-MP is therefore following ISO 20022, but in the specific way the industry has agreed.

The coverage of CGI-MP spans the main ISO 20022 message families that banks and corporates use every day. The pain family covers payment initiation. These are the messages a corporate sends to its bank to instruct payments, including credit transfers and direct debits. The pacs family covers payments clearing and settlement. These are the messages banks send to each other and to clearing systems to move money. The camt family covers cash management, including account statements, balance reports and notifications. Together, these three families cover the full life cycle of a payment, from instruction, through clearing, to reporting.

A bank uses CGI-MP usage guidelines when it builds or buys a system that sends or receives ISO 20022 messages. The guidelines tell the bank's developers and its vendors exactly how to populate each field. They cover which formats to use for dates, amounts and references, and how to handle common cases such as charges, remittance information and returns. The bank's testing then checks its messages against the guidelines, not just against the raw standard. A message that is valid ISO 20022 but does not follow CGI-MP may still be rejected by a counterparty that expects the CGI-MP usage. Following the guidelines is a practical necessity, not a nicety.

For a corporate customer, CGI-MP brings a direct benefit. A corporate that pays from accounts at several banks can use the same payment file format for all of them, as long as each bank supports CGI-MP. The corporate does not need to maintain a separate format per bank. Its treasury system does not need to know each bank's local quirks. That reduces cost, reduces errors, and makes it easier to change banks or add a new banking relationship. For banks, the benefit is similar: fewer bilateral variations to support, fewer mapping errors, and faster onboarding of new corporate customers.

CGI-MP relates to CBPR+ in a complementary way. CBPR+ is the Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus usage guideline, published by SWIFT, for cross-border payments over the SWIFT network. CGI-MP is broader. It covers corporate to bank and bank to bank usage across domestic and cross-border payments. The two are aligned. A bank should not treat them as competing standards.

The migration to ISO 20022 makes CGI-MP more important, not less. As banks move from MT messages to ISO 20022, the risk is that each bank migrates in its own way. The industry could end up with as many ISO 20022 flavours as it had MT flavours. CGI-MP is the guard against that. A bank that migrates with CGI-MP produces messages that counterparties can process straight through. The standard is the language. CGI-MP is the agreed dialect. Knowing the dialect is what makes straight-through processing work in practice.
