text:
FINplus is the SWIFT messaging channel that carries ISO 20022 messages between banks. It is the successor to FIN, the long established channel that carries MT messages. Where FIN carries MT messages, FINplus carries ISO 20022 messages. It uses the same SWIFT network, the same security, and the same store and forward model, but with a message format designed for richer data and for the modern payments landscape.

To understand FINplus, it helps to separate three things that are often confused: the network, the channel, and the message format. The network is SWIFT itself, the secure private network that banks use to exchange financial messages. The channel is the service on that network that carries a particular type of traffic. FIN is the channel for MT messages. FINplus is the channel for ISO 20022 messages. The message format is the content of the message itself, MT in the case of FIN, ISO 20022 in the case of FINplus. A bank connects to the SWIFT network once, and then uses FIN, FINplus, and other services over that connection as its business requires.

FINplus differs from FIN in the message format it carries, and in what that format allows. MT messages are compact, with fixed fields and limited space for remittance information and party details. That richness is the main reason for the move to FINplus.

FINplus also differs from API channels. FINplus is a store and forward messaging channel, like FIN. A bank sends a message, the network stores it, validates it, and forwards it to the receiver, and the sender receives an ACK or NACK. That model suits payment instructions that need to be processed in sequence, with a clear audit trail, and with the network's validation and non-repudiation. APIs and FINplus therefore serve different purposes, and a bank will use both. FINplus carries the payment instruction itself. An API may carry a status query or a pre-validation check around it.

The FINplus message structure follows the ISO 20022 standard. The usage of those elements for cross-border payments is defined by CBPR+, the usage guideline that sits on top of ISO 20022 for the SWIFT network. Getting those layers right is the core implementation task.

How a bank connects to FINplus depends on how it already connects to SWIFT. A bank with an existing SWIFT connection does not need a new network. The interface is the bank's gateway to the network. It must be able to handle the larger, more detailed ISO 20022 messages, to validate them, and to produce the ACK and NACK handling that FINplus requires. Banks that use a service bureau or a vendor platform will work with that provider to enable FINplus, but the mapping and testing remain the bank's responsibility.

The migration from FIN to FINplus is the industry's move from MT to ISO 20022 for cross-border payments. It is phased, not a single cutover. During the migration period, banks operate both channels. Some counterparties are ready for ISO 20022, others are still on MT, and the bank must be able to send the right format to the right counterparty. That coexistence period is complex. As more banks complete the migration, FIN traffic declines and FINplus becomes the normal channel for cross-border payments.

The practical risks during migration are worth naming. A payment sent in the wrong format to a counterparty that is not ready for it will be rejected or will need manual repair. The bank's own screening, sanctions and reconciliation systems must also be able to handle the richer ISO 20022 data, or the benefit of that data is lost. Testing with each counterparty, and a clear record of who is on which format, are the controls that manage those risks.

For a payments professional, FINplus is not just a technical change. It changes what data travels with a payment, and therefore what the bank can do with that payment. Richer party data improves sanctions screening. Structured remittance data improves reconciliation for the beneficiary. Clearer charge information improves transparency for the ordering customer.

SWIFT Universal Confirmation is the rule that every bank receiving a cross-border payment must confirm the outcome of that payment to the SWIFT Tracker. It applies to every supervised financial institution receiving an MT103 or a pacs.008, whether or not the bank is a gpi member. It is the commitment that closes the loop on a cross-border payment. The ordering bank sends the payment, the intermediary banks forward it, the beneficiary bank credits it, and the beneficiary bank confirms that it has done so. Without that confirmation, the payment is an open item, and the tracker cannot show that it has arrived.

The idea behind Universal Confirmation is straightforward. A tracking service is only useful if the final status is reported. Universal Confirmation fixes that by making the final confirmation mandatory for every bank receiving a cross-border payment.

Every bank receiving an MT103 or a pacs.008 must confirm the outcome to the Tracker within two business days of the value date, as credited (ACCC), rejected (RJCT), placed on hold, or transferred outside SWIFT. SWIFT measures each institution on confirming at least 80% of its weekly traffic inside that window. The confirmation is not optional, and it is not limited to large payments or to payments for particular customers. That universality is what gives the tracker its reliability. A customer who looks at the tracker can expect a final confirmed status, not a payment that simply stops updating.

The confirmation flow works in sequence. Each intermediary bank processes the payment and forwards it, updating the tracker as it does so. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the beneficiary account, and then sends a confirmation. That confirmation states that the payment has been credited, gives the amount credited and the value date, and notes any charges deducted. The confirmation travels back to the banks that handled the payment, and the tracker is updated to show the payment as confirmed.

Confirmations travel via the Universal Confirmations API, trck.001, or the Basic Tracker. MT199 was used for tracker status in the past, but SWIFT deprecated its use for tracker confirmations in November 2025, so new implementations should use the API or trck.001. The ordering bank does not need to know which channel was used. It needs the confirmation itself.

Deadlines matter, and they are set by the service rules rather than by each bank's convenience. The confirmation must reach the Tracker within two business days of the value date, and SWIFT measures each institution on confirming at least 80% of its weekly traffic inside that window. A beneficiary bank that confirms late is in breach of the service rules, and SWIFT monitors compliance across the community.

When a bank does not confirm, several things happen. The tracker shows the payment as unconfirmed, which the ordering bank and its customer can see. The ordering bank may chase the missing confirmation, often by sending an MT199 query to the bank that should have confirmed. The payment remains an open item in the ordering bank's systems, which creates reconciliation work and, in some banks, an exception that must be cleared manually. The bank that failed to confirm is in breach of its Universal Confirmation obligation, which SWIFT monitors. Repeated failures to confirm can affect the bank's standing in the service and can be raised by counterparties that depend on its confirmations.

There are legitimate reasons why a confirmation may be delayed. In those cases, the bank should report the status, for example by sending a status update that the payment is held, rather than staying silent. Silence is the problem. A reported hold is manageable. An unreported hold is not.

Why Universal Confirmation matters for tracking is clear from the customer's point of view. A bank that can show a confirmed credit gives its customer certainty, and that certainty is the service the customer is paying for. Without Universal Confirmation, gpi would be a service that shows movement but not arrival, and that would be of limited value. With it, gpi can show the full journey, from instruction to confirmed credit, and the customer can close the transaction with confidence. Confirm every cross-border payment you handle as the final bank, promptly, with the correct reference, the amount credited and the value date. Pass on confirmations you receive. Chase missing confirmations instead of leaving them open. Treat a missing confirmation as an exception to be worked, not as a routine gap.

SWIFT Payment Controls is a service that screens a bank's outgoing SWIFT payments in real time, before the money leaves the bank, and stops payments that look suspicious. It is a fraud prevention control that sits between the bank's payment system and the SWIFT network. Its purpose is to catch fraudulent or anomalous payments at the last point where they can still be stopped, before they are sent to another bank and become much harder to recover.

The need for such a control comes from how payment fraud works in practice. Fraud often starts inside the bank: a compromised credential, a fake invoice, or a business email compromise that changes a supplier's account details. By the time the payment reaches SWIFT it looks like an ordinary instruction, and once the beneficiary bank credits it, recovery means a recall request that may fail. The best point to stop that payment is before it leaves the bank, while the money is still in the customer's account. Payment Controls is designed for exactly that point.

The service works by checking each outgoing payment against a set of policies and rules the bank has defined. When the bank's payment system prepares a payment for sending over SWIFT, the payment is passed through Payment Controls first, through an interface between the payment system and the service, before it is released to the SWIFT network. The service returns a release or a hold in real time, so a clean payment is not delayed. If the payment fits the bank's normal pattern and passes its policies, it is released and sent on its way. If it does not fit, it is held for review.

The controls themselves fall into three broad groups. The first is policy controls. These are rules the bank sets about what is allowed. Examples are a maximum amount for a single payment, a list of countries or currencies the bank will not pay to without extra approval, a rule that payments above a threshold need a second approver, and a rule that first-time beneficiaries need extra checks. Policy controls are the bank's own business rules, expressed as checks the service applies automatically to every payment.

The second group is screening. Screening checks the payment against lists and data the bank uses to detect risk: sanctions lists, lists of known fraud accounts, the bank's own history of the customer's normal payments, and patterns such as a payment to a new country at an unusual hour or a round amount just below a reporting threshold. Screening is not a single check. It is a set of checks that run together, and a payment that fails any of them is held.

The third group is alerts. When a payment is held, the service raises an alert to the bank's operations or fraud team. The alert explains why the payment was held, which rule or check it failed, and what the payment details are. The team then reviews the payment, contacts the customer or the originating business if needed, and decides whether to release it or to reject it. The alert is the human step in the process. The service can hold a payment automatically, but the decision to release or reject it is made by a person who has looked at the facts.

When a payment is stopped, the flow is deliberate. The payment does not leave the bank. It sits in a held queue. The operations or fraud team is notified. If the payment is fraudulent, or cannot be verified as genuine, the team rejects it, and the money stays in the customer's account. The customer is then informed, and the bank's fraud team follows its own process for the attempted fraud.

The timing matters. A held payment is delayed, and a genuine payment that is held unnecessarily creates a customer service problem. A good implementation therefore tunes its rules so that genuine payments are rarely held, and held payments are reviewed quickly. A control that stops fraud but also stops genuine payments for hours is a control that will be bypassed or ignored, and that defeats its purpose.

Payment Controls fits with gpi and with fraud prevention more broadly. Gpi gives the bank and its customer visibility over where a payment is, and Universal Confirmation gives certainty that it has arrived. Payment Controls gives the bank assurance that the payment should have been sent in the first place. The three work together: Payment Controls checks the payment before it leaves, gpi tracks it while it moves, and confirmation proves it arrived. A bank that uses all three can tell its customer, with confidence, that a payment was checked, tracked and confirmed. It also fits with the bank's wider fraud prevention. It is an additional layer, at the point of exit, that catches what earlier controls may have missed. Know your bank's Payment Controls policies. When a payment is held, work the alert promptly, and do not release a payment you cannot verify. When a genuine payment is held repeatedly for the same reason, raise it so the policy can be tuned, rather than working around the control.

HVPS+ is a set of common ISO 20022 usage guidelines for high-value payment systems. It was created by the operators of the world's major high-value systems, working together, so that a pacs.008 or a pacs.009 means the same thing in New York, Frankfurt, London and Tokyo. It is not a payment system itself. It is a rulebook that sits on top of the ISO 20022 message standard and tells each high-value system exactly how to use it.

High-value systems needed their own rulebook because the ISO 20022 standard on its own is too flexible. The standard defines a message, but it allows many fields to be optional, many formats to vary, and many choices to be left to each implementer. That flexibility is fine for a single domestic market, but it breaks down when a payment has to move between systems, or when a bank has to build one interface that works for several systems. Two systems could both claim to use pacs.009 and still reject each other's messages because one expects a structured address and the other accepts free text, or because one requires a specific charge code and the other does not. HVPS+ removes that ambiguity by fixing the choices.

HVPS+ covers the core payment messages used in high-value settlement. The main ones are pacs.008 for customer credit transfers, pacs.009 for financial institution credit transfers, and pacs.002 for payment status reports, which carry acceptances and rejections back to the sender. It also covers the account reporting and liquidity messages in the camt family, such as camt.052 for intraday account reports, camt.053 for end of day statements, and camt.054 for debit and credit notifications. Liquidity management messages such as camt.050 are also in scope, because moving liquidity between accounts is a daily operation for every high-value participant.

The key rules in HVPS+ are about discipline in the data. Addresses must be structured, with town, country and postal code in their own fields rather than buried in free text lines, so that screening and routing can be automated. Agent identification must be precise, using BICs where they exist rather than names alone. Charges, remittance information and purpose codes follow agreed conventions so that the receiving system does not have to guess. Character sets are restricted, so that a character valid in one system cannot corrupt a message in another. Perhaps most important, HVPS+ defines which fields are mandatory, which are conditional and which are forbidden for each message in a high-value context, and it defines the exact reason codes to use when a payment is rejected, so that a rejection from one system is understood by the sender in another.

HVPS+ differs from CBPR+ in scope and in audience. CBPR+ is the rulebook for cross-border payments between banks, built around the correspondent banking chain. HVPS+ is the rulebook for the domestic high-value systems that actually settle the money at the end of that chain, the real-time gross settlement systems and the large-value clearing systems run by central banks and market infrastructures. The two rulebooks overlap deliberately. A cross-border pacs.008 that arrives under CBPR+ rules is often settled domestically under HVPS+ rules, and the guidelines are designed so that the data survives that handover without being re-keyed or truncated. If a field is mandatory under CBPR+, HVPS+ does not drop it, and if HVPS+ needs extra settlement detail, CBPR+ provides a place to carry it.

For a payments professional, HVPS+ matters because it is what makes straight-through processing possible in the high-value world. When a bank connects to a new high-value system, the first document its engineers and its operations team read is the HVPS+ usage guideline for that system. A message that follows HVPS+ will be accepted, validated and settled without manual repair. A message that ignores it will be rejected, queued, or repaired by hand, and in high-value payments a manual repair means delay, cost and operational risk on a payment that may be worth millions. Knowing the rulebook is therefore not an academic exercise. It is the difference between a payment that settles in seconds and one that sits in an exceptions queue.

text:
CBPR+ and HVPS+ are two rulebooks for the same ISO 20022 message standard, written for two different parts of the payment journey. CBPR+ governs cross-border payments between banks, the correspondent banking world. HVPS+ governs high-value domestic payment systems, the real-time gross settlement systems and large-value clearing systems that settle money in central bank funds. A single payment can be governed by both, one after the other, and knowing where one rulebook ends and the other begins is essential to working in international payments.

CBPR+ stands for Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus. It was developed by SWIFT together with the global banking community to replace the old MT message formats for cross-border traffic. It defines how banks use pacs.008 for customer payments, pacs.009 for bank to bank payments, pacs.002 for status reports and pacs.004 for payment returns, when the payment crosses a border. Its rules focus on the problems of the cross-border chain: identifying the debtor and creditor agents across several intermediary banks, carrying complete remittance and regulatory information through every hop, screening against sanctions lists, and making sure the data that left the ordering bank is the data that reaches the beneficiary bank.

HVPS+ covers the same message types, but for a different purpose. Its focus is settlement in a domestic high-value system. The questions it answers are about finality, liquidity and precision: which account is debited, which account is credited, what time the payment settles, what happens if the sending bank does not have enough liquidity, and how the system reports the settlement back. Its rules are stricter on data structure, because a high-value system settles in real time and cannot pause to ask what a free-text address means. Structured addresses, exact agent identification, restricted character sets and precise rejection codes are HVPS+ territory.

The two rulebooks overlap in the middle, and that overlap is deliberate. The messages are the same, pacs.008, pacs.009, pacs.002 and the camt reporting messages, and the two rulebooks were designed to be compatible, so a payment does not need to be rebuilt when it moves from one world to the other. Where they differ, the difference follows the job each one does. CBPR+ cares about the full payment chain and the completeness of the business information. HVPS+ cares about the settlement leg and the exactness of the settlement data. A field mandatory under CBPR+ for a regulator or a screening system will still be present when the payment reaches the HVPS+ system. A field that HVPS+ requires for settlement, such as a precise settlement account reference, can be carried through the CBPR+ chain without being stripped out.

At field level the difference is concrete. In a pacs.008, CBPR+ makes the debtor and creditor agents, the debtor and creditor accounts, the remittance information and the regulatory reporting fields mandatory or conditional, so the full chain can be screened and reconciled. HVPS+ keeps those fields but adds settlement precision: the settlement method and settlement account must be stated exactly, structured addresses are required rather than free text, agent identification must use BICs, and the message version must match the version the high-value system accepts. A payment that is valid under CBPR+ can still be rejected by an HVPS+ system if the address is unstructured or the settlement account is missing, and a payment that settles cleanly under HVPS+ can still fail a CBPR+ check if the remittance information was stripped out on the way in.

In practice, a bank must handle the handover between the two rulebooks every day. Take a typical payment: a corporate customer in London pays a supplier in Singapore. The London bank sends a pacs.008 under CBPR+ through the correspondent chain, and the Singapore bank must settle the Singapore dollar leg in its domestic high-value system under HVPS+ rules. The Singapore bank's payment hub has to map the CBPR+ message into the HVPS+ format, checking that every field the domestic system mandates is present, that the address is structured to HVPS+ standard, and that the agent identification matches what the domestic system expects. If a field is missing or in the wrong format, the payment is repaired or rejected before it reaches the settlement system, because a high-value system will not accept an ambiguous instruction.

A concrete mapping example shows the work. The CBPR+ pacs.008 arrives with the debtor agent identified by BIC, the creditor agent by BIC, an unstructured creditor address in free text, and a settlement method of INDA, meaning the payment settles through the instructing agent. The payment hub maps it to the HVPS+ format by converting the address to structured lines, confirming the settlement account from the settlement method, and checking the message version against the HVPS+ version in force. If the address cannot be structured, the payment is repaired by asking the sending bank for the structured form, or rejected with a pacs.002 giving the reason code, rather than being sent to the settlement system in a form it will refuse.

The migration context makes this comparison more than theoretical. The global move from MT to ISO 20022 happened on a shared timetable, with both rulebooks converging on the same message versions. Banks that built for only one rulebook discovered gaps at the handover, payments valid cross-border but invalid for domestic settlement, or settlement reports that could not be reconciled with the cross-border instruction. The lesson for any payments team is to design for both rulebooks from the start: validate inbound messages against CBPR+ at the border and against HVPS+ at the settlement system, keep the data complete through the whole journey, and test the handover explicitly rather than assuming that a message valid in one world is automatically valid in the other.

text:
RT1 is EBA Clearing's pan-European instant payment system. It clears and settles SEPA Instant Credit Transfers, known as SCT Inst, between banks across Europe, around the clock, every day of the year. If TIPS is the Eurosystem's instant settlement service, RT1 is the private-sector alternative, operated by EBA Clearing, which also runs the STEP2 and EURO1 systems. A bank offering instant euro payments will typically connect to one of the two, and many large banks connect to both.

RT1 differs from TIPS in one fundamental way: settlement. TIPS settles each payment individually in central bank money, in real time, on accounts held at the Eurosystem. RT1 settles on prefunded technical accounts. Each participating bank prefunds a technical account held for RT1 purposes, and payments are settled by moving funds between these technical accounts. Settlement is still final, in central bank money, but through a prefunded pool. Participants monitor their prefunded balance continuously and top it up when it runs low, because a bank whose technical account is empty cannot send further instant payments until it tops it up.

The payer's bank sends the payment instruction into RT1, which validates it and forwards it to the beneficiary's bank. The beneficiary's bank must respond within the scheme's time limit, confirming that the payment can be credited to the beneficiary's account. Once the positive response is received, RT1 settles the payment between the two banks' technical accounts and sends a confirmation back to the payer's bank. The whole end-to-end journey is designed to complete within a maximum of ten seconds.

The differences from TIPS matter in practice. TIPS is a Eurosystem service, operated by the central banks, settling directly in central bank money on the participant's TIPS account balance. RT1 is a commercial service operated by EBA Clearing, settling on prefunded technical accounts, and participants pay for the service commercially. TIPS is a pure settlement engine: the payer's bank and the beneficiary's bank exchange messages through TIPS itself. RT1 is a clearing and settlement system in one: it routes the messages between the banks and settles the funds. From a customer's point of view, the two are indistinguishable, the money arrives in seconds either way. From a bank's point of view, the choice involves cost, liquidity management, operational resilience and the bank's existing relationship with EBA Clearing.

What happens on a timeout or a reject is defined by the SCT Inst scheme and handled the same way on both systems. If the beneficiary's bank does not respond within the time limit, RT1 treats the payment as timed out and does not settle it; the payer's bank is informed with a negative status report, and the payer's account is not debited, or is credited back if a debit was already applied. If the beneficiary's bank actively rejects the payment, for example because the account is closed or the beneficiary name does not match, it sends a negative response, RT1 does not settle, and a pacs.002 status report carries the rejection reason back to the payer's bank. The payer's bank must then tell its customer clearly and quickly that the payment failed and why. There is also a recall process: if a payment was sent in error or is suspected of fraud, the payer's bank can send a recall request, and the beneficiary's bank must respond within the scheme's deadline and return the funds if they are still available.

RT1 matters because instant payments are now a baseline expectation, not a premium service. A bank that cannot receive SCT Inst payments in seconds will lose customers to one that can, and a bank that cannot send them will see its corporate customers route their urgent payments elsewhere. RT1 gives banks, including smaller banks that do not want a direct connection to TIPS, a route into instant payments through an established operator with a single connection, a single set of rules and a single prefunded account to manage. For a payments professional, the practical takeaway is to know which system your bank uses, how its prefunding is managed, what your timeout and reject handling looks like, and what your customer sees when a payment that was supposed to take seconds does not arrive.

text:
A Dedicated Cash Account, or DCA, is a cash account in the Eurosystem's TARGET services, set aside for one specific purpose. Unlike a Main Cash Account, which is the participant's general purpose account, a DCA holds liquidity only for the service it belongs to. There are three kinds: an RTGS DCA for high-value payments in T2, a TIPS DCA for instant payments, and a T2S DCA for securities settlement. Each DCA is linked to one Main Cash Account, and liquidity moves between the two as needed. The separation is deliberate: it ring-fences the liquidity for each service, so that a surge in instant payments cannot drain the funds needed for high-value settlement, and vice versa.

The Main Cash Account, or MCA, is the participant's central account in T2. It holds the participant's central bank money and minimum reserves, and it is where standing facilities are accessed and credit lines are drawn. A Technical Account belongs to a system or an ancillary system, not to a single participant, and settles that system's obligations, for example a clearing system that nets payments and settles the net amounts. A DCA sits between the two. It belongs to the participant, like the MCA, but it is dedicated to one service, so the liquidity on it can only be used for that service's transactions.

Each DCA has a clear job. The RTGS DCA holds the liquidity for high-value and urgent payments in T2: a pacs.009 sent debits it, and a pacs.009 received credits it. The TIPS DCA holds the liquidity for instant payments. Because instant payments run around the clock, including nights and weekends when the RTGS service is closed, the TIPS DCA must be funded in advance and monitored continuously. The T2S DCA holds the liquidity for securities settlement: it is debited when the participant buys securities and credited when it sells them.

Liquidity moves between the MCA and the DCAs through liquidity transfers, a daily job for a bank's payments operations team. A participant can move liquidity manually, with an immediate transfer instruction, or automatically, using standing orders that move a fixed amount at a fixed time each day, or floor and ceiling rules that trigger a transfer when a balance crosses a threshold. For example, a bank might set a rule that tops up its TIPS DCA automatically whenever the balance falls below a threshold, so that instant payments never stall overnight, and sweep surplus liquidity from its RTGS DCA back to the MCA at the end of the day. The message used for these transfers is camt.050.

What happens if a DCA runs out of funds depends on the service. In RTGS, a payment that cannot settle for insufficient funds is queued. It waits, and the system retries it as liquidity arrives, either from incoming payments or from a transfer from the MCA. The participant can reorder or cancel queued payments, but one still unsettled at the end of the business day is rejected, and the sender must inform its customer. In TIPS there is no queue, because instant payments must complete in seconds. If the TIPS DCA has insufficient funds, the payment is rejected immediately and a negative status report goes back to the payer's bank. Proper funding and automatic top-ups of the TIPS DCA are therefore a critical operational control. In T2S, a securities transaction that cannot settle for lack of cash is held and retried through the day, and may fail if the cash never arrives, creating a settlement fail that must be reported and resolved.

For a payments professional, DCAs are where liquidity management becomes concrete. It is not enough for the bank to have enough money overall. The money has to be in the right account at the right time. A bank with ample funds on its MCA but an empty TIPS DCA will still fail its customers' instant payments on a Saturday night. A bank that leaves too much on its RTGS DCA overnight earns nothing on it and may miss its reserve position. Getting the split right, automating the transfers, monitoring balances and having a clear procedure for a DCA running dry are the daily disciplines that keep a bank's payments flowing.

text:
The National Settlement Service, known as NSS, is the service operated by the Federal Reserve Banks that settles the money behind ACH payments in the United States. ACH files move payment instructions between banks, but those are only promises to pay until settlement happens. NSS is where the actual movement of funds between banks takes place, by debiting and crediting the reserve accounts banks hold at the Federal Reserve.

An ACH payment starts with the Originating Depository Financial Institution, the ODFI, sending a file of payment entries to an ACH operator. There are two ACH operators in the US: FedACH, run by the Federal Reserve, and the Electronic Payments Network, known as EPN, run by The Clearing House. The operator sorts the entries and delivers them to the Receiving Depository Financial Institution, the RDFI, which credits or debits its customer's account. The customer-facing side is done, but the banks still owe each other money, and that interbank obligation is what NSS settles.

Settlement works on net positions, not on individual payments. For each settlement cycle, the operator totals what each bank sent and received and works out a single net position per bank: a net debit if the bank owes money overall, or a net credit if money is owed to it. The operator then sends a settlement file to NSS containing one net entry per bank. NSS posts those entries to the banks' Federal Reserve master accounts. A net debit bank is debited, a net credit bank is credited, and because every debit has a matching credit, the system balances. The individual entries, which may number in the millions, are never posted one by one. Only the net position moves.

Timing matters because settlement does not happen at the same moment as the file exchange. ACH operates on settlement windows during the business day. Same-day ACH has several windows, so a file sent in the morning can settle the same day, while later files settle in a later same-day window or the next business day. Standard next-day ACH settles on the next business day. The RDFI typically makes funds available based on the settlement date, so a payment can show as received before the interbank money has moved. That gap is normal, and it is one reason banks manage their settlement positions carefully.

Settlement through NSS is final once posted. When NSS debits a bank's reserve account, that debit is a final transfer of central bank money, the safest form of settlement available. This finality is what makes ACH work: once settlement has happened, the receiving bank knows the money is genuinely its. Any later problem, such as a return or a reversal, is handled as a new ACH entry in a later cycle, not by undoing the settlement.

What happens if a bank cannot settle? A bank must have enough money in its Federal Reserve account, or access to intraday credit, to cover its net debit position. Banks monitor their positions through the day and manage liquidity so settlement entries clear. If an account cannot fund a settlement debit, the entry may be held, the bank is contacted to fund its account, and the ACH operator is informed. This is rare for a solvent bank, which holds balances and has access to daylight overdraft facilities, but it is a real operational risk. A bank that repeatedly struggles to fund settlement faces supervisory attention, because inability to settle signals serious liquidity trouble.

For a payments professional, the practical point is this: ACH is a deferred net settlement system, not a real-time gross settlement system like Fedwire. Payment instructions, customer credits, and interbank settlement are three separate events at different times. NSS is the final step that converts instructions into central bank money, and its netting design is what lets ACH process huge volumes cheaply. When you investigate a delayed payment, the answer usually lies in which settlement window the file fell into and whether the net position was funded, not in the payment instruction itself.

text:
Phixius is an information exchange platform operated by Nacha, the organisation that governs the ACH network in the United States. It does not move money. It moves information about payments between financial institutions and other participants, so a bank can check the facts about an account or a payment before sending an ACH entry. In simple terms, Phixius lets banks ask each other questions and get trusted answers, instead of sending a payment blind.

The problem is an old one. An ACH payment carries an account number and a routing number, but the originating bank cannot tell whether that account is open, belongs to the person named, or can receive that type of payment. A wrong account number, a closed account, or a name mismatch all produce a return, costing both banks time and money and delaying the payment. Fraud adds a further risk, since a fraudster with stolen account details can set up debits the victim never authorised. Phixius addresses both problems by letting banks validate information before sending.

The core use case is account validation. Before originating an ACH payment, a bank or its processor can ask Phixius to confirm the status of an account with the receiving bank. The receiving bank responds with information such as whether the account is open, whether it is the type of account claimed, and whether the account holder information matches. The exact data shared depends on the service and permissions in place, but the principle is the same: the originating bank gets a reliable answer from the institution holding the account, rather than relying on the details supplied by the originator alone.

Phixius also carries payment information. Beyond validation, it supports exchanging information connected to a payment, such as remittance detail that helps the receiving bank apply the payment correctly. This matters most in business to business payments, where the receiver needs to know which invoice a payment relates to. A standard platform avoids the errors of passing payment detail through informal channels or leaving it out entirely.

The flow end to end looks like this. First, an originator gives its bank the payment details, including the receiver's account and routing numbers. Second, the originating bank or its service provider sends a validation request through Phixius to the receiving bank. Third, the receiving bank checks the account and returns a response, typically within seconds. Fourth, the originating bank decides what to do: send the payment, correct the details and ask again, or hold the payment and contact the originator. Fifth, if everything checks out, the ACH entry is sent through the normal operator channels and settles through the National Settlement Service. Phixius sits before the payment, not inside it.

Phixius works on a hub model. A bank connects once to the platform, through its own systems or a service provider, and the platform routes each request to the right institution and returns the answer. With thousands of institutions in the US ACH network, point to point connections between all of them would be unworkable.

If the validation step fails, the payment does not go out, and that is the point. A failed validation might mean the account is closed, the account number does not exist, or the details do not match. In each case the originating bank can stop the payment before it becomes a return, correct the details, and resend. That is cheaper and faster than sending the payment, waiting for a return, and starting over. A fraudster testing stolen account details gets a rejection rather than a successful debit.

For a payments professional, Phixius matters because it attacks the two most expensive problems in ACH operations: returns and fraud. Every return generates exception handling, customer contact, and rework, and Nacha monitors return rates, with high rates attracting attention. Validating accounts before sending cuts return rates, improves the customer experience, and shrinks the window for fraud. Phixius does not replace the ACH network or the settlement system. It sits alongside them as the information layer that makes the money movement layer more reliable, and its value grows as more institutions participate, since a validation service is only as useful as the accounts it can check.

text:
Lynx is Canada's high value payment system and its real time gross settlement system, known as an RTGS. It is operated by Payments Canada, and settlement takes place in accounts at the Bank of Canada, so payments settle in central bank money. When a Canadian bank must pay another bank a large amount that must be final the same day, it normally goes through Lynx. Typical uses are interbank funding, securities settlement, foreign exchange settlement, and large corporate payments. It replaced the Large Value Transfer System, known as LVTS.

Under LVTS, many payments settled on a deferred net basis, with loss sharing arrangements and heavy reliance on collateral and bilateral credit limits. Exposures could build up during the day before final settlement. Lynx moves core settlement to real time gross settlement. Each payment is settled individually, in full, and in central bank money, as soon as it is processed and the paying bank has enough funds. Once settled, the payment is final and irrevocable.

Only direct participants hold a settlement account at the Bank of Canada and send payments directly into Lynx. Direct participants are mainly banks and other financial institutions that meet eligibility criteria set by Payments Canada and the Bank of Canada, including prudential standing, operational capability, and the ability to pledge eligible collateral. To join, an institution applies to Payments Canada, completes connection and testing, puts collateral arrangements in place, and opens its settlement account at the Bank of Canada. Smaller institutions reach Lynx indirectly, through a direct participant acting as settlement agent. Their payments are submitted by the agent bank, settlement takes place in the agent bank's account, and the underlying customer is settled separately on the agent bank's books.

A payment starts in the sending bank, which receives an instruction from its customer, for example a corporation paying a supplier or a bank settling a securities deal. The sending bank checks the instruction, verifies the account and the amount, and carries out sanctions, fraud, and anti money laundering controls. It checks that it has enough funds or available collateral backed liquidity in its Bank of Canada settlement account. It then sends a payment message into Lynx, carrying payer, payee, amount, value date, and reference. Lynx validates the message and the participant's authority to send it. If the checks pass and funds are available, the Bank of Canada debits the sender's settlement account and credits the receiver's account at the same moment, and Lynx confirms settlement to both sides.

Lynx uses ISO 20022 messages. The customer starts the chain with an instruction to its own bank, carried in a pain.001 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation message when sent electronically. The sending bank sends a customer payment into Lynx in a pacs.008 Customer Credit Transfer message, sent by the sending bank to Lynx for onward settlement to the receiving bank. A payment between banks for their own account, such as an interbank loan repayment, is carried in a pacs.009 Financial Institution Credit Transfer message, sent by the sending bank. Lynx replies with a pacs.002 Payment Status Report, sent by Lynx to the sending bank to confirm settlement, queuing, or rejection. If a payment must be returned, the receiving bank sends a pacs.004 Payment Return message. Banks reconcile with camt.052 and camt.053 account messages from the Bank of Canada.

Take a worked example. A corporate customer of Bank A pays CAD 25 million to a supplier who banks with Bank B. At Bank A, the entries are a debit of CAD 25 million to the corporate customer's account and a credit of CAD 25 million to Bank A's settlement account at the Bank of Canada. At the Bank of Canada, settlement is a debit of CAD 25 million to Bank A's settlement account and a credit of CAD 25 million to Bank B's settlement account, made at the same moment. At Bank B, the entries are a debit of CAD 25 million to Bank B's settlement account and a credit of CAD 25 million to the supplier's account.

If funds are not available, Lynx queues the payment and manages it through its settlement mechanisms. The Urgent Payment Mechanism, known as UPM, is for payments that must settle now, such as a payment linked to a securities settlement, and it gives these payments priority over other queued payments. For example, Bank A owes CAD 40 million for a securities purchase at a fixed time, and sends it through UPM so it settles ahead of routine queued payments. The Liquidity Saving Mechanism, known as LSM, is for payments where a short delay is acceptable, and it looks for offsetting payments. For example, Bank A owes Bank B CAD 100 million and Bank B owes Bank A CAD 80 million. With LSM offsetting, the two payments settle together and Bank A needs only CAD 20 million of net liquidity. The Reserved Collateral Mechanism, known as RCM, is a dedicated mechanism used only for payments to CDS Clearing and Depository Services Inc., settling obligations between the Bank of Canada and a participant. It is not a general tool for reserving collateral for any critical payment. The Real Time Mechanism, known as RTM, is the real time gross settlement path itself.

Banks manage Lynx liquidity actively through the day. They start with the balance in their Bank of Canada settlement account, add expected incoming Lynx payments, and plan outgoing payments against that forecast. They can add liquidity by pledging eligible collateral and by borrowing through Bank of Canada facilities where eligible. Incoming payments are the main source of intraday funds, so a delay in one large incoming payment can leave a bank short, and operations teams watch the queue and the account balance continuously. A bank that sees a shortfall can reprioritise its queue, move a payment to LSM, or bring in funds from its treasury desk.

Lynx operates during the Canadian business day, with opening and closing times and cut off times set by the operator and published in the system rules. Customer payments normally have an earlier cut off than payments between banks for their own account, because the receiving bank needs time to credit its customer. A payment submitted after its cut off is normally held for the next operating day, and unsettled queued payments expire or are returned under the system rules. Exact clock times are set by the operator and can change, so teams work from the published schedule for the day. If liquidity is short, a payment stays queued and Lynx retries it as new funds arrive. If the message has a format error, a wrong account, a sanctions hit, or a missing field, Lynx rejects it and the sending bank must correct and resend it. If a system fails, banks follow contingency procedures and notify Payments Canada and the Bank of Canada. In every case, a payment is not settled until Lynx confirms it, and a queued payment is not a paid payment.

title: CIPS: China's cross-border payment system
text:
CIPS, the Cross Border Interbank Payment System, is China's system for clearing and settling cross border payments in renminbi, known as RMB or CNY. It is operated by Cross Border Interbank Payment System Co., Ltd., based in Shanghai, under the supervision of the People's Bank of China. In simple terms, CIPS lets a bank outside China pay a bank inside China in RMB, or a Chinese bank pay a bank abroad in RMB, through a dedicated RMB system rather than only through correspondent banking. It supports the international use of the renminbi.

China built CIPS for practical reasons. Cross border RMB trade was growing, and exporters, importers, and investors needed a reliable, standardised way to pay in RMB across borders. Relying only on correspondent banks meant a payment could pass through several intermediaries, each adding time, cost, and a point of failure. China also wanted a system it could supervise directly, with its own operating hours, message standards, and settlement arrangements, so RMB payments would not depend entirely on systems run in other countries or on other currencies. CIPS was therefore designed for RMB only, open to banks in China and abroad, to support trade, investment, and financial market transactions.

CIPS has two types of participant. Direct participants hold a settlement account with CIPS and settle directly through the system. They are typically large banks, including Chinese banks and overseas branches or subsidiaries of foreign banks admitted as direct participants. Indirect participants do not hold a settlement account of their own. They access CIPS through a direct participant, which acts as their clearing bank and submits and receives payments on their behalf. This two tier model lets smaller banks use CIPS without a direct connection, while keeping settlement risk with supervised direct participants.

A bank that wants to join as a direct participant applies to the CIPS operator, meets the eligibility and technical requirements, completes connection and testing, and opens and funds its settlement account. A bank that wants to join as an indirect participant instead signs an agreement with a direct participant, which agrees to act as its clearing bank. The indirect participant needs a RMB account relationship with that clearing bank, agreed cut off times and message formats, and its own sanctions and anti money laundering controls, because the clearing bank will still screen the payments it submits. The two banks also agree how returns, queries, and fees are handled, since the indirect participant has no direct relationship with the CIPS operator.

A CIPS payment starts with a customer instruction, for example a European importer paying a Chinese supplier in RMB. The customer's bank checks the instruction, carries out sanctions, anti money laundering, and fraud screening, and confirms the account details. The sending bank then sends a payment message into CIPS, using ISO 20022 messaging standards. CIPS validates the message, checks that the sending participant has enough funds or an approved funding arrangement, and processes the payment for clearing and settlement. Clearing means matching and validating the payment, while settlement means moving the RMB between participant accounts. Once settlement is complete, CIPS confirms to both banks, and the receiving bank credits its customer.

CIPS messages follow ISO 20022. The customer's instruction to its own bank is carried in a pain.001 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation message when sent electronically. The sending bank sends the payment into CIPS in a pacs.008 Customer Credit Transfer message for a customer payment, or a pacs.009 Financial Institution Credit Transfer message for a bank to bank payment. CIPS sends a pacs.002 Payment Status Report back to the sending participant to confirm settlement, queuing, or rejection, so the sending bank knows whether the payment is final. If the payment must be sent back, the receiving participant sends a pacs.004 Payment Return message. Banks also use camt.052 and camt.053 account messages to reconcile their CIPS settlement account.

Take a worked example. A European importer who banks with Bank A in Europe pays RMB 10 million to a Chinese supplier who banks with Bank B in China. At Bank A, the entries are a debit of RMB 10 million to the importer's account and a credit of RMB 10 million to Bank A's CIPS settlement account. At CIPS, settlement is a debit of RMB 10 million to Bank A's settlement account and a credit of RMB 10 million to Bank B's settlement account, made when the payment settles. At Bank B, the entries are a debit of RMB 10 million to Bank B's CIPS settlement account and a credit of RMB 10 million to the supplier's account. If the importer banks with an indirect participant, its clearing bank is the direct participant debited at CIPS, and the two settle separately on their own books.

Liquidity management is central to CIPS because a participant can only settle payments it can fund. A direct participant funds its CIPS settlement account from its RMB balances, normally by moving RMB into the account from its onshore RMB account through China's domestic payment arrangements, and by receiving incoming CIPS payments during the day. Operations teams forecast outgoing payments, watch the balance and the queue, and top up the account before it runs low. When funds are short, CIPS queues the payment and retries it as new funds arrive, so a payment can sit waiting for an incoming payment or a top up. If funds still have not arrived by the cut off, the payment is rejected or held for the next operating day under the system rules, and the sending bank must tell its customer and agree new timing.

CIPS operates during published operating hours set by the operator, with cut off times for different types of payment. Customer payments normally have an earlier cut off than payments between banks, and payments that depend on a linked domestic leg or on another market's hours may have their own cut off. A payment submitted after its cut off is normally held for the next operating day, and queued payments that have not settled by the end of the operating day are dealt with under the system rules. Exact clock times are set by the operator and can change, so teams work from the published schedule for the day. CIPS must not be confused with SWIFT or with CNAPS. SWIFT is a messaging network that carries instructions but does not move money or settle a payment, while CIPS both processes the instruction and settles the RMB. CNAPS is China's domestic RMB system. If a CIPS payment fails, the cause decides the handling. A format error means CIPS returns it for correction and resending. Insufficient funds means it may be queued until liquidity arrives, or rejected at the cut off. A sanctions stop means it is held for review. Wrong beneficiary details mean the receiving bank returns it, and the sending bank must correct the details and send a new payment. In every case, the payment is not final until CIPS confirms settlement.

title: CHATS: Hong Kong's clearing house automated transfer system
text:
CHATS, the Clearing House Automated Transfer System, is Hong Kong's real time gross settlement system, known as an RTGS. It is operated under the oversight of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, known as the HKMA, Hong Kong's central banking institution. In simple terms, CHATS is how banks in Hong Kong settle large value, time critical payments between each other in central bank money, with each payment settled individually and in full as soon as it is processed.

What makes CHATS unusual is that it settles in more than one currency. The Hong Kong dollar CHATS is the core system for HKD payments. There are also separate CHATS systems for United States dollars, euros, and renminbi. Each currency has its own settlement accounts and arrangements, but all run on the same RTGS principle. A bank can pay another bank in USD through USD CHATS, for example to settle a foreign exchange deal, and the same applies to EUR CHATS and RMB CHATS. This reflects Hong Kong's role as an international financial centre, where banks routinely move several currencies in a day.

Settlement in CHATS takes place in settlement accounts held for that currency. For HKD, banks hold settlement accounts with the HKMA, and a payment settles by moving HKD from the sending bank's HKMA settlement account to the receiving bank's HKMA settlement account, so it settles in central bank money. For the other currencies, the HKMA appoints a settlement institution for each currency, and banks hold settlement accounts with that institution for that currency. A USD payment therefore settles in the banks' USD accounts with the USD settlement institution, and likewise for EUR and RMB. Each currency's accounts are separate, so a bank must fund each currency account on its own.

A CHATS payment starts in the sending bank. A customer instruction arrives, for example a corporation paying a supplier, a bank settling a securities transaction, or a bank meeting a foreign exchange obligation. The sending bank checks the instruction, carries out sanctions, anti money laundering, and fraud checks, and confirms it has enough funds in its settlement account for that currency. It then sends a payment message into CHATS. CHATS validates the message and checks the sending bank's settlement account. If funds are available, the payment settles immediately. The sending bank's account is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited at the same moment, and both banks receive a confirmation.

CHATS payments use ISO 20022 messages. The customer's instruction to its own bank is carried in a pain.001 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation message when sent electronically. The sending bank sends the payment into CHATS in a pacs.008 Customer Credit Transfer message when the payment is for a customer, and in a pacs.009 Financial Institution Credit Transfer message when the payment is between banks for their own account. CHATS sends a pacs.002 Payment Status Report back to the sending bank to confirm settlement, queuing, or rejection. If the payment must be sent back, the receiving bank sends a pacs.004 Payment Return message. Banks reconcile each currency account with camt.052 and camt.053 account messages.

Take a worked example in HKD. A corporate customer of Bank A pays HKD 50 million to a supplier who banks with Bank B. At Bank A, the entries are a debit of HKD 50 million to the corporate customer's account and a credit of HKD 50 million to Bank A's HKD settlement account with the HKMA. At the HKMA, settlement is a debit of HKD 50 million to Bank A's settlement account and a credit of HKD 50 million to Bank B's settlement account, made at the same moment. At Bank B, the entries are a debit of HKD 50 million to Bank B's HKD settlement account and a credit of HKD 50 million to the supplier's account. The same pattern applies in USD, EUR, or RMB, with settlement accounts at that currency's settlement institution.

If funds are not available, the payment is queued. CHATS manages the queue with liquidity saving features, including looking for payments that can be offset against each other, so two banks that owe each other can settle with less cash. For example, if Bank A owes Bank B HKD 60 million and Bank B owes Bank A HKD 45 million, offsetting lets the two payments settle together with only HKD 15 million of net liquidity from Bank A. Banks can reprioritise payments in the queue, inject liquidity, or wait for incoming payments. HKD liquidity can come from the bank's HKMA balance, incoming CHATS payments, or HKMA intraday facilities for eligible banks against eligible collateral. USD, EUR, and RMB liquidity must be funded separately in each currency.

The four currency systems differ in more than the currency code. HKD CHATS is the core domestic system, settles in accounts at the HKMA, and supports the widest range of local payments, including government payments, securities settlement, and interbank funding. USD CHATS settles in USD through its settlement institution, and is heavily used for foreign exchange settlement and trade payments, including payment versus payment links. EUR CHATS works the same way in euros, with a smaller volume and a focus on trade and foreign exchange. RMB CHATS settles RMB in Hong Kong and connects with mainland payment infrastructure so RMB can move onward into China. Operating hours and cut off times also differ by currency, because each system follows its own schedule and the hours of the markets it links to.

CHATS also links to other systems. In a payment versus payment link, known as PvP, the two legs of a foreign exchange deal settle together, so one currency is released only if the other is also released. This removes Herstatt risk, the risk that one side pays and the other fails. In a delivery versus payment link, known as DvP, a CHATS payment is linked to a securities transfer, so cash moves only if the securities move, and securities move only if the cash moves. Settlement finality is central to CHATS. Once a payment has settled, it is final and irrevocable. The receiving bank has the money in central bank money, and the sending bank cannot cancel or reverse it through the system. This finality is protected by Hong Kong law, including the Clearing and Settlement Systems Ordinance. Each currency CHATS has its own operating hours and cut off times, set by the operator and published in the system rules. A payment submitted after the cut off is normally held for the next operating day. A compliance stop means it is held for review. Wrong beneficiary details mean the receiving bank returns it. A system outage means banks follow contingency procedures and the HKMA coordinates the response, which may include extended hours. In all cases, a payment is not paid until CHATS confirms settlement.

text:
FCDPS, the Foreign Currency Domestic Payment System, is China's system for clearing and settling payments in foreign currencies between banks inside China. In simple terms, it lets a bank in Shanghai pay a bank in Beijing in United States dollars, euros or another foreign currency, without the payment having to leave China or pass through a chain of correspondent banks abroad. It is a domestic system, but the money it moves is not renminbi. It is foreign currency, held and settled inside China, for domestic use.

China needs this system because its economy uses foreign currency inside the country as well as across its borders. A Chinese exporter may hold dollars in a domestic account. A Chinese importer may need to pay a domestic supplier in dollars. A bank may need to settle a foreign currency loan, a foreign currency deposit, or a foreign currency trade between two domestic parties. Before a dedicated domestic system existed, those payments often had to be routed through correspondent banks, sometimes outside China, even though both payer and payee were inside China. That added time, cost and operational risk, and made the payment dependent on banks and cut offs abroad. FCDPS was created to keep those domestic foreign currency payments inside China, with one set of rules, one operating day and one settlement arrangement.

FCDPS is operated as part of China's payment system infrastructure under the supervision of the People's Bank of China, with the China Foreign Exchange Trade System involved in its operation. Participants are banks operating in China that are authorised to handle foreign currency business, including large Chinese commercial banks, joint stock banks, city commercial banks and Chinese branches of foreign banks, where they meet the requirements. Each participant holds settlement accounts for the foreign currencies it uses, and must meet eligibility, technical and risk management standards. Smaller banks that are not direct participants can access the system through a direct participant, in the same two tier pattern used by many other payment systems.

A payment starts with a customer instruction in a foreign currency, for example a company in Shenzhen paying a supplier in Guangzhou in United States dollars. The sending bank checks the instruction, checks that the customer holds enough of that currency, and carries out sanctions, anti money laundering, foreign exchange and fraud checks. Chinese foreign exchange rules matter here, because even a domestic payment in a foreign currency is subject to the reporting and control rules for foreign currency business. The bank then sends a payment message into FCDPS. The system validates the message, checks the sending bank's settlement account for that currency, and processes the payment for clearing and settlement. Clearing means validating and preparing the payment. Settlement means moving the foreign currency from the sending bank's account to the receiving bank's account. Once settlement is complete, FCDPS confirms to both banks, and the receiving bank credits its customer's foreign currency account.

The difference between FCDPS and CIPS is the first thing to get clear, because the names are easily confused. FCDPS is domestic and it handles foreign currency. CIPS is cross border and it handles renminbi. A payment through FCDPS has both payer and payee inside China, and the currency is a foreign currency such as USD or EUR. A payment through CIPS crosses the border, and the currency is RMB. A payment through CNAPS, China's domestic RMB system, has both parties inside China and the currency is RMB. If you can place a payment on those two axes, domestic versus cross border, and RMB versus foreign currency, you can decide which system is in the path. If a payment fails, the handling is familiar. A format error means correction and resending. Insufficient funds means queuing or rejection at the cut off. A compliance stop means review. Wrong beneficiary details mean a return. In every case, the payment is not final until FCDPS confirms settlement. Together, CNAPS handles domestic RMB, CIPS handles cross border RMB, and FCDPS handles domestic foreign currency, and that trio covers the main combinations a bank will meet in China.

text:
A smart contract is a program stored on a distributed ledger that moves money, or another digital asset, automatically when defined conditions are met. It is code with an if then structure. If the delivery is confirmed, then release the payment. If the deadline passes without delivery, then return the funds to the buyer. Once the code is deployed and the funds are locked in the contract, no person needs to press a button to make the payment happen, and no person can change the outcome by forgetting or refusing, unless the code itself allows a change.

A buyer and a seller agree the terms first, for example the price, the goods, the delivery date and the evidence that proves delivery. Those terms are then written as code. The buyer sends funds into the contract, and the contract locks them. When the agreed event happens, the contract checks its conditions and executes. If the conditions are met, it moves the funds to the seller. If they are not met by the deadline, it moves the funds back to the buyer. Suppose a buyer agrees to pay 50,000 for equipment from a seller, with delivery due in ten days. The buyer sends 50,000 into a smart contract. A delivery confirmation is recorded, and the contract checks that it matches the agreed terms, for example the correct order number, the correct quantity and a date on or before the deadline. If the check passes, the contract releases 50,000 to the seller.

A missed deadline is a designed outcome, not an error. The contract must have a clear rule for what happens when time runs out, often called a timeout or an expiry. When the deadline passes, the contract changes its state from waiting to expired, and the return of funds is triggered. That is why the evidence, the timing and the exact definition of delivery must be written carefully before deployment. A dispute state is the middle path between automatic release and automatic return. Some contracts allow a party to raise a dispute before the deadline, for example if the goods are damaged, incomplete or not as described. When a dispute is raised, the contract moves into a dispute state and stops the automatic release. The funds stay locked while the dispute is resolved.

An arbitrator is a named person or organisation who can decide the outcome in a dispute state. The arbitrator might be a bank, a platform operator, a trade body or a trusted third party named in the agreement. The arbitrator reviews the evidence, often off the ledger, and then sends a decision to the contract, for example release in full to the seller, return in full to the buyer, or split the funds between them. The contract then executes that decision. Funds can be locked if there is no fallback. If the contract has no rule for what happens when an expected event never arrives, and no dispute path and no arbitrator, the funds can sit in the contract forever, with no person able to move them. The buyer cannot get a refund, the seller cannot get paid, and the money is effectively frozen. A well written contract always includes a fallback: a deadline, a return path, a dispute state, or a named party who can trigger a resolution.

To learn a real world fact, such as whether goods were delivered, what the price of a currency was at a certain time, or whether a flight landed late, it needs an oracle. An oracle is a service or a mechanism that brings an outside fact onto the ledger so the contract can use it. An oracle might be a single data provider, a group of providers who vote, a bank system, a logistics system, or a sensor that reports a reading. The oracle sends a signed message to the ledger, and the contract reads that message as its input. Who runs the oracle matters as much as the code itself, because the contract will act on whatever the oracle says. When the oracle is wrong or delayed, the contract can make the wrong payment. If the oracle reports that delivery has happened when it has not, the contract will release the funds to the seller even though the buyer has received nothing. Good designs reduce this risk by using several independent oracles and requiring agreement, by using a trusted source both parties accept, by allowing a challenge period before the funds move, or by adding a dispute state that can pause the release.

First the parties agree the terms in plain language: the amount, the asset, the deadline, the delivery evidence, the dispute process and the fallback. Second a developer writes the code to match those terms exactly, and the parties review the code and the plain language terms side by side to check they match. Third the code is tested on a test network with small amounts and with failure cases, including late delivery, wrong evidence, a missing oracle feed and a dispute. Fourth the contract is deployed to the ledger, which means the code is stored on the ledger and given an address. Fifth the buyer sends funds to that address and the contract locks them. Sixth the oracle feeds the fact, for example the delivery confirmation, onto the ledger. Seventh the contract checks the fact against its rules. Eighth the contract executes: it releases the funds to the seller, returns them to the buyer, or moves into dispute.

Smart contracts run on several named platforms. Ethereum is the best known platform for smart contracts, and its contract language is widely used for tokens, escrow, lending and decentralised finance. Hyperledger Fabric supports smart contracts, called chaincode, in permissioned business networks, where the contract runs between identified banks or companies. Corda supports contracts between known parties, with the contract logic shared only with those who need to see it, which fits regulated payments and trade finance. When the buyer funds the contract, the buyer records: debit escrow receivable or funds held in smart contract 50,000, credit bank or token account 50,000. When the delivery is confirmed and the contract releases the funds, the ledger shows: debit smart contract escrow account 50,000, credit seller account 50,000. The buyer then records: debit equipment or purchases 50,000, credit escrow receivable 50,000. The seller records: debit bank or token account 50,000, credit sales revenue 50,000. If the contract returns the funds on a missed deadline, the ledger shows: debit smart contract escrow account 50,000, credit buyer account 50,000, and the buyer reverses the escrow entry.

text:
Distributed ledger technology, often shortened to DLT, is a way for several organisations to keep one shared record of transactions instead of each organisation keeping its own separate record and then reconciling the differences later. Each participant holds a copy of the same ledger, and new entries are added only when the participants agree, using agreed rules, that the entry is valid. A shared ledger aims to make that record consistent for everyone at the same time, so a payer, a payee and their banks do not end up with different versions of the same payment.

A blockchain is one type of distributed ledger, but the two terms are not the same. A distributed ledger is the general idea of a shared, replicated record. A blockchain is a specific way of organising that record, where transactions are grouped into blocks and each block is linked to the previous block, usually with a cryptographic fingerprint. Some distributed ledgers do not use blocks at all. A node is a computer that holds a copy of the ledger and can send and receive messages about new transactions. A validator is a node, or a participant operating a node, that takes part in the formal process of checking and approving new entries. Not every node is a validator. In a bank payment network, a validator might be a bank, a central bank, a market infrastructure operator, or another trusted participant that has been admitted to the network.

A permissioned ledger is a ledger where participants must be identified and approved before they can join, read, or write. A permissionless ledger is a ledger where anyone can join, usually without revealing a real world identity, and can in principle become a validator. Most payment use cases in regulated finance use permissioned ledgers, because banks must know their customers, apply sanctions screening, and be able to identify who made a payment if something goes wrong. A permissionless ledger gives openness and resistance to control by any single party, but it makes identity checks, privacy and legal accountability much harder.

Consensus is the process by which validators agree that a transaction is valid and should be added to the ledger. In proof of work, validators, often called miners, compete to solve a difficult mathematical puzzle. This is expensive because it uses a large amount of computing power and electricity, and settlement is relatively slow, often taking minutes and several blocks. In proof of stake, validators are chosen in part according to how much of the network asset they hold and have locked up as a stake, which they can lose if they act dishonestly. This uses far less energy and can settle faster, but it raises questions about concentration, because the largest holders have the most influence. Byzantine fault tolerance voting is a third model, widely used in permissioned payment ledgers. Validators exchange votes and agree on the order of transactions when a defined majority, often two thirds, agrees. This is fast and energy efficient, it can settle in seconds, and it can tolerate a minority of faulty or dishonest validators, but it works best when the number of validators is limited and known in advance.

Finality is the point at which a payment on the ledger can be treated as irreversible and settled. On some ledgers finality is probabilistic. A transaction becomes more certain as more blocks are added after it, because it becomes harder to rewrite history, but there is no single moment when the rules say it can never be reversed. On other ledgers finality is deterministic. Once the validators have voted and the transaction is committed, the rules say it is final, and it will not be reversed except through a new correcting transaction. Banks and market infrastructures usually prefer deterministic finality, because payment operations, liquidity management and legal certainty depend on knowing exactly when a payment has settled.

Corda is a distributed ledger designed for regulated financial institutions. It shares the details of a transaction only with the parties involved and those who need to see it, which fits banking privacy. Corda is used for interbank payments, trade finance, syndicated lending and the exchange of digital assets between known counterparties. Hyperledger Fabric is an open source permissioned ledger framework used to build private business networks. Fabric is used for payment and settlement pilots, trade finance, and reconciliation between banks and corporates. Ethereum is a public permissionless ledger that supports smart contracts and tokens, and it is widely used for digital assets, stablecoins and decentralised finance. A signed transaction follows a clear sequence. The payer creates a payment instruction, signs it with a private key, and sends it to the network. Validators check the signature and the balance, agree on the order, and include it in the ledger. Each node then updates its copy, so the payer balance falls and the payee balance rises in every copy at the same time.

Suppose a corporate called Acme holds tokenised money on a permissioned ledger and pays 100,000 to a supplier called Beta. Before the payment, the ledger shows Acme with 250,000 and Beta with 50,000. Acme signs the payment, the validators check the signature and the balance, agree, and commit the entry. The ledger now shows Acme with 150,000 and Beta with 150,000. The entries are: debit Acme token account 100,000, credit Beta token account 100,000. Tokenised money is a digital representation of a claim, not new money by itself. Cross border payment and delivery versus payment show why banks study DLT. Today a cross border payment often passes through correspondent banks, each keeping its own record, which adds time, cost and reconciliation breaks. On a shared ledger the banks could see the same payment state, so the payment could move in fewer steps. Delivery versus payment, often called DvP, is the exchange of an asset for payment so that one side does not settle without the other. On a ledger this can be an atomic exchange: the asset moves to the buyer and the money moves to the seller in the same ledger update, or neither moves. If Beta provides an incorrect ledger address, or Acme does not have enough balance when the transaction is checked, the transaction is not committed and the ledger does not change. If validators cannot reach the required majority, new transactions pause until agreement is restored. If Acme loses the private key that controls its token account, it may not be able to sign a payment at all, even though the ledger still shows the balance.
