text:
A crypto payment end to end is a payment that starts as fiat money in a bank account, becomes a crypto asset, moves on a blockchain, and then becomes fiat money again in another bank account. The full journey has four stages: the on-ramp, where fiat is exchanged for crypto; the wallet transfer, where the crypto moves from the payer to the payee; the on-chain confirmation, where the network agrees the transfer is final; and the off-ramp, where the crypto is exchanged back into fiat. Each stage has its own accounts, its own risks and its own reconciliation, and a failure at any stage can leave the payment stuck, lost or worth less than expected.

The on-ramp is the purchase of crypto with fiat money. The payer sends fiat to a crypto exchange or a broker, usually by bank transfer, card or another payment method supported by the exchange. The exchange receives the fiat, checks the identity of the payer, and then credits the payer with crypto at the agreed exchange rate, after deducting any fee. The accounting at the payer side is: debit crypto asset held at exchange, credit bank account, for the fiat amount paid.

The wallet is where crypto is held and controlled, and the key idea is custody. It holds the private keys that control crypto recorded on the blockchain. A hot wallet is a wallet connected to the internet, for example an exchange wallet, a mobile app or a browser wallet. It is convenient and fast, but it is exposed to online attack, phishing and malware. A cold wallet is a wallet kept offline, for example a hardware device or a paper record of the keys, disconnected from the internet until it is needed. It is much harder to attack remotely, but it is slower to use and it can be lost or damaged. In custodial custody, the exchange or a custodian holds the keys on behalf of the customer. In self custody, the customer holds the keys directly.

The wallet debit is the moment the payer instructs the transfer. The payer enters the payee wallet address, the amount of crypto, and the fee to pay to the network. The wallet signs the transaction with the payer private key. The signed transaction is broadcast to the network. The payee wallet address is a long string of characters, and it must be copied exactly. The payer must therefore check the address, the network, and the asset type before signing. Sending the right asset on the wrong network, or the wrong asset to an address that expects another asset, can make the funds unrecoverable.

On-chain confirmation is the process by which the network agrees the transfer is valid and records it. Validators or miners check the signature, check that the payer has enough balance, and include the transaction in a block. The first block that includes the transaction is the first confirmation. Each block added after it is another confirmation. Finality on chain means the point at which the payment is treated as settled and unlikely to be reversed. On some networks finality is probabilistic, and the payee waits for a number of confirmations, often six or more depending on the network and the value, before treating the payment as good. On other networks finality is deterministic, and the transaction is final once the validators have voted and committed it. The payee should not release goods, services or onward funds until the agreed number of confirmations has been reached. The off-ramp is the conversion of crypto back into fiat money. The payee sends the crypto to an exchange or a broker, sells it at the current rate, and asks for the fiat proceeds to be paid to a bank account. The off-ramp rate may be different from the on-ramp rate, because time has passed and the crypto price has moved.

Reconciliation is the matching of the on-chain transaction to the bank ledger. The payer must match the fiat debit at the on-ramp to the crypto purchase, the crypto purchase to the wallet transfer, and the wallet transfer to the on-chain transaction record. The payee must match the on-chain receipt to the crypto sale at the off-ramp, and the crypto sale to the fiat credit in the bank account. Each leg has a different reference: a bank transaction reference, an exchange order number, a wallet transaction hash, and a bank credit reference. Operations must link those four references into one payment record. Failure handling depends on where the failure happens. A wrong address is the most serious failure. If crypto is sent to an address that belongs to the wrong person, the transfer will confirm and there is usually no way to recall it. If crypto is sent to an address on the wrong network, the funds may be lost permanently. An insufficient fee is a different failure. If the payer sets the network fee too low, validators may ignore the transaction, and it can sit unconfirmed for hours or drop out of the queue. The payer may then need to resubmit with a higher fee. An exchange failure is a third case. If the exchange is down, freezes withdrawals, or fails during the on-ramp or off-ramp, the fiat or the crypto can be stuck inside the exchange until the exchange recovers.

Suppose a payer wants to pay the equivalent of 100,000 rupees. At the on-ramp, the payer sends 100,000 rupees to an exchange and receives crypto worth 99,000 rupees after fees and the exchange rate. The payer sends that crypto to the payee wallet, paying a network fee worth 500 rupees, so the payee receives crypto worth 98,500 rupees. At the off-ramp, the payee sells the crypto and receives 97,500 rupees in the bank account after fees and a small price fall. The payer spent 100,000, the payee received 97,500, and 2,500 was lost to fees and price movement. The entries are: payer debit crypto asset 99,000, debit exchange fees 1,000, and credit bank 100,000 at the on-ramp. When the payer sends the crypto, the send is: debit payment to payee 98,500, debit network fee expense 500, credit crypto asset 99,000. Payee debit crypto asset 98,500 on receipt, credit revenue (or amount payable) 98,500; payee debit bank 97,500 and debit loss on sale 1,000, credit crypto asset 98,500 at the off-ramp. Check the payee address character by character, and use a small test payment first for a new payee or a large amount. Set a fee that will get the transaction confirmed in the time the business needs. Agree in advance who bears the price movement and the fees at each stage. Record the transaction hash, the exchange order numbers and the bank references together. Keep the private keys secure, with a backup in a safe place, and know whether custody is with the exchange or with the customer.

A central bank digital currency, or CBDC, is digital money issued by a central bank. A domestic retail CBDC payment is a payment between people or businesses inside one country, using that digital money, settled in central bank money. This lesson is the operational flow: what happens step by step when a payer sends CBDC to a payee, what accounts are debited and credited, what messages or calls move between the systems, and what happens when a payment fails.

A retail CBDC payment starts in a wallet. A CBDC wallet is an app, or an account held with a bank or another authorised intermediary, that holds CBDC for a customer. The payer opens the wallet, enters the payee, usually by a wallet address, a phone number, a QR code or an account identifier, and enters the amount. The payer confirms the payment, often with a PIN, a biometric check, or another authentication step. At this point the payment is only an instruction. Validation is the next step, and it happens before any money moves. The wallet or the intermediary checks that the payer is who they claim to be, that the wallet has enough CBDC, that the amount is within any limits, and that the payee identifier is valid. If any check fails, the payment stops and the payer is told why.

Settlement in central bank money is the core of a CBDC payment. The payer CBDC account is debited and the payee CBDC account is credited. In accounting terms the entries are: debit payer CBDC wallet account, credit payee CBDC wallet account, for the full amount of the payment. Because CBDC is a direct liability of the central bank, the settlement is in central bank money, not in commercial bank money. Once that update is committed, the payment is settled. The payer balance falls immediately, the payee balance rises immediately, and the payee can use the funds without waiting for a clearing cycle. The system sends a confirmation to the payer and to the payee, usually as an in app notification, a text message, or a message back to the wallet. The confirmation includes the amount, the payee, the date and time, and a transaction reference that both parties can use if they need to query the payment later. The payer and payee wallets update their balances and their transaction histories.

The wallet sends a payment instruction to the intermediary or to the central bank system, using a secure API call that carries the payer identifier, the payee identifier, the amount, the currency, and a unique transaction reference. The intermediary or the central bank system validates the instruction and returns a response that says accepted, rejected, or held for review. If accepted, the system posts the debit and credit and returns a settlement confirmation with a settlement reference and a timestamp. The wallet then shows that confirmation to the payer and the payee. The full retail sequence is therefore: payer instruction, authentication, validation, debit and credit in central bank money, and confirmation to both parties.

A wholesale CBDC payment is a different flow for a different purpose. Suppose Bank A owes Bank B 10 million for a securities settlement, and both banks hold wholesale CBDC accounts at the central bank. Bank A sends a wholesale payment instruction through its system to the central bank wholesale ledger. The central bank validates the instruction, checks that Bank A has enough wholesale CBDC, and checks that the instruction matches the securities settlement instruction, for example the trade reference, the security, and the quantity. If the checks pass, the central bank posts: debit Bank A wholesale CBDC account 10 million, credit Bank B wholesale CBDC account 10 million. At the same time, the securities leg is settled: the securities move from Bank B to Bank A, or from the seller to the buyer, on the securities ledger.

The accounts involved in a wholesale flow are the wholesale CBDC accounts at the central bank, the securities accounts on the securities ledger, and the internal accounts of each bank that record the payment and the securities movement. Bank A records: debit securities held 10 million, credit wholesale CBDC account 10 million. Bank B records: debit wholesale CBDC account 10 million, credit securities held 10 million, with the customer or counterparty entries behind those totals. Bank A sends a payment instruction to the central bank, the central bank sends a settlement confirmation back to Bank A and to Bank B, and the securities system sends a settlement confirmation for the securities leg.

Failure handling in a retail CBDC payment depends on where the failure happens. If the payment fails at validation, for example the balance is too low or the payee identifier is invalid, no money moves. The payer is told the reason, corrects the instruction, and submits a new payment. The system uses the unique transaction reference to check whether the payment has already been settled, and if it has, it returns the original confirmation instead of posting a second debit. If the payment settles but the confirmation does not reach the payer or the payee, the payment is still settled, because the ledger update is the settlement, not the notification. The payer and payee can check the wallet balance and the transaction history to confirm the payment.

If Bank A does not have enough wholesale CBDC at the moment of settlement, the payment is queued or rejected, and Bank A must fund its account or arrange liquidity before resubmitting. If the securities leg fails, for example the securities are not available, the payment leg must not settle alone, because that would leave Bank A having paid without receiving the securities. The system therefore holds both legs together and settles them only when both are ready, or settles neither. A duplicate wholesale instruction must be detected by its unique reference and rejected, because a duplicate 10 million payment is a serious operational loss. Always check the payee identifier before confirming, because a CBDC payment settles immediately and cannot be recalled by pressing a button. Keep the transaction reference and the settlement reference together for reconciliation, and reconcile wallet balances to the central bank ledger daily. For a wholesale payment, confirm that the payment reference matches the securities reference before release, and confirm that both legs have settled before closing the trade.

text:
A cancellation in the direct payment method is a request by the ordering bank to stop a customer credit transfer that was sent straight from the ordering bank to the beneficiary bank, with no intermediary bank in between. The payment itself travels in one hop, so the cancellation also travels in one hop. The ordering bank asks the beneficiary bank to stop the payment and return the funds if they have not yet been credited to the beneficiary. The customer who ordered the payment is the person who starts the process, usually because the payment was sent in error, sent twice, sent to the wrong beneficiary, or is no longer needed. The cancellation does not undo a payment that has already been completed. It is a request, and the beneficiary bank must check the status of the payment before it can act on it.

The end to end flow starts when the ordering customer tells the ordering bank to cancel the payment. The ordering bank first checks its own records to confirm that the payment was sent, that it has not already been returned, and that the instruction is clear about which payment is meant. The bank identifies the payment by its reference, amount, currency, value date, ordering customer, and beneficiary details. If the payment is still inside the ordering bank and has not yet been released to the beneficiary bank, the ordering bank can stop it internally and no message needs to go out. In the direct method, however, the usual case is that the payment has already been sent, so the ordering bank must send a cancellation request to the beneficiary bank. The ordering bank then waits for the beneficiary bank to confirm what happened.

In ISO 20022 form the cancellation request is a camt.056, the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request. (The customer-facing equivalent, camt.055, is what a customer sends to its own bank; the bank then sends camt.056 to the next bank.) In MT form the equivalent is an MT192, which is the request for cancellation message. The ordering bank sends the camt.056 or the MT192 to the beneficiary bank, and it does so as soon as the customer asks, because every minute matters. The beneficiary bank replies with a camt.029, which is the resolution of investigation message, to say whether the cancellation succeeded or failed. In MT form the reply is an MT196, the Answers message, which states whether the cancellation was accepted or refused. An MT199 free-format message is only the fallback where a bank cannot generate an MT196. The beneficiary bank sends this reply after it has checked the payment and, if possible, stopped it. The ordering bank then tells the ordering customer the outcome, and credits the funds back to the customer if the cancellation succeeded.

The accounting entries show why the timing matters. When the original payment was sent, the ordering bank debited the ordering customer account and credited its own settlement account or its account with the beneficiary bank, depending on how the two banks settle with each other. The beneficiary bank, on receipt, debited its settlement account or its account with the ordering bank and credited a suspense or in transit account while it checked the payment. If the cancellation arrives before the beneficiary is credited, the beneficiary bank reverses that entry. It debits the suspense or in transit account and credits the settlement account, so the funds go back to the ordering bank. The ordering bank then debits its settlement account and credits the ordering customer account. The customer is back where they started, apart from any charges. If the beneficiary has already been credited, the entries are different, and the cancellation cannot simply reverse them, as explained below.

Cancellation is still possible while the payment is in flight or waiting to be credited at the beneficiary bank. It is possible while the beneficiary bank holds the funds in suspense, while the payment is queued for the next value date, and while the beneficiary bank is still checking the beneficiary details. It is too late once the funds have been credited to the beneficiary account and are available for the beneficiary to use. At that point the money belongs to the beneficiary, and the beneficiary bank cannot take it back without the beneficiary consent. The ordering bank must then ask the beneficiary, through the beneficiary bank, to return the funds voluntarily. The beneficiary may agree or refuse. If the beneficiary agrees, the return is made as a new payment from the beneficiary to the original ordering customer, or as a return under a pacs.004 if the scheme allows it. If the beneficiary refuses, the ordering bank has no payment system remedy left, and the matter becomes a commercial or legal dispute between the customer and the beneficiary.

If the cancellation fails, the ordering bank must tell the customer why, and what the next step is. A common failure is that the payment was already credited, as described above. Another failure is that the cancellation request itself is unclear, for example the reference does not match any payment, or the amount does not match. A third failure is that the beneficiary bank cannot find the payment because it was already returned for another reason. Charges can also arise. The beneficiary bank may charge for handling the cancellation, and the ordering bank may pass that charge to the customer. The original payment charges are not normally refunded, because the work of sending the payment was already done. The lesson for operations staff is to act at once, to identify the payment exactly, to use the right message, and to set the customer expectation clearly. A cancellation is a request to stop a payment, not a guarantee, and its success depends entirely on whether the funds have already reached the beneficiary.

text:
A cancellation in the serial payment method is a request to stop a customer credit transfer that travels through a chain of banks, one after the other, from the ordering bank through one or more intermediary banks to the beneficiary bank. In the serial method the payment instruction passes from bank to bank in sequence, and each bank in turn forwards it to the next bank in the chain. The cancellation must therefore travel back through the same chain, in reverse order, and each bank must stop the payment and pass the cancellation on to the bank before it. A cancellation that stops at only one bank in the middle leaves the rest of the chain still holding or forwarding the payment, so the whole chain has to be unwound step by step.

The end to end flow starts when the ordering customer asks the ordering bank to cancel the payment. The ordering bank checks its own records and confirms the payment details, including the reference, amount, currency, value date, and the full chain of banks named in the payment. If the payment has not yet left the ordering bank, it can be stopped internally. In the usual case it has already left, so the ordering bank sends a cancellation request to the next bank in the chain, which is the first intermediary bank. That bank checks whether it still holds the funds or has already forwarded them. If it still holds them, it stops the payment and sends the cancellation back to the ordering bank with a confirmation. If it has already forwarded them, it sends the cancellation request onward to the next bank in the chain. This continues, hop by hop, until the request reaches the beneficiary bank, which is the last bank in the chain.

In ISO 20022 form the cancellation request at each hop is a camt.056, the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request. (The customer-facing equivalent, camt.055, is what a customer sends to its own bank; the bank then sends camt.056 to the next bank.) In MT form the equivalent at each hop is an MT192, the request for cancellation. Each bank that receives a camt.056 or an MT192 sends its own camt.056 or MT192 to the next bank, so the request is reissued at every hop rather than simply forwarded as a single message. Each bank replies to the bank that sent it the request. In ISO 20022 form that reply is a camt.029, the resolution of investigation, stating whether the cancellation succeeded at that hop. In MT form the reply is an MT196, the Answers message, which states whether the cancellation was accepted or refused. An MT199 free-format message is only the fallback where a bank cannot generate an MT196. The replies also travel back hop by hop, so the ordering bank only gets a final answer after every bank in the chain has responded. The ordering bank then tells the ordering customer the outcome.

The accounting entries must be unwound at each bank in reverse order. When the original payment moved forward, each bank debited the account of the bank that sent it the payment and credited the account of the next bank, or credited a suspense account while it processed the instruction. Take a chain with an ordering bank, two intermediary banks, and a beneficiary bank. On the original payment the ordering bank debited the ordering customer and credited the first intermediary. The first intermediary debited the ordering bank and credited the second intermediary. The second intermediary debited the first intermediary and credited the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank debited the second intermediary and credited a suspense account, then the beneficiary. On cancellation, each entry is reversed at each bank. The beneficiary bank debits the suspense account and credits the second intermediary. The second intermediary debits the beneficiary bank and credits the first intermediary. The first intermediary debits the second intermediary and credits the ordering bank. The ordering bank debits the first intermediary and credits the ordering customer. The funds come back along exactly the same path they went out on.

Cancellation is still possible while the payment is anywhere in the chain before the beneficiary is credited. It is possible while an intermediary still holds the funds, while the payment is queued at an intermediary, and while the beneficiary bank holds the funds in suspense. It is too late once the beneficiary bank has credited the beneficiary account and the funds are available to the beneficiary. At that point the beneficiary consent is needed before any bank can take the funds back, and the beneficiary bank cannot simply reverse the credit. The ordering bank must ask, through the chain, for the beneficiary to agree to return the funds. If the beneficiary agrees, the return travels back through the chain as a return or as a new payment, depending on the scheme. If the beneficiary refuses, the cancellation fails at the final hop even though every earlier hop succeeded, and the ordering bank must explain this to the customer.

If the cancellation fails at any hop, the failure must be traced and reported clearly. One bank in the chain may have already forwarded the payment while another still holds it, so the status can differ from hop to hop. A common failure is a break in the chain, where one intermediary cannot identify the payment because the reference was changed or truncated as the payment moved forward. Another failure is a time limit, where an intermediary has already released the funds under its own cut off and cannot recall them. Charges can also accumulate, because each bank in the chain may charge for handling the cancellation, and those charges are deducted as the funds travel back. The customer may therefore receive back less than the original amount. The operational lesson is to send the cancellation at once, to trace it hop by hop, to confirm each bank reply before assuming the payment is stopped, and to tell the customer that a serial cancellation is slower and less certain than a direct cancellation, because every bank in the chain must act before the funds are safe.

text:
A cancellation in the cover payment method is a request to stop a customer credit transfer that is sent in two legs. The customer leg carries the payment instruction from the ordering bank to the beneficiary bank, and the bank to bank leg carries the actual funds, usually through a correspondent bank. In the cover method the beneficiary bank is told to pay the beneficiary, and a separate cover payment moves the money to fund that instruction. A cancellation in this method therefore has two things to stop, the customer instruction and the cover funds, and stopping only one of them leaves the payment half done. Both legs must be traced, and both legs must be stopped, for the cancellation to succeed.

The end to end flow starts when the ordering customer asks the ordering bank to cancel the payment. The ordering bank checks its records and identifies both legs of the payment, the customer instruction and the cover payment, by their references, amounts, currencies, and value dates. If neither leg has left the ordering bank, both can be stopped internally. In the usual case both legs have already been sent, so the ordering bank must send two cancellation requests. One request goes to the beneficiary bank to stop the customer instruction, and the other request goes to the correspondent bank, or to the next bank in the cover chain, to stop the cover funds. The two requests are sent at the same time, because a delay on either leg can let the payment complete on that leg while the other leg is stopped.

In ISO 20022 form the customer leg is a pacs.008, the customer credit transfer, and the cover leg is a pacs.009, the financial institution credit transfer, sent with the cover method indicator. The cancellation request for the customer leg is a camt.056, the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request, sent by the ordering bank to the beneficiary bank. (The customer-facing equivalent, camt.055, is what a customer sends to its own bank; the bank then sends camt.056 to the next bank.) The cancellation request for the cover leg is also a camt.056, sent by the ordering bank to the correspondent bank that holds the cover funds, or to the bank that is forwarding the cover. In MT form the customer leg is an MT103 and the cover leg is an MT202 with the cover method, and the cancellation request for each leg is an MT192, the request for cancellation. Each receiving bank replies with a camt.029 in ISO 20022 form, or an MT196 in MT form, to say whether the cancellation succeeded on that leg. The ordering bank must wait for both replies before it can tell the customer the final outcome.

The accounting entries show the two legs clearly. On the original payment the ordering bank debited the ordering customer account and credited its settlement account for the customer leg, and separately debited its internal settlement account and credited its Nostro account with the correspondent bank for the cover leg, because the correspondent will debit that Nostro to fund the beneficiary bank. The correspondent bank debited the ordering bank and credited the beneficiary bank, to fund the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank debited the correspondent and credited a suspense account, then credited the beneficiary. On a successful cancellation both legs are reversed. The beneficiary bank debits the suspense account and credits the correspondent, so the cover funds are not needed by the beneficiary bank. The correspondent bank debits the beneficiary bank and credits the ordering bank, returning the cover funds. The ordering bank debits the correspondent and credits the ordering customer account, so the customer is repaid. If only the customer leg is stopped but the cover leg has already been paid to the beneficiary bank, the beneficiary bank holds funds it cannot use for this payment, and those funds must be returned separately as a bank to bank return.

Cancellation is still possible while the beneficiary bank has not yet credited the beneficiary and while the correspondent bank still holds the cover funds. It is possible while either leg is in flight, queued, or held in suspense. It is too late on the customer leg once the beneficiary has been credited and the funds are available to the beneficiary, because the beneficiary consent is then needed before the credit can be reversed. It is too late on the cover leg once the correspondent has paid the beneficiary bank and the beneficiary bank has used those funds to credit the beneficiary, because the cover funds have already done their job. If one leg is stopped and the other leg is too late, the cancellation is only partly successful, and the ordering bank must explain exactly which leg failed and why. The beneficiary may need to agree to return the funds, and that return will itself travel as a new instruction and a new cover, or as a return under a pacs.004 where the scheme allows it.

If the cancellation fails, the reason must be traced to the correct leg. A common failure is a mismatch between the two legs, where the cover reference does not match the customer instruction, so the correspondent bank cannot link the cancellation to the cover payment. Another failure is timing, where the cover leg settles faster than the customer leg, so the funds arrive before the cancellation request does. Charges can arise on both legs, because the beneficiary bank may charge for stopping the customer instruction and the correspondent bank may charge for stopping the cover. Those charges are deducted from the returned funds, so the customer may receive back less than the original amount. The operational lesson is to treat a cover cancellation as two cancellations, to send both requests at once, to track both replies separately, and never to tell the customer the payment is cancelled until both legs are confirmed stopped. Stopping one leg alone is not a cancellation.

text:
An instant payment is a transfer that moves money from one bank account to another within seconds, at any hour of the day or night. Behind that speed sits a question of plumbing: does every payment pass through one central hub, or do banks connect with each other directly? In a hub model, a single central switch receives every payment, routes it to the receiving bank, clears it and arranges settlement. In a distributed or bilateral model, banks settle with each other directly, or through several links, and no single point handles every transaction. The choice shapes speed, resilience, cost and control, so it matters to every bank that joins an instant payment system.

In a hub model, the flow has four clear steps. First, the payer's bank checks the payer's balance and sends the payment instruction to the hub. Second, the hub validates the instruction, checks that the receiving bank is reachable, and forwards the instruction to the payee's bank. Third, the payee's bank credits the payee's account and confirms back to the hub. Fourth, the hub records the obligation between the two banks and settles it, usually by moving funds between settlement accounts the banks hold with the hub or with the central bank. Clearing, which is the exchange and validation of payment instructions, happens inside the hub. Settlement, which is the actual movement of money between banks, also happens through the hub, so each bank deals with one counterparty instead of dozens.

In a distributed or bilateral model, the flow is different. The payer's bank sends the instruction directly to the payee's bank, or through an intermediary the two banks have agreed on. Clearing happens between the two banks themselves: they exchange the instruction, validate it and agree the payment is good. Settlement also happens between the two banks, either immediately through accounts they hold with each other, or later through a periodic net settlement where many payments are added up and only the net difference moves. There is no single switch in the middle. Each pair of banks needs its own connection, its own agreement and its own settlement arrangement, which is why the model is called bilateral when only two banks are involved and distributed when many such links form a network.

Liquidity, the money a bank must have available to pay out, works differently in each model. In a hub model, each bank keeps funds in a settlement account with the hub or the central bank, and the hub draws on that balance as payments settle. The bank bears the liquidity need, but it funds one account, not many, and the hub can show it a single balance and a single queue of pending payments. In a distributed model, a bank must hold funds across every bilateral relationship it settles through, or hold enough in correspondent accounts to cover payments to each partner. That spreads liquidity thin and makes it harder to see the total position at a glance. Some distributed arrangements reduce this by netting payments over a period, so only the net amount moves, which lowers the liquidity need but adds a delay before final settlement.

Failure behaves differently too. When a hub goes down, every payment that depends on it stops, because there is no alternative path for the hub to hand the work to. That is the single point of failure risk, and it is why hub operators invest heavily in redundancy, backup sites and recovery procedures. A partial failure is also possible: the hub may accept instructions but be unable to settle them, leaving payments in an uncertain state until settlement resumes. When one bilateral link fails in a distributed model, only the payments between those two banks are affected, and the rest of the network keeps working. The affected banks can sometimes reroute through another bank or wait for the link to recover, but rerouting adds steps, time and cost, and there may be no agreed fallback route at all.

The trade-offs follow from these mechanics. A hub is usually faster to join, because a new bank connects once to the hub and can then reach every other member, which keeps onboarding cost low and makes the service quick to roll out. It gives the operator central control over rules, limits, fraud checks and dispute handling, which helps consistency but concentrates power and risk. A distributed model is more resilient to a single outage and gives banks more control over their own connections and counterparties, but it is slower and more expensive to build, because each new link needs its own agreement, testing and liquidity. India illustrates the hub model: NPCI operates the central switch for IMPS and UPI, so a payment from any member bank to any other member bank passes through NPCI for routing, clearing and settlement. A bank choosing between the models weighs these points: speed of rollout and simplicity against resilience and independence, and the cost of one shared settlement account against the cost of many bilateral ones.

text:
Six instant payment systems look similar from the outside: money moves in seconds, day and night. Underneath, they differ in clearing, settlement, liquidity needs, alias support, and failure handling. This lesson compares IMPS in India, Faster Payments in the United Kingdom, TIPS in the Eurozone, FedNow and RTP in the United States, and NPP in Australia, then draws out when a bank would choose each model.

IMPS, the Immediate Payment Service in India, is run by NPCI and works as a hub. A payment passes through NPCI's central switch, which clears it and routes it to the receiving bank. Settlement happens through settlement accounts, with banks funding their positions so payments settle immediately. Each member bank must keep enough in its settlement account to cover outgoing payments, and NPCI's central position makes funding simple: one account, one balance. IMPS supports alias-style addressing through the mobile number and MMID combination that predates UPI. If a payment times out, the payer's bank must check the status before retrying, because a blind retry can create a duplicate. Reversals follow defined dispute and return procedures.

Faster Payments in the United Kingdom is hub based and operated centrally. Clearing happens through the central infrastructure, and settlement happens through accounts at the Bank of England on a deferred net basis, normally three times each banking day. Banks manage their net debit positions against those cycles; settlement is not prefunded per payment. The central infrastructure completes a transaction between two participating members within 15 seconds, including acknowledgement, although the receiving bank may take up to two hours to credit the beneficiary where checks are needed. Faster Payments does not have a native proxy directory of its own; account numbers and sort codes remain the addressing method, though banks can layer alias features on top. On failure, a payment that does not complete within the expected window is reported as failed or pending, and the sending bank must resolve its status before telling the customer the outcome, so a payment is never sent twice by mistake.

TIPS, the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement service of the Eurosystem, settles in central bank money, which is the strongest form of settlement, because the money moves between accounts held at the central bank itself. A payment is cleared and settled in one step: TIPS checks the payer bank's central bank balance, moves the funds to the payee bank's account, and confirms. There is no deferred netting, so the liquidity need is the balance each bank holds at its central bank, funded by holding reserves. TIPS supports proxy addressing through the Mobile Proxy Lookup service, which links a mobile number to an account across participating countries. If a payment cannot settle, for example because the payer bank lacks funds, it is rejected immediately rather than queued, so the payer knows at once and no duplicate can arise from a retry.

FedNow, operated by the Federal Reserve in the United States, is a hub model that also settles in central bank money. Participating banks hold master accounts at the Federal Reserve, and each payment moves funds between those accounts in real time, so clearing and settlement happen together. The liquidity need is the balance in the master account, and banks manage it by monitoring their position and transferring funds in as needed, including outside normal business hours. FedNow itself has no directory service, so alias addressing is not a native FedNow feature. A bank can offer alias-based payments over FedNow by using a private-sector directory to resolve the alias to routing and account details; the Federal Reserve has said a native alias directory is a possible future enhancement. When a payment fails or times out, FedNow reports the status so the sending bank can determine whether the payment settled before deciding to retry, and duplicate detection helps prevent the same instruction settling twice.

RTP, the Real-Time Payments network in the United States, is operated by The Clearing House and works as a hub with prefunded settlement. Member banks fund a joint settlement account at the Federal Reserve, and each payment draws on the sending bank's prefunded position, so settlement is immediate and final. The liquidity need is the prefunded balance each bank maintains, and banks top it up as it is drawn down. RTP has no native alias directory for credit transfers. Alias addressing on RTP is available through the alias-based Request for Payment utility and third-party token services, where an enrolled mobile number or email token stands in for bank details. If a payment times out, the network returns a clear status, and the sending bank must check it before retrying, because a retry of a settled payment would duplicate it. Reversals are not automatic; they follow the network's rules for returns and disputes.

NPP, the New Payments Platform in Australia, is a hub model with a central switch operated for the industry, and settlement happens through the Reserve Bank of Australia, so it settles in central bank money. Payments are cleared centrally and settled between banks' exchange settlement accounts, which banks fund to cover outgoing payments. NPP is the home of PayID, so alias addressing is a core feature rather than an add-on: a payment can be addressed to a mobile number, email address or business number, and the payer sees the payee's registered name before confirming. NPP also carries rich data with each payment, which suits business payments that need a reference. On failure, a payment that does not settle is reported with a status the sending bank can act on, and duplicate handling plus the PayID name check reduce the chance of a payment going to the wrong person or being sent twice.

Failure handling follows a common pattern across all six. A timeout means the sender does not know whether the payment settled, so the correct action is always to check the status first and only then retry; a blind retry is the main cause of duplicates. A duplicate is prevented by unique transaction identifiers that let the receiving bank recognise and reject a second copy of the same instruction. A reversal is not a feature of instant settlement itself, because settlement is final, so returning money needs a separate instruction, either a new payment from the recipient or a formal return under the scheme's rules. The practical difference is how quickly the status comes back.

Each model fits a different need. IMPS suits a market that needs a single national hub with simple onboarding and broad reach. Faster Payments suits a market that values a fast service level backed by central bank settlement. TIPS suits Eurozone banks that want central bank money settlement. FedNow suits a US bank that wants the Federal Reserve as settlement counterparty. RTP suits a US bank that prefers a private-sector network with prefunded settlement and alias support. NPP suits an Australian bank that wants alias addressing and rich data. The trade-offs: central bank money settlement is the safest but demands central bank balances; prefunded settlement is fast but ties up liquidity; alias addressing improves the customer experience but depends on directory quality; and a single hub is simple to join but concentrates operational risk.

The T2 ISO 20022 message catalogue is the complete set of ISO 20022 messages used by TARGET2, known as T2, for real-time gross settlement and central bank liquidity management in the euro area. T2 replaced the earlier TARGET2 system with a consolidated platform that separates the Real-Time Gross Settlement service, called RTGS, from the Central Liquidity Management service, called CLM. Every payment, liquidity transfer, status report and notification in T2 is carried by a named ISO 20022 message, and each message has a defined sender, a defined receiver, a defined trigger and a defined place in the processing flow. Learning the catalogue means knowing, for each message, who sends it, when it is sent, and what the receiver does with it.

The pacs.008, Financial Institution to Financial Institution Customer Credit Transfer, is the customer payment message in T2. It is sent by the debtor bank, on behalf of its customer, to the creditor bank, through the RTGS service, when a customer payment must settle in central bank money on the same day. The pacs.008 carries the debtor and creditor customer details, the debtor and creditor agent details, the amount, the currency, the value date and any remittance information. A typical use is a corporate customer paying a supplier in another euro area country with same-day value, where the two banks have no direct account relationship and need central bank settlement.

The pacs.009, Financial Institution Credit Transfer, is the bank-to-bank payment message in T2. It is sent by one bank to another bank, through RTGS, when the payment is the banks own obligation rather than a customer payment. Typical uses are interbank lending, settlement of a financial market transaction, payment of a fee or a margin call, or a bank covering its own account. The pacs.009 carries the debtor agent and creditor agent, the amount and the settlement details, but it does not carry an underlying customer as the originator.

The pacs.002, Payment Status Report, is the status message in T2. It is sent by the RTGS service, or by the receiving bank, to the sending bank, to report the processing outcome of a pacs.008 or pacs.009. A pacs.002 can confirm that a payment has been accepted, settled, queued, rejected or cancelled. It is sent when the payment status changes, for example when a payment is queued because of insufficient liquidity and later settles when liquidity arrives, or when a payment is rejected because of a validation error. The sending bank uses the pacs.002 to update its own payment status, to inform its customer, and to decide whether to retry, repair or cancel the payment.

The pacs.004, Payment Return, is used when a settled payment must be returned. It is sent by the receiving bank, through RTGS, to the original sending bank, when the receiving bank cannot apply the funds, for example because the creditor account is closed, the account details are wrong, or the payment is returned under a recall agreement. The pacs.004 carries the original payment reference so the sending bank can match the return to the original pacs.008 or pacs.009, and the return reason. The return is itself a settled payment in the opposite direction, so it creates a new settlement in central bank money. Banks must handle pacs.004 returns promptly, because the customer funds are in transit until the return settles.

Liquidity in T2 is moved with camt.050 and confirmed with camt.025. The camt.050, Liquidity Credit Transfer, is sent by a bank, or by the central bank on behalf of a bank, to move liquidity between accounts in T2. A bank sends a camt.050 to move funds from its CLM main cash account to its RTGS dedicated cash account before the RTGS day starts, to move funds back at the end of the day, or to move funds between RTGS accounts during the day. A bank can also send a camt.050 to move liquidity to or from its TIPS dedicated cash account. The camt.025, Receipt, is sent by the T2 service back to the sender of a camt.050, or of another instruction, to confirm that the instruction was accepted and executed, or to report that it was rejected.

Account reporting and notifications in T2 use camt.052, camt.053 and camt.054. The camt.052, Bank to Customer Account Report, is an intraday statement sent by the T2 service to a bank, showing the account balance and the transactions posted so far during the day. The camt.053, Bank to Customer Statement, is the end-of-day statement, showing the full day activity and the closing balance for a CLM or RTGS account. The camt.054, Bank to Customer Debit Credit Notification, is sent when a single debit or credit is posted to an account, and it tells the bank exactly which payment or liquidity transfer caused the entry.

Two further camt messages handle exceptions. The camt.056, FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request, is sent by the original sending bank to request cancellation of a payment that has not yet settled, or to request a recall of a payment that has already settled. The receiving bank, or the RTGS service, responds with a camt.029, Resolution of Investigation, which states whether the cancellation or recall was accepted or rejected, and the reason.

The admi messages, Administration messages, cover system and service events rather than payments. An admi message is sent by the T2 service to a participant to report a system event, for example a change in the RTGS business day schedule, a system start or close, a broadcast about a service disruption, or a notification that a participant account has been blocked or unblocked. The most commonly seen admi messages are system event notifications that tell all participants that the RTGS day has opened, that a cut-off is approaching, or that the service will close at a stated time.

Which messages belong to RTGS, CLM and TIPS follows the service that holds the account. RTGS uses pacs.008 and pacs.009 for payments, pacs.002 for status, pacs.004 for returns, camt.056 and camt.029 for cancellation and recall, and camt.052, camt.053 and camt.054 for account reporting on RTGS dedicated cash accounts. CLM uses camt.050 for liquidity transfers into and out of the main cash account, camt.025 for receipts, and camt.052, camt.053 and camt.054 for reporting on the main cash account. CLM does not carry customer payments: a pacs.008 is an RTGS message, not a CLM message. TIPS, the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement service, uses pacs.008 for instant payments and pacs.002 for status, in a TIPS-specific processing flow with immediate settlement, and camt.050 is used to fund and defund the TIPS dedicated cash account from CLM or RTGS. The catalogue works only when each message is sent to the right service, at the right time, by the right party.

text:
An MT103 reject is what happens when a customer credit transfer is rejected before the money moves. The ordering bank sends an MT103 to instruct the next bank to pay the beneficiary, but the receiving bank checks the instruction and finds a problem that stops it from processing the payment. The payment is rejected, the funds never leave the ordering bank, and the ordering customer is told that the payment did not go through. A reject is different from a return. A return happens after the money has moved. A reject happens before it moves, so there is nothing to send back, because nothing was sent in the first place in settlement terms.

The end to end flow starts when the ordering customer instructs the ordering bank to pay a beneficiary. The ordering bank checks the instruction, debits the customer in its own books if its process requires it, and sends the MT103 to the next bank, which may be the beneficiary bank directly or an intermediary bank. The receiving bank validates the MT103 on arrival. It checks that the beneficiary details are complete and usable, that the account number or IBAN is in a valid format and belongs to an account the bank can credit, that the currency is one the bank can process, that the amount is within limits, and that the value date is valid and not in the past. It also checks its own sanctions and compliance screening, its internal rules on the ordering customer, and whether the payment instruction is complete and unambiguous. If any of these checks fail, the receiving bank rejects the payment instead of forwarding it or crediting the beneficiary.

The messages involved are the MT103 itself, the pacs.002 status report in ISO 20022 form, and the MT199 in MT form. The ordering bank sends the MT103 to the receiving bank. The receiving bank sends back a pacs.002, which is the payment status report, to tell the ordering bank that the payment was rejected and why. In MT form the receiving bank sends an MT199, a free format message, with the same information. The pacs.002 carries the status of rejected and a reason described in words, for example that the beneficiary account is invalid, that the beneficiary details are incomplete, that the currency is not supported, or that the payment failed a compliance check. The ordering bank receives the pacs.002 or MT199 and tells the ordering customer that the payment was rejected and what needs to be corrected. The ordering bank does not need to tell the beneficiary, because the beneficiary was never expecting funds that were never sent, although in practice the ordering customer may tell the beneficiary that the payment will be late.

The accounting entries are simple, because the money never moved between banks. At the ordering bank, when the payment was instructed, the bank may have debited the ordering customer account and credited an internal payment in transit account, pending release of the MT103. On rejection, the ordering bank reverses that entry. It debits the payment in transit account and credits the ordering customer account, so the customer has the full amount back. The receiving bank makes no customer accounting entry at all, because it never credited the beneficiary and never received settlement funds for this payment. It may record the rejected instruction in its own logs for audit and compliance, but there is no debit or credit to a customer account and no Nostro movement. This is the key difference from a return, where several banks must reverse entries that have already been posted.

If the reject happens, the ordering customer can correct the problem and send the payment again. If the beneficiary account number was wrong, the customer supplies the correct account. If the beneficiary name was incomplete, the customer supplies the full name. If the currency was not supported on that route, the customer chooses a supported currency or a different route. If the payment failed a compliance check, the customer may need to supply supporting information about the purpose of the payment or the relationship with the beneficiary, and the bank will decide whether the payment can proceed. The re sent payment is a new MT103 with a new reference, and it goes through the same checks again. The customer should not simply send the same instruction again without change, because the same check will fail again.

Charges on a reject are normally limited. The receiving bank may charge for handling a rejected instruction, and the ordering bank may pass that charge to the customer, but there is no charge for returning funds between banks, because no funds moved. The ordering bank should also tell the customer promptly, because a rejected payment can cause a missed deadline, a late fee from the beneficiary, or a broken commercial commitment. The operational lesson is to validate the MT103 before sending it, to check the beneficiary account and currency with the customer at the point of instruction, and to act on a pacs.002 reject at once. A reject is good news in one sense, because the money is still safe at the ordering bank, but it is still a failed payment, and the customer needs a clear reason and a clear path to send it correctly.

text:
An MT103 return is what happens when a customer credit transfer comes back after the money has already moved. The ordering bank sent the MT103, the payment travelled through the chain, and the beneficiary bank or an intermediary bank then sent the funds back, because the payment could not be completed as instructed. A return is different from a reject. A reject happens before the money moves, so there is nothing to send back. A return happens after the money has moved, so the funds must travel back along the chain, with accounting entries reversed at each bank, before the ordering customer is repaid.

The end to end flow starts when the ordering bank sends the MT103 to the next bank in the chain. The payment moves forward, bank by bank, and each bank debits the previous bank and credits the next bank, or credits a suspense account while it processes the instruction. The problem is discovered after the funds have moved. The beneficiary bank may find that the beneficiary account is closed, that the account number does not match the beneficiary name, that the beneficiary has refused the payment, or that the payment cannot be credited for a compliance reason that only became clear on receipt. An intermediary bank may also return the payment if it cannot forward it, for example because the next bank in the chain is unable to receive it. The bank that discovers the problem stops the payment and starts the return leg, sending the funds back to the bank that sent them the payment.

The messages involved are the original MT103, the pacs.004 return message in ISO 20022 form, and the MT199 or a new MT103 in MT form. In ISO 20022 form the customer credit transfer is a pacs.008, and its return is a pacs.004, the payment return message, sent by the bank returning the funds to the bank that sent them the payment. The pacs.004 carries the original payment reference, the amount being returned, and the reason for the return described in words, for example that the beneficiary account is closed, that the beneficiary refused the payment, or that the account details do not match. In MT form there is no dedicated return message for an MT103, so the returning bank normally sends an MT199 to explain the return, and sends the funds back with a new MT103 in the reverse direction, or with an MT202 if the return is bank to bank. Each bank in the chain that receives the return passes it on to the previous bank, until it reaches the ordering bank. The ordering bank then tells the ordering customer that the payment was returned and why.

The accounting entries reverse the original payment at each bank. Take a chain with an ordering bank, one intermediary bank, and a beneficiary bank. On the original payment the ordering bank debited the ordering customer and credited the intermediary. The intermediary debited the ordering bank and credited the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank debited the intermediary and credited a suspense account, and then found it could not credit the beneficiary. On the return the beneficiary bank debits the suspense account and credits the intermediary, sending the funds back. The intermediary debits the beneficiary bank and credits the ordering bank. The ordering bank debits the intermediary and credits the ordering customer account. The customer is repaid, apart from any charges deducted on the way back. If the return passes through more banks, each bank makes the same pair of entries, debiting the bank it is returning funds to and crediting the bank it received them from, in reverse order.

Charges on a return can reduce the amount the customer receives back. Each bank in the chain may deduct a charge for handling the return, and the beneficiary bank may deduct a charge for the work of checking and returning the payment. Those charges are taken from the returned amount as it travels back, so the ordering customer may receive less than the original amount. The ordering bank must show the customer the amount returned and each charge deducted, so the customer can see why the repayment is smaller. The customer should also be told that charges on the original payment are not normally refunded, because the work of sending the payment was already done, even though the payment did not reach the beneficiary.

Partial returns are possible, although they are less common than full returns. A partial return happens when only part of the original amount is returned, for example because the beneficiary bank was able to credit part of the payment but not the rest, or because a charge or a deduction was taken from the amount before the return. In a partial return the pacs.004 states the amount being returned, which is less than the original amount, and the ordering bank credits the customer with that returned amount only. The rest of the payment is treated as completed, and the customer must decide whether to send a new payment for the shortfall, or to accept the partial credit. The operational lesson is to treat a return as a payment in reverse, to trace it hop by hop, to check the reason in words before telling the customer, and to explain the charges clearly. A return means the money moved and came back, so the customer needs to know not only that it failed, but how much came back and why.

text:
An MT202 reject is what happens when a bank to bank payment is rejected before the money moves. An MT202 is a general financial institution transfer, sent by one bank to another bank to move funds for the sending bank own account, or on behalf of another financial institution. It is not a customer payment, so there is no ordering customer and no beneficiary customer in the instruction. When the receiving bank checks the MT202 and finds a problem, it rejects the instruction, the funds never leave the sending bank, and the sending bank must decide what to do next. A reject is different from a return, where the funds have already moved and must be sent back.

The end to end flow starts when the sending bank decides to move funds to another bank. The reason may be to fund a Nostro account, to settle a position, to cover a customer payment that will be made by the receiving bank, or to move liquidity between the bank own accounts. The sending bank sends the MT202 to the receiving bank, instructing it to credit the account named in the instruction. The receiving bank validates the MT202 on arrival. It checks that the account to be credited is valid and can receive the funds, that the currency is one it can process, that the amount is within limits, that the value date is valid, and that the instruction is complete and unambiguous. It also runs its own compliance and sanctions screening on the sending bank and on the instruction. If any check fails, the receiving bank rejects the MT202 instead of crediting the account.

The messages involved are the MT202 itself, the pacs.002 status report in ISO 20022 form, and the MT199 in MT form. In ISO 20022 form the bank to bank payment is a pacs.009, the financial institution credit transfer, and a reject is reported with a pacs.002, the payment status report, carrying the status of rejected and the reason described in words. In MT form the sending bank sends the MT202, and the receiving bank sends an MT199, a free format message, to say that the payment was rejected and why. The reason may be that the account to be credited does not exist, that the account is closed, that the currency is not supported, that the amount exceeds a limit, or that the instruction failed a compliance check. The receiving bank sends this reply promptly, so the sending bank knows at once that the funds have not moved and can take the next step.

The accounting and funding position is the key point of an MT202 reject. When a bank sends an MT202, it expects to release Nostro funding, which means it expects its account with the receiving bank, or its settlement account, to be debited to fund the payment. On a reject, that Nostro funding is not released. The sending bank makes no debit to its Nostro account and no credit to the receiving bank, because the receiving bank never accepted the instruction. If the sending bank had already earmarked the funds in its own books, for example by debiting an internal funding account and crediting a payment in transit account, it reverses that entry on receipt of the reject. It debits the payment in transit account and credits the internal funding account, so the funds are available again for another use. The receiving bank makes no accounting entry, because it never credited any account and never received settlement funds.

What the sending bank does next depends on the reason for the reject. If the account details were wrong, the sending bank corrects the account and sends a new MT202 with the correct details. If the currency was not supported, the sending bank chooses a supported currency or a different receiving bank. If the amount exceeded a limit, the sending bank may split the payment or seek approval for a larger amount, following its own internal rules. If the reject was for a compliance reason, the sending bank must investigate, supply any missing information, and decide whether the payment can be sent at all. The re sent payment is a new MT202 with a new reference, and it goes through the same checks again. The sending bank should not send the same instruction again without change, because the same check will fail again.

If the MT202 was intended to fund a customer payment, the reject has a knock on effect. The customer payment that depended on this funding cannot proceed until the funding is in place, so the sending bank must either fix the MT202 quickly or find another way to fund the customer payment. The sending bank operations team should therefore treat an MT202 reject as urgent, tell the team that owns the underlying purpose of the funds, and record the reject for audit. The lesson is that a bank to bank reject is clean in accounting terms, because no funds moved, but it can be serious in business terms, because the liquidity or the cover that the payment was meant to provide is still missing, and the next step must be taken without delay.

text:
An MT202 return is what happens when a bank to bank payment comes back after the money has already moved. One bank sent an MT202 to another bank to move funds for its own account or for another financial institution, the receiving bank accepted and processed the instruction, and then the funds were sent back, because the payment could not be completed as instructed or because the receiving bank could not use the funds as intended. A return is different from a reject. A reject happens before the money moves, so there is nothing to send back. A return happens after the money has moved, so the funds must travel back, with accounting entries reversed at each bank, before the sending bank is repaid.

The end to end flow starts when the sending bank sends the MT202 to the receiving bank. The receiving bank credits the account named in the instruction, or holds the funds in suspense while it checks the instruction. The problem is discovered after the funds have moved. The account to be credited may be closed, the account number may not match the account holder, the receiving bank may be unable to apply the funds for the purpose stated in the instruction, or a compliance check that only became clear on receipt may prevent the receiving bank from keeping the funds. The receiving bank then starts the return leg, sending the funds back to the sending bank, and telling the sending bank why the payment was returned.

The messages involved are the original MT202, the pacs.004 return message in ISO 20022 form, and the MT199 with a new MT202 in MT form. In ISO 20022 form the bank to bank payment is a pacs.009, the financial institution credit transfer, and its return is a pacs.004, the payment return message, sent by the returning bank to the bank that sent the payment. The pacs.004 carries the original payment reference, the amount being returned, and the reason for the return described in words, for example that the account is closed, that the account details do not match, or that the funds cannot be applied as instructed. In MT form there is no dedicated return message for an MT202, so the returning bank normally sends an MT199 to explain the return, and sends the funds back with a new MT202 in the reverse direction. The sending bank receives the MT199 and the new MT202, checks that the amount and reference match the original payment, and updates its own records.

A worked example makes the entries clear. Bank A in London sends an MT202 for one million in the stated currency to Bank B in New York, to fund Bank A Nostro account with Bank B. On the original payment Bank A debits its Nostro account with Bank B for one million and credits its internal funding account for one million, so the Nostro balance rises by one million. Bank B, on receipt, debits its settlement account for one million and credits its Vostro account for Bank A for one million, so the funds are now available to Bank A in New York. Bank B then finds that the Nostro account named in the instruction is closed, following a recent account change that Bank A had not recorded. Bank B cannot credit the closed account, so it returns the funds. On the return Bank B debits its Vostro account for Bank A for one million and credits its settlement account for one million, sending the funds back. Bank A, on receipt, debits its internal funding account for one million and credits its Nostro account with Bank B for one million, so the one million is back where it started. The MT202 is normally sent to the bank holding the funds being moved, not to the bank whose Nostro is being funded, unless Bank A holds a separate funding account at Bank B. If the return passes through an intermediary bank, that bank makes the same pair of entries in reverse, debiting the bank it returns funds to and crediting the bank it received them from.

A return is used instead of a new payment when the purpose is to undo the original payment, rather than to make a fresh payment for a new purpose. If Bank B simply sent a new MT202 to Bank A for a new purpose, that would be a new payment, with a new reference and a new business reason, and the original payment would still stand as completed. A return, by contrast, is linked to the original payment by its reference and its reason, and it tells both banks and their auditors that the original payment did not complete as intended. This linkage matters for reconciliation, for audit, and for reporting, because it shows that the funds went out and came back for the same instruction. A return is therefore the right choice when the account was wrong, when the funds cannot be applied, or when the receiving bank cannot keep the funds. A new payment is the right choice when the business purpose has changed and a fresh movement of funds is needed.

Charges on an MT202 return can reduce the amount repaid. The returning bank may deduct a charge for handling the return, and any intermediary bank may deduct a charge as the funds travel back. Those charges are taken from the returned amount, so the sending bank may receive back less than the original amount. The sending bank must record the amount returned and each charge, and tell the team that owns the funds why the repayment is smaller. The sending bank must also decide the next step. If the account was closed, it must obtain the correct account and send a new MT202. If the funds cannot be applied as instructed, it must clarify the purpose with the receiving bank before sending again. If the return was for a compliance reason, it must investigate before any re send. The operational lesson is to treat an MT202 return as a reversal, not as a new payment, to reconcile it against the original instruction by reference and amount, and to act at once, because the liquidity that the original payment was meant to provide is still missing until a correct payment is sent.

text:
An unauthorised SEPA Direct Debit collection is a collection taken from a debtor account without a valid mandate from the debtor. The 13-month unauthorised refund rule gives the debtor the right to claim a full refund of that collection for up to 13 months after the date the account was debited. The clock starts on the debit date, not on the date the debtor notices the collection, and the refund covers the full amount of the unauthorised collection. This is a consumer and debtor protection rule under the SEPA Direct Debit scheme and the Payment Services Directive, and it applies even when the collection itself was processed normally through the clearing system.

The 13-month rule is different from the better known 8-week refund for authorised collections, and confusing the two is a common operational error. An authorised collection is one where a valid mandate existed, but the debtor disputes the amount or the timing, or simply changes their mind within the permitted window. For an authorised collection, the debtor has 8 weeks from the debit date to ask their bank for a refund, and the bank must refund it without asking for a reason, provided the claim is inside the 8 weeks. An unauthorised collection has no valid mandate at all, so the debtor is not limited to 8 weeks. The debtor has 13 months, and the claim is not a no-questions refund. The debtor must state that no mandate was given, and the bank must investigate whether a mandate existed.

The claim process starts with the debtor contacting their own bank, the debtor bank, and stating that the collection was unauthorised. The debtor identifies the collection by date, amount, creditor name and creditor identifier, and confirms that no mandate was signed or that the mandate relied on does not cover that collection. The debtor bank records the claim, checks its own records for a mandate copy or a mandate reference, and contacts the creditor bank through the scheme refund process. The creditor bank then asks the creditor to produce evidence of the mandate. The evidence is normally the signed mandate form, or the electronic mandate record with the debtor identifier, the mandate reference, the date of signature and the creditor identifier. If the creditor cannot produce a valid mandate, the refund is paid.

Who bears the loss depends on where the failure sits. If no mandate ever existed, the creditor bears the loss, because the creditor collected money it had no right to collect. The debtor bank refunds the debtor, the creditor bank debits the creditor bank account or recovers from the creditor, and the creditor is left without the funds. If a mandate did exist but the creditor bank or the creditor stored it incorrectly, the party that failed to produce or retain the mandate evidence bears the operational loss, even though the underlying debt may still be owed through another route. The creditor can then pursue the underlying amount through normal commercial means, but cannot simply re-present the same direct debit without a fresh agreement.

A refusal is a different flow from a refund, and it happens before settlement rather than after it. A refusal means the debtor bank refuses to execute the collection before interbank settlement takes place. The debtor may have instructed the bank not to pay, the account may be closed, or the bank may have a standing instruction to refuse collections from that creditor. In a refusal, the funds never leave the debtor account through the direct debit channel, and the collection never reaches settlement. The refusal is reported back through the clearing system so the creditor bank and the creditor know the collection did not proceed.

Refusal, reject and return are three distinct outcomes, separated by timing. A reject happens before interbank settlement, when a technical or validation check fails, for example an invalid IBAN, a missing mandate reference, a duplicate file, or a file received after the cut-off. A refusal also happens before interbank settlement, but it is a business decision by the debtor bank or the debtor, not a technical validation failure. A return happens after interbank settlement, when the funds have already moved and must be sent back, for example because the account was closed after settlement, the account had insufficient funds at the point of return processing, or the debtor claims a refund after settlement. The timing matters because it decides which message is used, who holds the funds at each stage, and how quickly the creditor learns the collection failed.

The messages involved follow that timing. The creditor bank sends the collection instruction to the clearing and settlement mechanism in a pacs.003 direct debit instruction, normally one business day before the due date for a first or one-off collection and on the agreed presentation timetable for recurrent collections. The debtor bank, on receiving the instruction, checks the account and the mandate position. If it refuses, it sends a pacs.002 payment status report carrying a refusal reason back through the clearing system to the creditor bank. If the collection is rejected for a technical reason, a pacs.002 is also used, with a reject reason code. If the collection settles and is later returned, the debtor bank sends a pacs.004 payment return. The creditor bank passes the outcome to the creditor, normally in a camt.054 bank to customer debit or credit notification or in the creditor bank account statement, so the creditor can update its receivables ledger.

The timeline for a refusal is short. The debtor bank decides on or before the due date, the pacs.002 refusal is returned through the clearing system on the settlement cycle, and the creditor bank informs the creditor, normally on the same business day or the next business day, depending on the creditor bank reporting cycle. The next step for the creditor is to contact the debtor directly, find out why the collection was refused, and agree another payment method, such as a bank transfer or a card payment. The creditor should not simply re-present the same direct debit. If the debtor has withdrawn the mandate, the creditor must stop presenting collections under that mandate reference entirely and record the cancellation.

In practice, the two flows test different controls. The 13-month refund tests mandate storage, mandate evidence and the creditor ability to prove authorisation months after the event. The refusal flow tests daily operational awareness: the creditor must read the pacs.002 and pacs.004 reports every day, reconcile them to the expected collections file, and follow up refused items the same day. A creditor that ignores refusals for a week will keep shipping goods or providing services against invoices that were never paid, and will lose the chance to collect by another method while the debtor is still contactable.
