text:
The SEPA Direct Debit settlement model is the set of rules that moves money from debtor accounts to creditor accounts on the due date of a collection, through a clearing and settlement mechanism, most commonly STEP2, and then through the banks central bank accounts. Settlement is the point at which the interbank obligation is discharged: the debtor bank owes the creditor bank the value of the collections that were presented and not refused or rejected, and that obligation is settled in central bank money on the settlement date. The creditor is credited and the debtor is debited on the basis of that settlement, not on the basis of the file being sent.

The clearing and settlement mechanism, or CSM, sits between the creditor bank and the debtor bank. The creditor bank sends a file of collection instructions, in pacs.003 messages, to the CSM. The CSM validates the file, sorts the instructions by debtor bank, and forwards them to each debtor bank. The debtor bank checks each instruction against the debtor account and the mandate position, and returns refusals and rejects before settlement. The CSM then calculates a net settlement position for each bank: the total value of collections that bank is due to receive as a creditor bank, less the total value it must pay as a debtor bank. That net position is settled in central bank money, normally through TARGET, on the settlement date.

STEP2 is the main pan-European CSM for SEPA Direct Debit, operated as a retail clearing system with several settlement cycles each business day. Each cycle has a cut-off time for file submission, a processing window in which files are validated and distributed, and a settlement time at which the net positions for that cycle are settled. A creditor bank that misses the cut-off for one cycle must wait for the next cycle, which can push the due date.

Presentation timing drives the settlement date. A recurrent collection is normally presented to the CSM one business day before the due date, known as D minus 1, where D is the due date. A first or one-off collection is also normally presented on D minus 1 under the current scheme rules, although older scheme versions required earlier presentation for first collections, and some creditor banks still submit first collections earlier for operational safety. The debtor bank receives the instruction in time to check it before the due date. On the due date, the collections that were not refused or rejected are settled: the debtor bank account is debited and the creditor bank account is credited. The value date for the debtor is normally the due date, and the value date for the creditor is normally the due date as well, so that neither side gains or loses a day of value on a normal collection.

The accounting entries show the flow clearly. On the due date, the debtor bank debits the debtor customer account and credits its internal settlement account for the collection amount. The creditor bank debits its internal settlement account and credits the creditor customer account. At the CSM level, the debtor bank settlement account is debited and the creditor bank settlement account is credited in central bank money for the net settlement amount. For cross-bank collections, the interbank leg is essential, because the debtor bank does not hold the creditor account and the creditor bank does not hold the debtor account.

A worked example makes the timing concrete. A utility creditor has 10,000 customers each owing 50 euro for a monthly bill, a total of 500,000 euro, due on Monday 15 September. The creditor bank prepares a pacs.003 file on Friday 12 September and submits it to STEP2 on that day, which is D minus 1 in business day terms, because Saturday and Sunday are not business days for this purpose. STEP2 validates the file on Friday, distributes the instructions to the debtor banks, and the debtor banks check the accounts. On Monday 15 September, the due date, the debtor banks debit the 10,000 debtor accounts for 50 euro each, and STEP2 settles the net positions: each debtor bank pays its share into the settlement system, and the creditor bank receives 500,000 euro less any refusals, rejects and returns. The creditor bank then credits the utility creditor account with the settled amount on Monday 15 September, and the utility marks those 10,000 invoices as paid.

If a debtor bank refuses 200 of those collections, for 10,000 euro, the refusal is reported in a pacs.002 before settlement, and the settlement amount is reduced to 490,000 euro. The 200 debtors are not debited, and the utility must follow up those 200 invoices separately. If a further 50 collections, for 2,500 euro, are returned after settlement because the accounts were closed, the debtor banks send pacs.004 payment returns after settlement, and the creditor bank debits the utility account for 2,500 euro and reports the returns in a camt.054 notification. The utility final settled amount for that due date is therefore 487,500 euro, and the receivables ledger must show 250 unpaid invoices, not 10,000 paid invoices.

Settlement can fail, and the failure handling is part of the model. If a debtor bank does not have sufficient central bank liquidity to meet its net settlement obligation, the settlement for that cycle can be delayed or partially settled, depending on the CSM rules and the TARGET settlement arrangements. The CSM will normally retry in a later cycle on the same day, and the affected collections will settle late rather than not at all. If a creditor bank file is rejected in full because of a format error, no collections from that file settle, and the creditor bank must correct and resubmit the file, which may move the due date. If an individual collection is rejected, only that collection fails, and the rest of the file settles normally. The creditor bank is responsible for reconciling the settlement amount received against the file total, investigating any difference the same day, and reporting the outcome to the creditor so the creditor ledger matches the bank account.

The tie to STEP2 processing is therefore direct: STEP2 is not just a message switch, it is the place where presentation, validation, distribution, refusal handling and net settlement come together. The creditor bank file submission cut-off decides whether a collection makes the intended due date. The debtor bank response window decides whether a refusal is reported before settlement or becomes a return after settlement. The STEP2 settlement cycle decides when the creditor bank receives the funds and can credit the creditor. A creditor that understands this chain can plan its billing run, its file submission time and its reconciliation, and can explain to a debtor why a collection debited on a Monday was presented on the previous Friday, and why a refused collection never appears on the debtor statement at all.

text:
An accounting entry for a payment is a pair of equal and opposite postings, a debit and a credit, recorded in the books of a bank. Every payment that moves value must balance at each bank that touches it: total debits must equal total credits at that bank, for that payment, at each step. If a bank debits a customer account, it must credit another account for the same amount. If it debits its Nostro account, which is its own account held at another bank, it must credit another account for the same amount. This lesson works through the entries step by step, so you can trace EUR 50,000 from the sender to the receiver and back again, and see exactly where the money sits at each moment.

The worked example is a customer payment. Sara holds an account at Bank A in Frankfurt. She instructs Bank A to pay EUR 50,000 to Lee, who holds an account at Bank B in Singapore. Bank A and Bank B do not hold accounts with each other. Both hold accounts with a correspondent bank, Bank C. Bank A holds a Nostro account at Bank C, which is Bank A's own money held at Bank C. Bank C holds a Vostro account for Bank A, which is the same account seen from Bank C's side, and a Vostro account for Bank B. The payment travels as an MT103, or pacs.008 in ISO 20022, from Bank A to Bank B through Bank C. There are no charges in this example, so the full EUR 50,000 reaches Lee.

Step 1 takes place at Bank A, the ordering bank. When Sara's instruction is accepted, Bank A debits Sara's customer account for EUR 50,000 and credits its internal clearing account, also called a suspense or settlement account, for EUR 50,000. The debit reduces Sara's balance by EUR 50,000. The credit parks the money inside Bank A while the payment is prepared. Debits equal credits at Bank A: EUR 50,000 on each side. Bank A then sends the MT103. To fund the payment at the correspondent, Bank A debits its internal clearing account for EUR 50,000 and credits its Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000. Again the step balances. After these two postings, Sara's account is EUR 50,000 lower, the clearing account is back to zero, and Bank A's Nostro at Bank C is EUR 50,000 lower, because Bank A has now told Bank C to pay that amount onward.

Step 2 takes place at Bank C, the correspondent bank. Bank C receives the instruction and moves the money between the two Vostro accounts it holds. Bank C debits the Vostro account of Bank A for EUR 50,000 and credits the Vostro account of Bank B for EUR 50,000. The debit reduces what Bank C owes Bank A by EUR 50,000. The credit increases what Bank C owes Bank B by EUR 50,000. Total debits equal total credits at Bank C: EUR 50,000 on each side. No customer account is touched at Bank C.

Step 3 takes place at Bank B, the beneficiary bank. Bank B receives the MT103 and credits its customer. Bank B debits its Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000 and credits Lee's customer account for EUR 50,000. The debit reduces Bank B's balance at Bank C by EUR 50,000, because Bank B has now used that balance to pay Lee. The credit increases Lee's balance by EUR 50,000. Debits equal credits at Bank B: EUR 50,000 on each side. The payment is now complete: Sara is EUR 50,000 lower, Lee is EUR 50,000 higher, and every debit has a matching credit.

A bank to bank payment works the same way, but there is no customer at either end. Suppose Bank A now owes Bank B EUR 50,000 of its own money, for example to settle a loan or a foreign exchange deal. Bank A sends an MT202, or pacs.009 in ISO 20022, which is a payment between banks for their own account, not for a customer. At Bank A, the entry is debit the internal settlement account for EUR 50,000 and credit the Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000. At Bank C, the entry is debit the Vostro account of Bank A for EUR 50,000 and credit the Vostro account of Bank B for EUR 50,000. At Bank B, the entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000 and credit the internal settlement account for EUR 50,000. Each bank balances. The difference from the MT103 is only who the money belongs to: in the MT103 the money belonged to Sara and then to Lee, while in the MT202 the money belongs to Bank A and then to Bank B. The accounts used are the same kinds of accounts, Nostro, Vostro and settlement, and the discipline is the same.

The return leg reverses the flow. Suppose Lee's account was closed, or Bank B cannot apply the payment, so Bank B returns the EUR 50,000. The return travels as a pacs.004, a payment return. At Bank B, the entry is debit Lee's customer account for EUR 50,000, or debit the internal clearing account if the money was parked there and never credited to Lee, and credit the Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000. At Bank C, the entry is debit the Vostro account of Bank B for EUR 50,000 and credit the Vostro account of Bank A for EUR 50,000. At Bank A, the entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for EUR 50,000 and credit Sara's customer account for EUR 50,000. Each bank balances again, and after the return every account is back where it started: Sara has her EUR 50,000 back, Lee has nothing extra, and the Nostro and Vostro balances are restored. A return is not a new payment. It is the exact reversal of the original entries, in the opposite direction, for the same amount.

Three checks will keep you right on any MT103 or MT202. First, name the bank before you name the account, because the same word means different things at different banks: a Nostro at Bank A is Bank A's money at Bank C, while a Vostro at Bank C is Bank C's liability to Bank A. Second, check that each bank balances at each step, not just at the end, because a payment can balance overall while one bank is out of balance in the middle, and that is where breaks and reconciliation differences come from. Third, remember that the MT103 and the MT202 are instructions, not money. The money moves when the correspondent debits one Vostro and credits the other, and when each bank posts its Nostro entry.

text:
Some SWIFT messages move money, some ask for money, some cancel a payment, and some ask a question. The accounting entries are different in each case, and the most common mistake is to post money entries for a message that moves no money at all. This lesson works through each message in turn: a charge claim with MT191, a cancellation with MT192, a query and its answer with MT195 and MT196, and Nostro funding with MT210. The worked example uses USD 10,000 for a payment and USD 150 for a charge claim.

Start with MT191, the request for payment of charges. Suppose Bank A sent a customer payment of USD 10,000 by MT103 to Bank B, and Bank B incurred USD 150 of charges that Bank A had agreed to pay. Bank B sends an MT191 to Bank A claiming USD 150. The MT191 itself moves no money, so no Nostro or Vostro account is debited or credited when it is sent. Bank B may record the claim in its own books as an accrual: debit Charges Receivable, an internal asset account, for USD 150 and credit Charges Income for USD 150. That entry balances at Bank B, but it is only a record that money is owed, not a movement of cash. Bank A may record debit Charges Expense USD 150 and credit Charges Payable USD 150.

The money moves when Bank A pays the claim, and it pays it with an MT202, a bank to bank payment. Assume Bank A and Bank B both hold accounts with correspondent Bank C, as in the MT103 lesson. At Bank A, the entry is debit Charges Payable for USD 150 and credit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 150. The debit clears the liability Bank A recorded when the claim arrived. The credit reduces Bank A's Nostro balance by USD 150. At Bank C, the entry is debit the Vostro account of Bank A for USD 150 and credit the Vostro account of Bank B for USD 150. At Bank B, the entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 150 and credit Charges Receivable for USD 150. The credit clears the receivable Bank B recorded when it sent the claim. Each bank balances at USD 150.

Next is MT192, the request for cancellation. The entries depend entirely on timing: whether the payment has settled or not. Case one is cancellation before settlement. Suppose Bank A sent an MT103 for USD 10,000, but the payment has not yet settled at the correspondent, and Bank A asks Bank B to cancel it with an MT192, or camt.056 in ISO 20022. Because no money has moved between banks, there are no Nostro or Vostro entries to reverse. At Bank A, the money is still in the internal clearing account, so the entry is debit the clearing account for USD 10,000 and credit the customer's account for USD 10,000. At Bank B there is no entry at all if the payment was never credited.

Case two is cancellation after settlement, and here the entries are real. Suppose the USD 10,000 has already settled and Lee has already been credited at Bank B, and Bank A then asks for the money back. Bank B cannot simply delete the credit. It must return the funds, and the return travels as a pacs.004. At Bank B, the entry is debit Lee's customer account for USD 10,000 and credit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 10,000. At Bank C, the entry is debit the Vostro account of Bank B for USD 10,000 and credit the Vostro account of Bank A for USD 10,000. At Bank A, the entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 10,000 and credit Sara's customer account for USD 10,000. Each bank balances.

Now MT195 and MT196, the query and its answer. Suppose Bank A sent the USD 10,000 payment, Lee says it has not arrived, and Bank A sends an MT195 to Bank B asking for the status. Bank B replies with an MT196 giving the answer. No money moves on either message, and no accounting entries are posted at either bank, for a simple reason: a question does not change any balance. Bank A does not debit or credit any account when it sends the query, and Bank B does not debit or credit any account when it answers. The same rule applies to an MT199, a free format message: it carries words, not value, so it never posts a debit or a credit by itself.

Finally, MT210, the notice to receive, which is used for Nostro funding. Suppose Bank A needs to fund its Nostro account at Bank C so it can send the USD 10,000 payment, and it transfers USD 10,000 from its own settlement account to its Nostro account. Bank A sends an MT210 to Bank C to advise that the funds are coming. At Bank A, the funding entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 10,000 and credit the internal settlement account for USD 10,000. The debit increases Bank A's Nostro balance, because Bank A now holds more money at Bank C. The credit reduces Bank A's settlement account by the same amount. The entry balances. At Bank C, when the funds arrive, the entry is debit the settlement account for USD 10,000 and credit the Vostro account of Bank A for USD 10,000. The credit increases what Bank C owes Bank A by USD 10,000. The entry balances at Bank C.

Once the Nostro is funded, the payment itself is sent exactly as in the MT103 lesson, and it uses the funded balance. At Bank A, the entry is debit the customer's account for USD 10,000 and credit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 10,000. At Bank C, the entry is debit the Vostro account of Bank A for USD 10,000 and credit the Vostro account of Bank B for USD 10,000. At Bank B, the entry is debit the Nostro account at Bank C for USD 10,000 and credit the customer's account for USD 10,000. The funding and payment steps must not be netted into one, or the audit trail is lost.

The pattern across all five messages is simple enough to use as a check. MT191 asks for money, so it records a receivable and a payable, and the money moves later by MT202. MT192 cancels a payment, so before settlement it releases a hold with no cash entries, and after settlement it needs a full return with Nostro and Vostro entries at each bank. MT195 and MT196 ask and answer a question, so they post no entries at all. MT210 advises funding, so it posts a debit to the Nostro and a credit to the settlement account at the funding bank, and a credit to the Vostro at the receiving bank. In every case, name the bank, name the account, state the debit and the credit, and check that they are equal. If they are not equal, the entry is wrong, and no message type can fix it.

title: How the ISO 20022 migration changes compliance: screening, truncation and reporting
text:
ISO 20022 is the global standard for financial messaging, and its migration changes compliance because it changes the data compliance teams work with. The older MT messages carried names and addresses as unstructured free text, often shortened to fit, with little distinction between the debtor, the ultimate debtor, and an intermediary passing the payment on. ISO 20022 messages carry the same information in structured fields: separate elements for debtor, creditor, ultimate debtor, ultimate creditor, purpose, and remittance information. Screening, matching and reporting all depend on data quality, and ISO 20022 gives compliance systems far richer and more consistent data than MT ever did. The migration is therefore not only a technical change of format: it changes what a compliance team can see, must screen, and must report.

The biggest improvement is in the debtor and creditor fields. In an ISO 20022 payment message, the debtor is identified with a full name, a structured address split into street, building number, town and country, and an identification block carrying a legal entity identifier, a national registration number, or a bank identifier code. The creditor is identified the same way. Alongside them, the message can carry the ultimate debtor, on whose behalf the payment is made, and the ultimate creditor, who finally receives the funds. A purpose code explains why the payment is made, using standard codes for trade, services and salaries. A screening engine can now match a full structured name and address instead of guessing which free text line holds the name and which holds the town. It screens the ultimate parties as well as the direct parties, closing a gap MT left open: a payment that looked clean on the named debtor and creditor could hide a sanctioned ultimate beneficiary.

Screening improves, but false positives remain a real problem. A richer name field means more characters to match, and a partial or phonetic match against a sanctions list still generates an alert a human must clear. Structured addresses create new mismatches: a town spelled one way in the payment and another way on a sanctions list fails an exact match and may trigger a fuzzy match for review. The ultimate party fields add parties to screen, which helps detection but raises alert volume, because every extra party is another chance of a coincidental match. Naming differences also survive: a person with no family name, a company trading under several names, or a name written in a different order can still confuse a matching engine. Alert volumes often rise early in migration, not because payments are riskier, but because the engine sees more data and screens more parties. Teams must plan for that rise, staff the alert queue, and resist loosening the rules just to cut it, because that reopens the gap the migration was meant to close.

The biggest operational risk is truncation in MT to MX conversion. In transition, a payment often starts as MT, is converted to MX, and may be converted back before reaching its destination. An MT name field holding 35 characters is cut when the name is longer, and a four-line address is squeezed into elements with no slot for every line. The truncated data travels on, and the receiving bank screens and matches the shortened version. That breaks screening: a name cut mid-way can miss a sanctions match the full name would have caught, and an address without its town can fail a geographic check. It also breaks reconciliation: remittance data the beneficiary needs to match the payment to an invoice may arrive incomplete, so the payment sits in suspense while the missing detail is chased. The fix is to map fields before migration, not after: for each MT field, agree its MX element, what happens when the source is longer than the target, and whether overflow goes to a supplementary field or a manual log. Where the target system cannot accept the full data, the bank must decide in advance whether to reject the payment, hold it for enrichment, or pass it on with a warning, and record the decision.

Remittance data loss is where customers feel the migration first. In MT, remittance information was one block of free text, often truncated, and beneficiaries regularly received payments they could not match to invoices. ISO 20022 allows structured remittance information, with separate fields for invoice numbers, dates, amounts and tax references. But that benefit only appears when the whole chain carries the structured data: if any party converts back to MT or truncates the remittance block, the data is lost and the beneficiary returns to manual matching. Remittance data is also evidence: when a regulator asks why a payment was made, it is part of the answer, and a payment arriving stripped is harder to explain. Operations teams should therefore treat remittance data as part of the compliance record, test that it survives the journey, and raise a defect when it does not.

Reporting quality improves like screening, but only if data is captured correctly. Regulators receive reports built from payment data: transaction, suspicious activity, large value and tax exchange reports. Under MT, reports were built from free text that had to be parsed, and two banks could report the same payment differently because they read the unstructured lines differently. Under ISO 20022, reports are built from structured fields, so debtor name, creditor name, country codes and purpose code are the same in every report of the same payment. That consistency makes reporting more reliable and easier for a regulator to compare across banks. It also makes errors more visible: a wrong country code, a mismatched purpose code, or a missing ultimate creditor field now stands out where a vague free text line never did. Teams should expect regulators to ask sharper questions about data quality, and to test whether reported data matches payment data, because the format lets them do so.

A practical migration checklist: first, map every field: for each MT field carrying compliance data, record its ISO 20022 element, length limit, and overflow rule. Second, retune screening: test the engine on the new data, measure the change in alert volumes, and adjust matching thresholds deliberately, with sign off. Third, test with truncated data: send test payments with long names, addresses and remittance references through the full chain, and confirm what arrives. Fourth, screen the ultimate parties from the start: make sure the ultimate debtor and creditor fields are populated and screened, not left empty. Fifth, protect remittance data: confirm it survives the journey and is stored in the payment record. Sixth, validate reporting: run regulatory reports on migrated data, compare them with old data, and investigate every difference before it reaches a regulator. Seventh, train the operations team on the new alerts: a false positive from a structured address mismatch looks different from a free text one, and the team must know how to clear it and when to escalate. Migration is a multi year programme, and compliance is not a phase at its end. Teams that treat field mapping, screening retuning and truncated data testing as migration work from day one keep payments moving, alerts manageable, and reports able to stand up when a regulator reads them.

text:
Linking instant payment systems across borders means connecting the fast payment system of one country to the fast payment system of another, so that a payment sent from an account in one country arrives in an account in another country within seconds. In plain language, it takes the instant payment experience people already have at home, where money moves between banks in seconds at any hour, and extends it across a border. The sender pays in their own currency from their own bank, and the receiver gets the money in their own currency in their own bank, almost immediately. Behind that simple experience sits a link between two national systems, plus currency conversion and settlement between them.

There are two main ways to connect two instant systems. The first is a bilateral link, where the two systems connect directly to each other. The sending system and the receiving system agree the rules, the message formats, the conversion arrangement and the settlement arrangement between themselves, and payments flow directly from one to the other. The second is a hub or platform in the middle, where several national systems all connect to one shared platform. Each system connects once, to the hub, and the hub routes payments between any two systems connected to it. A bilateral link is simpler to build for two countries, but each new country needs a new link. A hub is harder to build at the start, but each new country only needs one connection to join the whole network. Both models exist in practice, and a country can take part in more than one link at the same time.

Currency conversion in the link is one of the hardest parts. The sender pays in one currency and the receiver is paid in another, so someone must convert the amount, and someone must set the exchange rate. The conversion can be done by the sending bank, by the receiving bank, or by a provider in the middle, such as a foreign exchange liquidity provider that holds balances in both currencies. The rate must be agreed before the payment is sent, so the sender knows exactly how much the receiver will get, and the conversion must happen fast enough not to break the promise of an instant payment.

Settlement between the systems is the other hard part. When a payment crosses the link, the receiving system pays the receiver immediately, but the sending system owes the receiving system the money. That obligation must be settled, and the link must define how. Settlement can happen in central bank money, where each system holds an account with its own central bank and the central banks settle between themselves, or it can happen through commercial banks that hold accounts in both currencies, or through prefunded accounts where each side holds a balance with the other and payments draw down that balance. Prefunding is common in instant links because it is fast and simple, but it ties up liquidity, since money sits idle in the prefunded account waiting to be used. Whatever the method, settlement must be final and it must keep pace with the flow of payments, so that the receiving system is never left holding a large unpaid balance.

The roles of the sending and receiving system operators are distinct. The sending system operator checks the sender, validates the payment, applies its own rules on limits and screening, converts or routes the payment into the link, and confirms to the sender that the payment has gone. The receiving system operator receives the payment from the link, checks the receiver, applies its own rules, credits the receiver's account, and confirms receipt back through the link. Both operators must agree on message standards, on what information travels with the payment, on how errors are handled, and on who is responsible when something goes wrong. The two operators also share responsibility for keeping the link available around the clock, because instant systems run at all hours and a cross-border link cannot close for the night.

Examples of live links and pilots show both models in action. Bilateral instant links connect the fast payment systems of two countries directly, and several such links are live, letting people send money between the two countries in seconds using their domestic payment apps. Project Nexus is a hub model: it is a project to build a shared platform that lets national instant payment systems connect once and reach all the other systems on the platform, with the design work coordinated internationally. mBridge is a platform built around central bank digital currencies, where central banks and commercial banks settle cross-border payments on a shared ledger, and it has run pilots involving several central banks. These examples are described here at concept level: the point is the model each one uses, not the detail of any single launch.

Failure handling is critical, because an instant payment must never leave money in limbo. The most common failure is a timeout in one leg: the sending leg completes but the receiving leg does not confirm in time, or the receiving system is temporarily unavailable. In that case the link must define a clear outcome, either the payment is completed once the receiving system recovers, or it is reversed and the sender is refunded in full. A conversion failure is similar: if the exchange rate cannot be applied, or the liquidity provider cannot deliver the receiving currency, the payment must not go ahead, and the sender must get their money back. The return path matters as much as the outward path. If a payment is sent to the wrong account, or the receiver rejects it, the money must be able to travel back across the link to the sender, with the conversion reversed and the sender refunded. Every link therefore needs agreed timeouts, agreed reversal rules, and a way for the two operators to reconcile payments that are in an uncertain state.

Why this matters for cross-border payments is straightforward. Today, a cross-border payment usually travels through correspondent banks, takes hours or days, costs a fee at each step, and gives the sender little visibility on when it will arrive or how much the receiver will get. Linking instant systems offers a different future: payments that arrive in seconds, cost less because there are fewer intermediaries, and tell the sender upfront what the receiver will get. For people sending money home to family, for small businesses paying suppliers abroad, and for anyone who expects payments to work as fast as a message, that difference is large. The challenges are real: conversion, settlement, liquidity, operating hours, compliance screening across borders, and agreement on common standards. But the direction is clear. Domestic instant payments have already changed what people expect from a payment, and linking those systems across borders is how that expectation is extended to the rest of the world.

title: FATCA, GATCA and the Common Reporting Standard in full: forms, withholding and payment impact
text:
FATCA is a United States law that requires financial institutions outside the United States to identify accounts held by US persons and report information about them to the US tax authority, the Internal Revenue Service. CRS, the Common Reporting Standard, is the OECD standard that does the same job on a global scale: participating jurisdictions collect information on accounts held by tax residents of other participating jurisdictions and exchange it automatically each year. GATCA is the informal name for this global version of FATCA, applying the same idea, automatic exchange of tax information, across many countries at once. Together, they mean tax residence is now a standard data point collected at onboarding, and information flows from the bank to its local tax authority and then to the tax authority where the account holder is resident.

At onboarding, the bank must establish the tax residence of every new customer. This is done through a self-certification, a signed statement in which the customer declares the countries where they are tax resident and provides a tax identification number for each of them. The bank does not take the statement at face value. It checks the declaration against the other information it holds, such as address, place of birth, nationality and phone number. If the documents point in a different direction from the self-certification, the bank must ask for clarification or further evidence. These conflicting signals are known as indicia. For example, a customer declaring residence in one country but giving a phone number and mailing address in another has created an indicium to resolve first. The bank records the determination and the evidence, in case a regulator asks how the decision was reached.

Two families of forms sit at the centre of the process. A US person, which includes US citizens and US tax residents, completes a W-9. The W-9 asks for the person's name, address and US taxpayer identification number, and it certifies that the number is correct and that the person is not subject to backup withholding. A non-US person completes a form from the W-8 series. The W-8 asks for name, country of citizenship, permanent residence address, tax identification number and date of birth, and certifies that the person is not a US person. Different versions cover individuals, entities and treaty claims, but the purpose is always the same: to establish tax status so the bank knows whether withholding or reporting applies. For CRS there is no single global form: each jurisdiction uses its own, asking the same core questions, refreshed if the customer moves to a new country.

Due diligence differs by account type. For an individual, the bank relies on the self-certification plus the indicia check, and looks for any sign the declared residence is wrong. For an entity account, the bank must first classify the entity: a financial institution, an active trading or services business, or a passive entity earning mainly investment income such as dividends, interest or rent. That matters because a passive entity cannot be reported on its own: the bank must look through it to the natural persons who control it. These controlling persons are typically significant owners, directors, or the settlors and beneficiaries of a trust. Each controlling person must self-certify, and if one is tax resident in a reportable jurisdiction, the entity account becomes reportable because of that person. Pre-existing accounts are reviewed in stages, high value accounts first, using existing records and electronic searches for indicia.

A reportable account is held by a person tax resident in a reportable jurisdiction, or an entity account with a controlling person who is. Once an account is reportable, the bank collects a defined set of information each year: the name, address, tax identification number and date and place of birth of the holder and any controlling persons, the account number, the bank name, and the year-end balance. It also reports income paid in during the year, split by type, such as interest and dividends, and for custodial accounts the gross proceeds from sales. This goes to the bank's local tax authority, which exchanges it automatically with the tax authority of each jurisdiction where the holder is resident. The exchange happens once a year, automatically: no request from the other country is needed, and the holder is not asked for permission. The chain is bank to local authority to foreign authority, and a rejected file must be corrected and resent.

The sharpest edge of FATCA is its withholding mechanism. A financial institution that does not comply with FATCA is treated as non-participating, and US source income paid to it is subject to a 30 percent withholding tax. It applies to US source payments such as interest and dividends, deducted at source before the money reaches the recipient. The paying agent withholds the 30 percent, remits it to the Internal Revenue Service, and reports the payment and amount withheld. The recipient receives only the remaining 70 percent and must claim any refund or treaty relief through their own tax filing. The same logic reaches individuals: if a customer refuses a W-9 or a valid W-8, or provides information the bank cannot rely on, the account may be treated as undocumented and withholding applied to its US source payments. The 30 percent rate is fixed by law, with no negotiation and no discretion at the bank level.

An undocumented account is one where the bank cannot establish the tax status of the holder. This happens when the customer never returns the self-certification, returns one that is incomplete or contradictory, or the bank finds indicia it cannot resolve. The consequences escalate in stages. First, the bank chases the documentation, sends reminders, and restricts the account from certain actions until the form arrives. Second, if the customer still does not comply, the account is classified as undocumented or recalcitrant, and the bank reports it as such to its tax authority, including the balance. Third, US source payments into the account become subject to the 30 percent withholding described above. In the most serious cases, the bank may close the account, because the reporting and reputational risk outweighs the value of the relationship.

US source income to an undocumented recipient is held back until the 30 percent is deducted. A payment to or from an account with expired tax documentation, for example an out of date W-8, can be stopped at screening until the form is renewed. A reportable payment, such as a large cross-border transfer, is flagged, enriched with tax data, and included in the annual exchange file. When a payment is stopped, the operations team follows a fixed sequence. First, they identify the reason, visible in the payment hub. Second, they ask the customer or relationship manager for the missing or expired document. Third, they decide whether to release it with withholding, hold it for the document, or return it to the sender. Fourth, they record the decision and the amount withheld, if any. Tax status is no longer a back-office matter: a missing form can stop a payment in flight, and the operations team decides whether it moves, moves with tax deducted, or does not move at all.

text:
A proxy payment, also called an alias payment, lets a payer send money using an easy identifier instead of a bank account number. The identifier, or alias, can be a virtual payment address, a mobile number, a national ID number or a QR code. The payer types the alias, the system looks it up in a directory, finds the account it points to, and sends the payment to that account. The alias is not the account itself; it is a pointer to it. That separation is the whole idea, because it hides account details, reduces typing errors and lets people be paid with information they already know, like a phone number.

In India, the virtual payment address, or VPA, is the alias used by UPI. A VPA looks like a name followed by an at sign and a handle, for example a name plus the handle of the user's payment app or bank. To register one, a user creates it inside a UPI app, and the app's payment service provider bank records the mapping between the VPA and the user's bank account with NPCI, which runs the addressing directory. To pay, the payer enters the VPA, the payer's bank asks the directory to resolve it, and the payment is routed to the linked account. The user can create more than one VPA, can change which account a VPA points to, and can delete a VPA. Because the VPA never reveals the account number, the payer cannot see the payee's bank details, which protects privacy but also means the payer must trust the directory to resolve the alias correctly.

In Australia, PayID is the alias for the New Payments Platform, or NPP. A PayID can be a mobile number, an email address or an Australian Business Number, and a person registers it through their bank, choosing which account it points to. The bank records the mapping in the PayID addressing service, which NPP operates. When a payer enters a PayID, the payer's bank queries the addressing service, receives the payee's account details and the payee's registered name, and shows that name to the payer before the payment is sent, so the payer can confirm they have the right person. One PayID can point to only one account at a time, and moving it to another account requires updating the registration. The name display step is a deliberate safety feature: it catches typing mistakes before money moves.

In Thailand, PromptPay uses a national ID number or a mobile number as the alias. A person registers through their bank, linking their ID number or mobile number to one bank account. To pay, the payer enters the recipient's ID or mobile number, the system resolves it to the linked account, and the payment is sent. PromptPay is closely tied to government disbursements, so citizens commonly register their ID number to receive welfare payments and refunds directly into a bank account. The alias set is deliberately small, just the ID or the mobile number, which keeps registration simple and makes the service easy to explain, but it also means a person cannot create a separate alias for each purpose the way a VPA user can.

A mobile number on its own is the most common alias worldwide, because almost every adult has one and it is easy to remember and share. The mechanism is the same in every system: the user registers the number with their bank, the bank stores the mapping in a directory, and a payer who enters the number triggers a lookup that returns the linked account. The risk is that mobile numbers change hands. When a person gives up a number, the operator may reassign it to someone else, and if the old owner never removed the alias registration, a payment addressed to that number can reach the wrong person. Systems handle this by asking banks to confirm the registered name before sending, by expiring stale registrations, or by requiring the owner to revalidate the number periodically. The payer should always check the displayed name where the system shows one.

A QR code is an alias in visual form. A merchant displays a code that encodes a payment address, and the payer scans it with a payment app instead of typing anything. There are two kinds. A static QR code is printed once and always points to the same merchant and account; the payer enters the amount after scanning. A dynamic QR code is generated fresh for each transaction and already contains the amount, and sometimes the transaction reference, so the payer only confirms and pays. Registration means the merchant obtains the code from their bank or payment provider, which links the code to the merchant's account. When scanned, the app resolves the code to that account and sends the payment. A static code is cheap and simple but cannot carry a per-transaction amount, so a payer can type the wrong amount. A dynamic code removes that error but needs a screen or printer at the point of sale. A damaged or swapped code can also misdirect a payment, which is why merchants are advised to verify the code and the payer to check the displayed merchant name.

When an alias is wrong or reused, the outcome depends on the system. If the alias does not exist in the directory, the payment is rejected before any money moves, which is the safe result. If the alias exists but points to the wrong person, because a number was reassigned or a VPA was mistyped to a valid but different address, the money can reach the wrong account, and recovery depends on the receiving bank's cooperation and local rules. If an alias was deleted and then recreated by someone else, a payment sent to the old alias reaches the new owner. The five models compare as follows. A VPA is flexible and private, since a user can hold several and change them, but it reveals nothing about the payee, so a typo can go unnoticed. PayID trades some flexibility for safety, because the payee's name is shown before sending. PromptPay is the simplest, with only an ID or a mobile number, and it works well for government payments. A plain mobile number is the most universal alias but carries the reassignment risk. A QR code removes typing entirely, which suits merchant payments, but it depends on the physical code being genuine. The shared lesson is that an alias is only as safe as its directory, its registration discipline and the confirmation step the payer sees before the money moves.
